Voters will elect representatives from all 435 [[List of United States congressional districts|congressional districts]] across each of the fifty [[U.S. state]]s, and five of the six [[Non-voting members of the United States House of Representatives|non-voting delegates]] from the [[Washington, D.C.|District of Columbia]] and the inhabited [[Insular area|U.S. territories]]. Special elections are also being held on dates throughout 2026. Numerous other federal, state, and local elections, including [[2026 United States Senate elections|elections to the Senate]], will be held on this date. The winners of this election will serve in the [[120th United States Congress]], with seats apportioned among the states based on the [[2020 United States census]] and revised district maps as a result of the [[2025–2026 United States redistricting]]. Primary elections for all 435 House seats, and five of the six non-voting delegate seats were held starting on March 3, and concluded on September 15, 2026. ==Retirements== ===Summary=== 60 representatives and two non-voting delegates (26 Democrats and 36 Republicans) have announced their retirement, 29 of whom (9 Democrats and 20 Republicans) are retiring to run for other offices. In 2026, most states will use the same districts created in the [[2020 United States redistricting cycle|redistricting cycle following the 2020 census]], which were first used in the 2022 elections. Maps have changed or would change in several states, often due to legal challenges made based on partisan or racial [[Gerrymandering in the United States|gerrymandering]].{{Table alignment}} As of {{monthyear}}, several states have seen challenges to their [[List of United States congressional districts|congressional district]] maps that were put in place during the [[2020 United States redistricting cycle|redistricting cycle]] brought upon by the results of the 2020 census. In [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Arkansas|Arkansas]], a federal court dismissed a case against their congressional map that argued the map did not comply with the [[Voting Rights Act]].{{cite web |last=Grajeda |first=Antoinette |date=2025-06-06 |title=Federal panel rules in favor of state in Arkansas congressional redistricting lawsuit |url=https://arkansasadvocate.com/2025/06/06/federal-panel-rules-in-favor-of-state-in-arkansas-congressional-redistricting-lawsuit/ |access-date=2025-07-23 |website=Arkansas Advocate |language=en-US}} The [[Supreme Court of Florida|Florida Supreme Court]] dismissed a challenge regarding the Florida's congressional map, finding a new plurality-Black congressional district would be against federal law.{{cite web |title=In boon for House GOP, Florida Supreme Court sides with DeSantis, upholds congressional map |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/07/17/florida-supreme-court-sides-with-desantis-upholds-congressional-map-00459893 |access-date=2025-07-23 |website=Politico |date=July 17, 2025}} In [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Georgia|Georgia]], litigation is still ongoing regarding appeals to the newly drawn congressional map that was used in the 2024 elections. However, it was not resolved before the filing deadline for the 2026 Congressional elections.{{cite web |last=Cook |first=Brianna |date=2025-01-22 |title=Georgia's redistricting maps return to court, challenging voting rights protections |url=https://wgxa.tv/news/state-news/georgias-redistricting-maps-return-to-court-challenging-voting-rights-protections-gerrymandering-legislative-congressional-brad-raffensperger |access-date=2025-07-23 |publisher=WGXA |language=en}} In [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Louisiana|Louisiana]], litigation remained unresolved.{{cite web |last=Howe |first=Amy |date=2025-06-27 |title=Supreme Court punts decision on Louisiana's congressional map to next term |url=https://www.scotusblog.com/2025/06/supreme-court-punts-decision-on-louisianas-congressional-map-to-next-term/ |access-date=2025-07-23 |website=SCOTUSblog |language=en-US}} In South Carolina, the [[South Carolina Supreme Court]] ruled that partisan gerrymandering is not in violation of the state's constitution, keeping the maps in place.{{cite web |last=George |first=Dustin |date=September 17, 2025 |title=State Supreme Court rules partisan gerrymandering constitutional |url=https://www.wspa.com/news/state-news/state-supreme-court-rules-partisan-gerrymandering-constitutional/ |access-date=September 17, 2025 |publisher=[[WSPA-TV]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251017092625/https://www.wspa.com/news/state-news/state-supreme-court-rules-partisan-gerrymandering-constitutional/ |archive-date=October 17, 2025 |url-status=dead}} In [[Texas]], a trial was held in federal court in [[El Paso, Texas|El Paso]] to determine whether its congressional map discriminated against Black and Latino voters in violation of the VRA,{{cite web |last=Kamal |first=Sameea |date=May 21, 2025 |title=Federal trial opens to determine whether Texas discriminated in redrawn redistricting maps |url=https://www.texastribune.org/2025/05/21/texas-redistricting-map-court-challenge-discrimination/ |access-date=August 21, 2025 |work=[[The Texas Tribune]]}} but the case was paused pending expected new maps in the state.{{cite web |date=August 20, 2025 |title=League of United Latin American Citizens v. Abbott |url=https://thearp.org/litigation/lulac-v-abbott/ |access-date=August 21, 2025 |website=The American Redistricting Project}} In [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Utah|Utah]], a partisan gerrymander case resulted in a map which creates a safe Democratic district comprising the majority of [[Salt Lake County]] following a district court ruling.{{cite web |last=Aerts |first=Lindsay |date=November 11, 2025 |title=Redistricting ruling: Judge rules against Utah legislature and picks plaintiffs map 1 for Utah's 2026 midterms |url=https://www.abc4.com/news/politics/inside-utah-politics/redistricting-ruling-judge-rules-against-utah-legislature-and-picks-plaintiffs-map-1-for-utahs-2026-midterms/ |access-date=November 11, 2025 |publisher=[[KTVX]]}} In [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Wisconsin|Wisconsin]], a challenge to the state's current congressional map, arguing it was an unlawful partisan gerrymander, was dismissed by the [[Wisconsin Supreme Court]].{{cite web |date=2025-06-25 |title=Wisconsin Supreme Court refuses to hear challenges to the state's congressional district boundaries |url=https://apnews.com/article/wisconsin-redistricting-congress-supreme-court-65f1b019febe9ca0d0db234b975b3445 |access-date=2025-07-23 |publisher=Associated Press |language=en}} A new map was required in [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Ohio|Ohio]] due to the Congressional Redistricting Procedures Amendment to Section XI of the [[Constitution of Ohio|state's constitution]], resulting in two districts becoming more Republican leaning. ===Out-of-cycle partisan redistricting efforts=== [[Greg Abbott|Governor Greg Abbott]] called a [[special session]] of the [[Texas Legislature]] to redraw its congressional districts, leading to the Texas Legislature passing new maps resulting in 5 new Republican-leaning districts.{{cite web |last=Yang |first=Maya |date=August 29, 2025 |title=Texas governor signs new redistricting bill, setting up loss of Democratic seats in US House |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/aug/29/texas-governor-greg-abbott-signs-redistricting-bill |access-date=August 29, 2025 |work=[[The Guardian]]}} On November 18, a panel of the [[United States District Court for the Western District of Texas|District Court for the Western District of Texas]] issued a preliminary injunction blocking the new map, putting the former map back in place,{{cite web |last1=Schouten |first1=Fredreka |last2=Cohen |first2=Ethan |date=November 18, 2025 |title=Federal court bars Texas from using new Republican-friendly US House map in midterms |url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/11/18/politics/texas-redistricting-trump-court-ruling |access-date=November 18, 2025 |publisher=[[CNN]]}} but the Supreme Court later placed an administrative stay on the ruling, allowing the new maps to stand.{{cite web |last=Sherman|first=Mark|date=December 4, 2025|title=Supreme Court allows Texas to use a congressional map favorable to Republicans in 2026|publisher=Associated Press|url=https://apnews.com/article/supreme-court-redistricting-texas-trump-02b07b477b153f23ed5c387f2f9ae0c4|access-date=February 15, 2026}} [[Ron DeSantis|Governor Ron DeSantis]] has expressed interest in redrawing [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Florida|Florida's]] congressional map, and the Florida House has created a special redistricting committee.{{cite web |last=Rohrer |first=Gray |title=Florida Gov. DeSantis says he's ready for redistricting – with or without new census |url=https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/local/state/2025/08/11/desantis-uthmeier-redistricting-census/85608955007/ |access-date=2025-08-11 |website=Tallahassee Democrat |language=en-US}} [[Mike Kehoe|Governor Mike Kehoe]] of [[Missouri]] called a special session on August 29, 2025, which redrew the solid Democratic [[Missouri's 5th congressional district|5th district]] to a solid Republican district, allowing the GOP to pick up a seat.{{cite web |last=Hines |first=Lani |date=2025-09-28 |title=Gov. Mike Kehoe signs gerrymandered congressional map into law |url=https://www.komu.com/news/state/gov-mike-kehoe-signs-gerrymandered-congressional-map-into-law/article_fdc64bd2-0dac-4daf-8000-ec599620b4f8.html |access-date=2025-09-28 |publisher=KOMU 8 |language=en}} However, on September 3, the [[Missouri Supreme Court]] unanimously ruled that the referendum on the new maps was sufficient and must be put on the ballot, thus leaving the 2022 maps in place for the 2026 elections.{{Cite news |last=Keller |first=Rudi |date=September 3, 2026 |title=Missouri Supreme Court blocks gerrymandered congressional map, orders referendum vote |url=https://missouriindependent.com/2026/09/03/missouri-supreme-court-blocks-gerrymandered-congressional-map-orders-referendum-vote/ |access-date=September 3, 2026 |work=Missouri Independent}} Republican state legislative leaders in [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in North Carolina|North Carolina]] announced a redraw of the state's congressional districts to make the 1st congressional district more Republican leaning. Talks and efforts about redistricting occurred in [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Nebraska|Nebraska]], [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in New Hampshire|New Hampshire]], [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Indiana|Indiana]], and [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Kansas|Kansas]], but either failed or did not gain traction.{{cite web |last=Pellish |first=Aaron |date=2025-08-08 |title=Kelly Ayotte rules out redistricting for New Hampshire |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/08/08/kelly-ayotte-rules-out-redistricting-for-new-hampshire-00501207 |access-date=2025-08-11 |website=[[Politico]]}}{{cite web |last=II |first=Juan Salinas |date=2025-08-06 |title=Nebraska might join national 'wildfire' of mid-decade redistricting • Nebraska Examiner |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2025/08/06/nebraska-might-join-national-wildfire-of-mid-decade-redistricting/ |access-date=2025-08-11 |website=[[Nebraska Examiner]] |language=en-US}} Democrats have threatened to retaliate against attempts to mid-decade redistrict for partisan gain and have stated the possibility of redrawing the congressional maps in blue states. In [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in California|California]], the [[California State Legislature|state legislature]] drafted a map eliminating five Republican districts to combat Texas's plan, which was approved by voters. In [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Virginia|Virginia]], members of the [[Virginia General Assembly|General Assembly]] announced a plan on October 23, 2025 to begin the process to redraw the state's congressional districts before the 2026 elections.{{cite web |date=2025-10-23 |title=Virginia Democrats Plan to Redraw House Maps in Redistricting Push |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/23/us/politics/virginia-democrats-redistrict.html |access-date=2025-10-23 |language=en}} Democratic governor [[Wes Moore]] of [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Maryland|Maryland]] unsuccessfully pursued redistricting in his state. Redistricting has been considered in [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Colorado|Colorado]], [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in New Jersey|New Jersey]], and [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in New York|New York]]. Legal and political challenges make redistricting before 2026 highly unlikely.{{cite web |last=Toomer |first=Lindsey |date=2025-12-09 |title=In shift, Sen. The '''2026 Alaska gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[Governor of Alaska|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Alaska|lieutenant governor of Alaska]]. A nonpartisan [[top-four primary]] election occurred on August 18, 2026, in which four candidates would advance to a [[Ranked-choice voting in the United States|ranked-choice]] general election.<ref>{{cite web|title = Primary Election Information|url = https://www.elections.alaska.gov/Core/primaryelectioninformation.php|website = Alaska Division of Elections|access-date = 2024-12-15|quote = Primary elections are held on the third Tuesday in August of even numbered years.|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220504030110/https://www.elections.alaska.gov/Core/primaryelectioninformation.php|archive-date = May 4, 2022|url-status = dead}}</ref> Incumbent governor [[Mike Dunleavy (politician)|Mike Dunleavy]] is term-limited and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term.

==Primary election==

===Campaign===
The primary featured a crowded field of 17 candidates. Candidates at times struggled to distinguish themselves, while Alaska's [[Nonpartisan primary#Alaska|nonpartisan primary]] and [[Ranked-choice voting in the United States#Alaska, 2022–present|ranked-choice voting]] system were credited with encouraging more positive campaigning. As a result, candidates often emphasized areas of agreement, particularly with members of their own party.<ref name="standout">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=In Alaska’s crowded race for governor, candidates struggle to stand out as primary nears |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/08/in-alaskas-crowded-race-for-governor-candidates-struggle-to-stand-out/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=August 9, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260810164447/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/08/in-alaskas-crowded-race-for-governor-candidates-struggle-to-stand-out/ |archive-date=August 10, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Republican Bernadette Wilson called on Republican candidates to withdraw if they advanced to the general election but received fewer votes than another Republican, though she was the only candidate to pledge to do so herself. Democrats [[Tom Begich]] and [[Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins]] similarly discussed the possibility of one withdrawing after the primary to consolidate Democratic support behind the other.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=James |title=After Alaska’s ‘final four’ primary, a silent primary may decide who’s on the ballot in November |url=https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/14/after-alaskas-final-four-primary-a-silent-primary-may-decide-whos-on-the-ballot-in-november/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Alaska Beacon]] |date=August 14, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260818213201/https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/14/after-alaskas-final-four-primary-a-silent-primary-may-decide-whos-on-the-ballot-in-november/ |archive-date=August 18, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The race also saw heavy spending. Republicans [[Treg Taylor]] and Matt Heilala, the party's two highest-spending candidates, largely self-funded their campaigns. Heilala contributed $1.4 million to his campaign, while Taylor contributed $600,000. Taylor's contribution violated an Alaska campaign finance deadline, though he argued that the restriction was unconstitutional.<ref name="spending"/> 

Kreiss-Tomkins spent more than any other candidate and reported the largest number of individual Alaskan contributors, although most of his funding came from outside the state, including employees of [[Anthropic]] and others connected to the artificial intelligence industry.<ref name="spending" /><ref name="standout" /> Begich raised approximately $1.2 million, more than half of which came from two wealthy Alaskan donors.<ref name="spending">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Candidates in Alaska’s open governor’s race spend big ahead of Tuesday’s primary |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/12/candidates-in-alaskas-open-governors-race-spend-big-ahead-of-tuesdays-primary/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=August 13, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260814183245/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/12/candidates-in-alaskas-open-governors-race-spend-big-ahead-of-tuesdays-primary/ |archive-date=August 14, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== General election ==
===Campaign===
After initially finishing second in the primary, Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, allowing fifth-place finisher Taylor to advance to the general election.<ref name=BegichWithdrawal/> However, the Alaska Public Offices Commission recommended against certifying Taylor's candidacy after finding that his financial disclosure did not substantially comply with state law.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |date=August 28, 2026 |title=Alaska campaign watchdog says Treg Taylor should not be allowed to run for governor |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/28/alaska-campaign-watchdog-says-treg-taylor-should-not-be-allowed-to-run-for-governor/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260829081050/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/28/alaska-campaign-watchdog-says-treg-taylor-should-not-be-allowed-to-run-for-governor/ |archive-date=August 29, 2026 |access-date=August 29, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}}</ref> On August 31, [[Lieutenant Governor of Alaska|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Nancy Dahlstrom]] declined to certify Taylor, temporarily elevating his running mate, Candice English, to the gubernatorial nomination; English subsequently selected Taylor's wife, Jodi Taylor, as her running mate.<ref name="Taylor">{{cite web |last=Samuels |first=Iris |date=August 31, 2026 |title=Treg Taylor disqualified from ballot as pressure grows for consolidated governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/31/pressure-grows-for-a-consolidated-gop-field-in-alaska-governors-race-as-deadline-nears/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260831200254/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/31/pressure-grows-for-a-consolidated-gop-field-in-alaska-governors-race-as-deadline-nears/ |archive-date=August 31, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}}</ref>  On September 4, Dahlstrom reversed her decision and announced that Taylor would be certified after a preliminary review by the Alaska Department of Law raised questions about whether the financial disclosure requirements had been applied consistently.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Samuels |first=Iris |title=Treg Taylor is back in Alaska’s race for governor after election officials reverse decision |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/04/treg-taylor-is-back-in-alaskas-race-for-governor-after-election-officials-reverse-decision/ |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=Anchorage Daily News}}</ref>

In the general election campaign, Taylor softened his messaging and attempted to appeal to independent and Democratic voters. Kreiss-Tomkins pledged that Democrats, Republicans, and independents would be equally represented in his cabinet and emphasized endorsements from [[Moderate Republicans (modern United States)|moderate Republicans]]. In contrast, Wilson criticized [[Bipartisanship in United States politics|bipartisanship]] and said that bipartisan coalitions in the [[Alaska legislature]] had been ineffective.<ref name="Refine">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Heeding ranked choice voting, candidates refine their strategies in Alaska governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/16/heeding-ranked-choice-voting-candidates-refine-their-strategies-in-alaska-governors-race/ |access-date=September 18, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 17, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260917151432/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/16/heeding-ranked-choice-voting-candidates-refine-their-strategies-in-alaska-governors-race/ |archive-date=September 17, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Taylor and Bronson called upon Republican voters to rank all three Republicans in the race, while Wilson urged her supporters not to rank other candidates and renewed her calls for the other Republicans to drop out.<ref name="Refine"/><ref name="WilsonCalls">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Wilson again calls on her Republican opponents to drop out of Alaska governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/18/wilson-again-calls-on-her-republican-opponents-to-drop-out-of-alaska-governors-race/ |access-date=September 19, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 18, 2026}}</ref>

While the three Republican candidates generally agreed on most issues, including opposition to new taxation proposals from Kreiss-Tomkins, Wilson was alone in advocating for a return to paying out full [[Permanent Fund Dividend|Permanent Fund dividends]] according to the statutory formula. Incumbent governor [[Mike Dunleavy (politician)|Mike Dunleavy]] had made a similar promise  during his [[2018 Alaska gubernatorial election|2018]] campaign, but his efforts to implement the proposal had been unsuccessful. In fact, dividends reached a record low during Dunleavy's administration. The other candidates argued that following the statutory formula would be unaffordable for the foreseeable future.<ref name="WilsonCalls"/>

The candidates also diverged on the issue of [[Data center|data centers]]. Bronson and Taylor were generally supportive of data centers, portraying them as an economic opportunity provided they generated their own electricity and did not drive up energy costs. Despite receiving large campaign contributions from donors connected to the artificial intelligence industry, Kreiss-Tomkins advocated for a moratorium on data center construction until a regulatory framework could be developed. He also supported regulation of artificial intelligence more broadly. Wilson also opposed data centers, highlighting their environmental impact and arguing that Kreiss-Tomkins could not be trusted on the issue.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=James |title=Where do Alaska’s four governor candidates stand on data centers? |url=https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/09/18/where-do-alaskas-four-governor-candidates-stand-on-data-centers/ |access-date=September 21, 2026 |work=[[Alaska Beacon]] |date=September 18, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260920011937/https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/09/18/where-do-alaskas-four-governor-candidates-stand-on-data-centers/ |archive-date=September 20, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

{{Election box total no change | votes= | percentage=100.00}} {{Election box end}} == Challenges to Tuberville's eligibility == Alabama's governors, unlike its U.S. senators, must satisfy three conditions set out in Article V, Section 117 of the [[Constitution of Alabama]]:
The governor and lieutenant governor shall each be at least thirty years of age when elected, and shall have been citizens of the United States ten years and resident citizens of this state at least seven years next before the date of their election.{{Cite web|title=SECTION 117|url=https://law.justia.com/constitution/alabama/CA-245654.html|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[Justia]]}}
Throughout Tuberville's gubernatorial campaign, many have alleged that he does not satisfy the seven-year residency condition, which would render him ineligible to hold the office. === Background === [[File:Map of Alabama and Florida with Lee County, AL and Walton County, FL highlighted.png|thumb|Tuberville owns residences in Lee County, Alabama, and Walton County, Florida.]] Tuberville is originally from Arkansas. In addition to his 9-year tenure at [[Auburn University]] in Alabama, Tuberville's football coaching career variously placed him in Florida, Mississippi, Texas, and Ohio.{{Cite news |last=Brassil |first=Gillian R. |date=2020-07-15 |title=Tuberville Advances: Will Alabama Send an Auburn Coach to the Senate? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/15/sports/tommy-tuberville-alabama-auburn.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} In July 2017, having retired from coaching and joined [[ESPN]] as an analyst, Tuberville recorded a promotional video at his residence in [[Santa Rosa Beach, Florida]], in which he says, "Six months ago, after 40 years of coaching football, I hung up my whistle and moved to Santa Rosa Beach, Florida, with the white sands and the blue water. What a great place to live."{{Cite web |last=Volner |first=Derek |date=2017-07-19 |title=Greetings from the beach: New ESPN, ABC CFB analyst Tommy Tuberville |url=https://www.espnfrontrow.com/2017/07/greetings-beach-new-espn-abc-cfb-analyst-tommy-tuberville/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=ESPN Front Row |language=en-US}} Tuberville purchased the 4,000-square-foot Florida residence through an [[Limited liability company|LLC]] in 2004,{{Cite news |last=Hakim |first=Danny |date=2020-10-12 |title=Tommy Tuberville’s Financial Fumbles |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/12/us/elections/senate-alabama-tuberville-jones.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} and its value was estimated Actually, I live in Auburn, but living mostly in [[Washington, D.C.|D.C]]., you know, during the week."{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iPdiCn7lUl4 |title=Alabama Sports Hall of Fame interviews: Tommy Tuberville |date=2026-05-08 |last=ABC 33/40 |access-date=2026-07-10 |via=YouTube}} === Challenges from Ken McFeeters === [[File:Ken McFeeters - Ralph Chapoco, Alabama Reflector.jpg|thumb|300x300px|Ken McFeeters announced a lawsuit against Tuberville on March 24, 2026.]] On January 27, 2026, after the filing deadline for the Republican Party primary had passed, Tuberville's gubernatorial primary opponent, Ken McFeeters, submitted a challenge to the [[Alabama Republican Party]], formally alleging that Tuberville did not satisfy the state's residency requirement. McFeeters alleged in his petition that Tuberville primarily resides at his beachfront house in Santa Rosa Beach, Florida.{{Cite web|author=NBC 15|title=Tuberville's Alabama residency formally challenged by gubernatorial opponent|url=https://mynbc15.com/news/local/tubervilles-alabama-residency-questioned-gop-urged-to-decide-on-eligibility|date=January 27, 2026|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[WMTV]]}} A spokesperson for Tuberville described the challenge as "a ridiculous PR stunt from a desperate candidate,"{{Cite web|last1=Davis|first1=Kayla|title=Republican candidate challenges Sen. Tommy Tuberville's residency, saying he lives in Florida|url=https://www.wvtm13.com/article/tuberville-mcfeeter-senator-alabama-governor-election/70176207|date=January 28, 2026|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[WVTM]]}} and Tuberville dismissed the allegation, stating, "What a joke. I guess they think, you know, I hadn't done my homework."{{Cite web|last1=Conlon|first1=Riley|last2=Higdon|first2=Michal|title='What a joke': Sen. Tommy Tuberville dismisses challenge to his Alabama residency|url=https://www.wvtm13.com/article/tuberville-residency-governor-challenge-alabama-florida/70193402|date=January 29, 2026|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[WVTM]]}} The Alabama Republican Party's 21-member steering committee reviewed the challenge on February 2, 2026, and rejected it, clearing the path for Tuberville to be on the primary ballot.{{cite web |last1=Marie Fogel |first1=Apryl |title=ALGOP steering committee votes down Tuberville, Wahl ballot challenges |url=https://1819news.com/news/item/algop-steering-committee-votes-down-tuberville-wahl-ballot-challenges |website=1819 News |access-date=2 February 2026 |date=February 2, 2026}} In a press release following the committee's decision, Tuberville's campaign chairman Jordan Doufexis celebrated that "common sense has prevailed and this made-up 'residency' hoax will be put to bed for good."{{Cite web |last=Press |first=Coach Tuberville |date=2026-02-02 |title=ALGOP Unanimously Votes to Dismiss Ridiculous "Residency" Challenge Against Coach Tuberville |url=https://www.coachforgovernor.com/post/algop-unanimously-votes-to-dismiss-ridiculous-residency-challenge-against-coach-tuberville |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Coach Tommy Tuberville for Governor |language=en}} In March 2026, McFeeters announced on the steps of the [[Alabama State Capitol|Alabama Capitol]] that he had filed a lawsuit against Tuberville in the [[Covington County, Alabama|Covington County]] Circuit Court.{{Cite web |last=Chapoco |first=Ralph |date=2026-03-24 |title=Republican gubernatorial candidate files lawsuit against U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/03/24/republican-gubernatorial-candidate-files-lawsuit-against-u-s-sen-tommy-tuberville/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} McFeeters, though not a lawyer, litigated the case ''[[Pro se legal representation in the United States|pro se]]'' and listed “God’s Law Team” as his law firm in the complaint.PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT TUBERVILLE’S MOTION TO DISMISS AND MOTION FOR THRESHOLD DETERMINATION OF CONSTITUTIONAL ELIGIBILITYhttps://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/lagniappemobile.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/c/1e/c1e5cf02-ffb6-499b-a514-fd3140bd74ce/6a0c7e77a1d9f.pdf.pdf{{Cite web |last=Chapoco |first=Ralph |date=2026-03-24 |title=Republican gubernatorial candidate files lawsuit against U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/03/24/republican-gubernatorial-candidate-files-lawsuit-against-u-s-sen-tommy-tuberville/ |access-date=2026-07-10 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} McFeeters pledged that he would drop out of the race if Tuberville released records demonstrating proof of residency.{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Claire |date=2026-03-25 |title=McFeeters files lawsuit challenging Tuberville’s residency |url=https://aldailynews.com/mcfeeters-files-lawsuit-challenging-tubervilles-residencyr/ |access-date=2026-07-15 |website=Alabama Daily News |language=en-US}} Tuberville did not release any records, and the lawsuit was dismissed for improper venue on May 18, 2026, the day before the primary election.{{Cite web |last=Chapoco |first=Ralph |date=2026-05-20 |title=Judge dismisses lawsuit challenging Tommy Tuberville's eligibility to be governor |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/05/19/judge-dismisses-lawsuit-challenging-tommy-tubervilles-eligibility-to-be-governor/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} On May 27, 2026, the week after the primary election, McFeeters filed another challenge with the Alabama Republican Party, arguing that the party should void Tuberville's nomination on eligibility grounds.{{Cite web |last=JOHNSON |first=SCOTT |date=2026-05-27 |title=Candidate seeks to void Tuberville nomination |url=https://www.lagniappemobile.com/news/alabama/election_2026/candidate-seeks-to-void-tuberville-nomination/article_eeee2816-55e1-499c-88d1-e9994197cacd.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Lagniappe Daily |language=en}} The party's Candidate Committee voted to proceed with the contest, surprising McFeeters, who said he was "totally shocked."{{Cite web |last=JOHNSON |first=SCOTT |date=2026-06-01 |title=ALGOP advances Tuberville nomination challenge |url=https://www.lagniappemobile.com/news/alabama/algop-advances-tuberville-nomination-challenge/article_ce1da93a-071a-4c52-9cd5-d0fe5b246228.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Lagniappe Daily |language=en}} During the proceedings, Tuberville produced seven years of heavily redacted Alabama tax returns, from 2018 to 2024.{{Cite web |last=Barrett |first=Anna |date=2026-06-02 |title=Tuberville submits income tax returns, expert says it's not enough to prove residency |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/06/02/tuberville-submits-income-tax-returns-expert-says-its-not-enough-to-prove-residency/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} However, by failing to adequately redact scannable [[PDF417|PDF417 barcodes]] in the corners of the document, the unredacted contents of the tax returns were inadvertently made available to the |url=https://www.lagniappemobile.com/news/alabama/campaign-exposes-tuberville-s-tax-financial-history/article_578d2e17-d57a-4863-8682-3e3b65fe9a3a.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Lagniappe Daily |language=en}} McFeeters, unconvinced that the tax returns sufficiently demonstrated proof of residency, shared plans to continue his challenge, telling [[AL.com]], “I want his wife to tell me, with a A woman like that is not going to share a bathroom.”{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Ruth Serven |date=2026-06-02 |title=Tuberville releases long-awaited tax returns, says he’s lived in Alabama since 2018 |url=https://www.al.com/news/2026/06/tuberville-releases-long-awaited-tax-returns-says-hes-lived-in-alabama-since-2018.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=al |language=en}} Following an internal closed-door hearing on June 14, 2026, the Alabama Republican Party Candidate Committee unanimously dismissed the challenge.{{Cite web |last=Knowles |first=Sawyer |date=2026-06-15 |title=Alabama Republican Party rules that Tuberville fully meets residency requirements |url=https://256today.com/alabama-republican-party-rules-that-tuberville-fully-meets-residency-requirements/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=256 Today |language=en-US}} In July 2026, McFeeters filed a second lawsuit with similar allegations in the [[Jefferson County, Alabama|Jefferson County]] Circuit Court.{{Cite web |last=Shelley |first=Jonathan |date=July 30, 2026 |title=Back to court: Ken McFeeters sues (again) over Tuberville's residency, eligibility for governor |url=https://www.rocketcitynow.com/article/news/state/back-to-court-ken-mcfeeters-sues-again-over-tubervilles-residency-eligibility-for-governor/525-4cec25e8-bc59-4143-9721-479fa17644dc}} The case was dismissed on August 18, 2026 for lack of jurisdiction.{{Cite web |last=Moon |first=Josh |date=2026-08-20 |title=Another Tuberville residency challenge has been dismissed |url=https://www.alreporter.com/2026/08/20/another-tuberville-residency-challenge-has-been-dismissed/ |access-date=2026-08-20 |website=Alabama Political Reporter |language=en-US}} On August 13, 2026, McFeeters additionally filed a federal lawsuit, which was dismissed one day later for lack of [[Standing (law)|standing]].{{Cite web |last=Shelley |first=Jonathan |date=August 14, 2026 |title=Judge dismisses federal lawsuit seeking to block Sen. Tuberville's run for governor |url=https://www.rocketcitynow.com/article/news/local/judge-dismisses-federal-lawsuit-seeking-to-block-sen-tubervilles-run-for-governor/525-dca50942-69d5-43d0-85b6-dc0f2678ce49}} === Quo warranto lawsuit === [[File:Barry Ragsdale - Anna Barrett, Alabama Reflector.jpg|thumb|219x219px|Birmingham lawyer Barry Ragsdale is an attorney for the plaintiffs.]] On June 17, 2026, plaintiffs Brook Dorgan and Justin LeBlanc filed a lawsuit against Tuberville in the [[Montgomery County, Alabama|Montgomery County]] Circuit Court, which seeks a [[Quo warranto|writ of ''quo warranto'']] to invalidate Tuberville's candidacy. The complaint, citing voter registration records, tax records, campaign finance records, and quotes from Tuberville himself, alleges that Tuberville has not consistently maintained residence at his Auburn, Alabama property.{{Cite web |title=EXPEDITED COMPLAINT FOR QUO WARRANTO AND DECLARATORY RELIEF |url=https://whnt.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/06/Tuberville-Residency-Challenge-Lawsuit.pdf}} The complaint requested an expedited jury trial, with plaintiffs' attorney Barry Ragsdale saying on a podcast, "We think that your average person who sits on a jury is just never, ever going to believe the stories that Tuberville makes up about where he lives."{{Cite web |title=Barry Ragsdale on the Tuberville Lawsuit |url=https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/barry-ragsdale-on-the-tuberville-lawsuit/id1845915473?i=1000774023089 |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Apple Podcasts |language=en-US}} Tuberville filed a motion to dismiss the suit on June 22, 2026.{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Claire |date=2026-06-23 |title=Tuberville files motion to dismiss in latest residency case |url=https://aldailynews.com/tuberville-files-motion-to-dismiss-in-latest-residency-case/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Daily News |language=en-US}} On July 9, 2026, Montgomery County Circuit Judge Brooke Reid dismissed the lawsuit for insufficient jurisdiction.{{Cite web |last=Barrett |first=Anna |date=2026-07-09 |title=Tommy Tuberville residency lawsuit dismissed by Montgomery judge |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/07/09/tommy-tuberville-residency-lawsuit-dismissed-by-montgomery-judge/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} The dismissal order cites a lack of case law concerning whether ''quo warranto'' may be applied for party nominees. However, Reid did affirm that the state constitution allows the judiciary to determine whether an individual satisfies the "clearly set forth and unambiguous" requirements to hold office, which Tuberville's lawyers had disputed. Reid did not render a verdict on the underlying question of Tuberville's eligibility. On July 14, 2026, Ragsdale filed an appeal to the [[Supreme Court of Alabama|Alabama Supreme Court]].{{Cite web |title=Barry Ragsdale appeals dismissed lawsuit challenging Tuberville’s… |url=https://1819news.com/news/item/barry-ragsdale-appeals-dismissed-lawsuit-challenging-tubervilles-residency-to-alabama-supreme-court |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=[[1819 News]] |language=en-US}} The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in a 7-0 ruling.{{Cite web |title=Alabama Supreme Court rules 7-0 for Tuberville, ends ‘residency hoax’ in courts for good |url=https://yellowhammernews.com/alabama-supreme-court-rules-7-0-for-tuberville-ends-residency-hoax-in-courts-for-good/ |access-date=2026-10-09 |website=[[Yellowhammer News]] |language=en-US}} == See also == *[[2026 United States elections]] *[[2026 Alabama elections]] ==Notes== {{notelist}} '''Partisan clients'''

{{ElectionsAZ}}
The '''2026 Arizona gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Arizona]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Katie Hobbs]] is seeking a second term. She is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[United States House of Representatives|congressman]] [[Andy Biggs]].

[[Primary elections]] took place on July 21, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}}</ref> Hobbs secured the Democratic nomination unopposed. Biggs secured the Republican nomination over congressman [[David Schweikert]] with 73.6% of the vote.<ref name=results>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/arizona-governor-results|title=Arizona Governor Primary Results|work=[[NBC News]]|access-date=July 22, 2026}}</ref>  

Following the passage of Proposition 131 in the [[2022 Arizona elections|2022 elections]], this will be the first gubernatorial election in Arizona in which candidates will be required to nominate a [[running mate]] for the newly established position of [[Lieutenant Governor of Arizona|lieutenant governor]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Arizona will elect its first lieutenant governor in 2026. What to know about the role |first=Stacey |last=Barchenger |work=[[The Arizona Republic]] |date=September 21, 2023 |access-date=October 14, 2024 |url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/arizona/2023/09/21/arizona-will-elect-its-first-lieutenant-governor-in-2026-what-to-know/70848159007/}}</ref> This will be one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]].
{{toclimit|3}}

== Background ==
Arizona is considered to be a [[purple state]] at both the federal and statewide level. After [[Joe Biden]] carried the state narrowly in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Arizona|2020 presidential election]],<ref>[https://www.cnn.com/2020/11/12/politics/biden-wins-arizona Biden carries Arizona, flipping a longtime Republican stronghold], CNN, November 13, 2020</ref> [[Donald Trump]] carried the state of Arizona by 5.5 points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Arizona|2024 presidential election]].<ref>[https://news.sky.com/story/us-election-how-big-a-win-was-this-for-donald-trump-13250701 US election: How big a win was this for Donald Trump?], Sky News, January 20, 2025</ref> Democrats control both [[U.S. Senate]] seats in Arizona<ref>[https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/11/12/democrat-gallego-wins-arizona-senate-race-defining-republican-majority Democrat Gallego wins Arizona, Republicans hold 53-47 US Senate majority], Al Jazeera, November 12, 2024</ref><ref>[https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/mark-kelly-wins-senate-race-in-arizona Mark Kelly wins Senate race in Arizona], PBS, November 12, 2022</ref> and hold the governorship, secretary of state office, and attorney general office.<ref>[https://apnews.com/article/2022-midterm-elections-arizona-governor-hobbs-ceadb2bf55f1d5ec4760f423f1af0204 Hobbs wins Arizona governor's race, flipping state for Dems], AP News, November 14, 2022</ref><ref>[https://www.multistate.us/insider/2024/11/6/post-election-republicans-add-to-strong-hold-of-state-governments Post-Election: Republicans Add to Strong Hold of State Governments], MultiState.US, November 6, 2024</ref> Meanwhile, Republicans maintain a majority in the [[Arizona Senate]] and [[Arizona House of Representatives]],<ref>[https://coppercourier.com/2024/11/20/arizona-legislature-republican-2025/ Republicans maintain total control of the Arizona Legislature. Here's what you need to know.], The Copper Courier, November 20, 2024</ref> and control 6 of the 9 [[U.S. House of Representatives|House of Representatives seats]] in the state.<ref>[https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/05/arizona-congressional-races-election-results/75904496007/ Republicans keep 6-3 majority in Arizona's US House delegation], AZ Central, November 13, 2024</ref> Democrats have characterized this race as key to establishing a Democratic [[Government trifecta|trifecta]] in Arizona for the first time in 60 years.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Romo |first=Renee |date=2025-12-12 |title=Democrats hoping for Arizona legislature trifecta |url=https://www.kold.com/2025/12/12/democrats-hoping-arizona-legislature-trifecta/ |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=[[KOLD-TV|KOLD]] |language=en}}</ref>

==Green primary==
===Background===
The [[Green Party of Arizona]] disavowed candidate Risa Lombardo, accusing her of being a Republican running to draw votes from Katie Hobbs. Lombardo, a former precinct committee member for the [[Arizona Republican Party]] and wife of a Republican activist, denied the accusations. Her campaign received services from firms and attorneys with connections to Republicans. The party supported a write-in candidate in the July 21st primary, but Lombardo obtained the nomination.<ref name="Lombardo1">{{cite news |last1=Sievers |first1=Caitlin |title=‘Sham’ Green Party candidates tied to GOP machine as they funnel cash to a mystery company |url=https://azmirror.com/2026/07/27/sham-green-party-candidates-tied-to-gop-machine-as-they-funnel-cash-to-a-mystery-company/ |access-date=September 4, 2026 |work=[[Arizona Mirror]] |date=July 27, 2026}}</ref>

In early September, it was reported that the Arizona Attorney General’s Office was investigating allegations that Lombardo's campaign, among others, had used fraudulent donations with falsified voter information to obtain public funding.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sievers |first1=Caitlin |title=Three candidates now face a criminal probe over public campaign funding fraud allegations |url=https://azmirror.com/2026/09/01/three-candidates-now-face-a-criminal-probe-over-public-campaign-funding-fraud-allegations/ |access-date=September 4, 2026 |work=[[Arizona Mirror]] |date=September 1, 2026}}</ref>

An election will be held in the [[United States|U.S.]] state of [[California]] on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[governor of California]]. The nominees are [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former secretary of health and human services [[Xavier Becerra]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] political commentator [[Steve Hilton]]. Democratic incumbent [[Gavin Newsom]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third term.

The statewide [[Nonpartisan primary|top-two primary election]] was held on June 2, 2026, with Becerra and Hilton advancing to the general election among the 61 candidates on the ballot.<ref name="Certified List">{{cite web|url=https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-primary/cert-list-candidates.pdf|title=Certified List of Candidates for June 2, 2026, Primary Election|website=[[Secretary of State of California]]|date=March 26, 2026}}</ref> Republicans have not won a gubernatorial race in California since [[2006 California gubernatorial election|2006]].

==Primary election==
===Campaign===
Sixty-one candidates qualified for the primary ballot. California uses a [[Nonpartisan primary|top-two primary]] system in which all candidates, regardless of party, appear on the same ballot, with the top two advancing to the general election.<ref name="Segura 2026">{{Cite news |last=Segura |first=Daniella |date=April 3, 2026 |title=California governor primary guide with candidates dates, voting info |url=https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/04/03/california-governor-primary-election-guide-2026/89409390007/ |access-date=April 11, 2026 |work=[[The Desert Sun]]}}</ref>

Among Republicans, [[Riverside County Sheriff's Department|Riverside County sheriff]] [[Chad Bianco]] and political commentator [[Steve Hilton]] emerged as the leading candidates, while the Democratic field remained fragmented. This raised concerns that two Republicans could advance to the general election.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ocregister.com/2025/12/26/californias-very-odd-election-year-starts-with-republicans-possibly-leading-the-governors-race/|title=California's very odd election year starts with Republicans possibly leading the governor's race|last=Walters|first=Dan|work=[[The Orange County Register]]|language=en-US|date=December 26, 2025|access-date=January 12, 2026}}</ref><ref name="Politico 2026">{{Cite web |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/09/californias-governor-race-mess-00817776 |title=8 Democrats and no front-runner: California's governor race is a mess |language=en |date=2026-03-09 |access-date=2026-03-11|website=Politico}}</ref> Those concerns eased after President [[Donald Trump]] endorsed Hilton, increasing the chance of a Democrat making it into the runoff because some Bianco supporters would likely shift their support to Hilton due to Trump's endorsement.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Collins |first=Terry |date=April 10, 2026 |title=Trump endorsed former Fox host. It could tip balance in this CA race. |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/04/10/trump-endorsement-steve-hilton-california-governor/89498710007/ |access-date=April 11, 2026 |work=[[USA Today]]}}</ref>

Before Swalwell's exit from the race, polls showed that the three Democrats with the greatest amount of public support were representative [[Eric Swalwell]], hedge fund manager and [[Tom Steyer 2020 presidential campaign|2020 presidential candidate]] [[Tom Steyer]], and former representative [[Katie Porter]].<ref name="Politico 2026" /> Other notable Democrats running included former [[mayor of Los Angeles]] [[Antonio Villaraigosa]], former HHS Secretary and [[California Attorney General|state attorney general]] [[Xavier Becerra]], [[Mayor of San Jose, California|mayor of San Jose]] [[Matt Mahan]], and [[California State Superintendent of Public Instruction|superintendent of public instruction]] [[Tony Thurmond]].<ref name="Segura 2026" /> Former Vice President [[Kamala Harris]] and U.S. Sen. [[Alex Padilla]] opted against running for governor, despite speculation by the media to the contrary.<ref name="Politico 2026" />

====Canceled debate====
A debate scheduled for March 24, 2026, hosted by the [[USC Center for the Political Future]], [[KABC-TV]], and [[KMEX-DT]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Debate for California Governor Includes CPF and ABC7|url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/center-for-political-future/news/california-governor-debate-2026/|date=March 14, 2026| publisher=[[USC Center for the Political Future]]}}</ref> was ultimately canceled hours before it was set to begin.<ref name="Austin 2026">{{cite news|title=University cancels California governor debate after accusations of bias from candidates of color|url=https://apnews.com/article/california-governor-debate-usc-candidates-bias-91539c81a8ecaf8612c0eacd04dc1312|first=Sophie|last=Austin|date=March 26, 2026| publisher=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref> Using a formula developed by USC political science professor [[Christian R. Grose]] that combined fundraising and polling data, only six candidates were invited: Republicans Bianco and Hilton, and Democrats Mahan, Porter, Steyer, and Swalwell.<ref>{{cite news|title=USC cancels California governor debate after excluding candidates of color|url=https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/usc-cancels-california-gov-debate-22093688.php|first=Anabel|last=Sosa|date=March 26, 2026| publisher=[[SFGate]]}}</ref> The selection drew criticism from chairs of the black and Latino caucuses, particularly because no nonwhite candidates qualified and because Mahan's strong fundraising offset weaker polling. USC and over 50 scholars defended the formula, but the debate was canceled after organizers could not agree to expand the field.<ref name="Austin 2026" />

{{pp|small=yes}} {{Short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Colorado gubernatorial election | country = Colorado | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2022 Colorado gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Colorado gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | image1 = AG Phil Weiser.jpg | nominee1 = [[Phil Weiser]] | running_mate1 = Lesley Dahlkemper | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | image2 = Victor Marx (52125665777) (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Victor Marx]] | running_mate2 = George Markert | map_image = | map_caption = | title = [[Governor of Colorado|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jared Polis]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsCO}} The '''2026 Colorado gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Colorado]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Jared Polis]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. [[Primary elections]] took place on June 30, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} In the Democratic primary, Colorado Attorney General [[Phil Weiser]] defeated U.S. senator [[Michael Bennet]]. If elected, Weiser would be the second consecutive Jewish governor after Polis. The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] has not won a gubernatorial election in Colorado since [[2002 Colorado gubernatorial election|2002]] nor a statewide office since 2016.{{Cite news |last=Times |first=The New York |date=2017-08-01 |title=Colorado University Regents-At-Large Results: Heidi Ganahl Leads |url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/2016/results/colorado-university-regents-at-large |access-date=2026-04-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Republican nominee [[Victor Marx]]'s candidacy has been mired in controversy; Marx has made a number of dubious claims and has notably stated he is unsure how many people he has killed.{{Cite web |date=May 27, 2026 |title=Full interview: Colorado Republican gubernatorial candidate Victor Marx |url=https://www.9news.com/video/news/politics/full-interview-colorado-republican-gubernatorial-candidate-victor-marx/73-c7e83d54-e098-41c0-b4fb-15457b261b06 |website=9News |language=en-US |access-date=May 29, 2026}} Leading to the Republican primary, both of Marx's opponents indicated they would refuse to endorse him if he won the nomination.{{Cite web |last=Luning |first=Ernest |date=May 27, 2026 |title=Republicans Kirkmeyer, Bottoms say they won’t back Marx if he wins Colorado’s gubernatorial primary |url=https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/05/27/republicans-kirkmeyer-bottoms-say-they-wont-back-marx-if-he-wins-colorados-gubernatorial-primary/ |website=Colorado Politics |language=en-US |access-date=July 21, 2026}} == Democratic primary == === Candidates === To move forward to the primary, candidates had to petition onto the ballot or achieve 30% or more at the [[Colorado Democratic Party]] State Assembly. Primary elections took place on August 11, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Ned Lamont]] is running for a third term, winning the Democratic nomination in August 2026.{{Cite news |last=Vigdor |first=Neil |date=2026-08-12 |title=Ned Lamont Wins the Democratic Primary for Connecticut Governor |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/11/us/politics/connecticut-primary-governor-lamont-elliott.html |access-date=2026-08-12 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Lamont is one of the most popular governors in the United States, with a 63% approval rating as of October 2025, according to [[Morning Consult]];{{Cite web |title=U.S. Governor Approval Rating Tracker |url=https://pro.morningconsult.com/trackers/governor-approval-ratings |access-date=2025-11-15 |website=Morning Consult Pro |language=en}} however, a [[University of New Hampshire]] poll from May 2025 found that 44% of Connecticut voters believe he should not run for a third term.{{Cite web |last=Craven |first=John |date=June 5, 2025 |title=Gov. Lamont 'seriously' considering running for a rare third term |url=https://connecticut.news12.com/gov-lamont-seriously-considering-running-for-a-rare-third-term |website=News 12 Connecticut}} [[Connecticut House of Representatives|State representative]] [[Josh Elliott (politician)|Josh Elliott]] challenged Lamont in the primary as a [[Progressivism in the United States|progressive]].{{Cite news |last=Putterman |first=Alex |title=State Rep. Josh Elliott announces campaign for governor, promising to tax CT's wealthy |url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-josh-elliott-governor-lamont-primary-challenge-20768829.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260206022833/https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-josh-elliott-governor-lamont-primary-challenge-20768829.php |archive-date=2026-02-06 |url-status=live |access-date=2026-02-06 |work=CT Insider |language=en}} {{toclimit|4}} ==Democratic primary== While incumbent [[List of governors of Connecticut|governor]] [[Ned Lamont]] initially had expressed doubts about running for a third term,{{Cite news |last=Haar |first=Dan |title=Dan Haar: Will he run? Lamont interview reveals doubts about a third term for Connecticut governor |url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-gov-ned-lamont-third-term-20243961.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250701001417/https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-gov-ned-lamont-third-term-20243961.php |archive-date=2025-07-01 |url-status=live |access-date=2025-11-15 |work=CT Insider |language=en}} he announced that he would run for re-election in November 2025.{{Cite web |last=Pazniokas |first=Mark |date=2025-11-14 |title=Today, the curtain goes up on Ned Lamont's bid for a third term |url=https://ctmirror.org/2025/11/14/gov-lamont-reelection-third-term-announcement/ |access-date=2025-11-15 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}} [[Connecticut House of Representatives|State representative]] [[Josh Elliott (politician)|Josh Elliott]] had already launched a bid to primary Lamont, believing that Connecticut needed a more [[Progressivism in the United States|progressive]] leader.{{Cite news |last=Craven |first=John |date=2025-07-14 |title=Democrat Josh Elliott launches bid for governor, promising big shift from Lamont |url=https://connecticut.news12.com/2025/07/14/democrat-josh-elliott-launches-bid-for-governor-promising-big-shift-from/4fXhwKnBB4lof6pdqcoKJs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518211332/https://connecticut.news12.com/2025/07/14/democrat-josh-elliott-launches-bid-for-governor-promising-big-shift-from/4fXhwKnBB4lof6pdqcoKJs |archive-date=2026-05-18 |access-date=2026-05-18 |work=News 12 Connecticut}} At the Democratic State Convention on May 16, 2026, at [[The Bushnell Center for the Performing Arts|The Bushnell]] in [[Hartford, Connecticut|Hartford]], Lamont defeated Elliott for the [[Democratic Party of Connecticut|state party]] endorsement, 1,468 votes (74.6%) to 501 (25.4%). However, Elliott surpassed the 15% of delegates needed to get on the ballot for the primary, which took place on August 11;{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Andrew |date=2026-05-16 |title=CT Dems endorse Lamont for 3rd term, but he faces primary |url=https://ctmirror.org/2026/05/16/lamont-clinches-ct-democratic-party-endorsement-but-will-face-primary/ |access-date=2026-05-18 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}} Lamont was the first incumbent governor to face a primary since [[Ella Grasso]] in [[1978 Connecticut gubernatorial election|1978]]. {{Elections in Florida sidebar}}
The '''2026 Florida gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Florida]]. [[Primary elections]] took place on August 18, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates |archive-date=May 9, 2026 |access-date=August 5, 2025 |website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref> Incumbent governor [[Ron DeSantis]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term.

[[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] have won every gubernatorial election in Florida since [[1998 Florida gubernatorial election|1998]]. If he wins, Byron Donalds would become the first [[List of minority governors and lieutenant governors in the United States|African American governor]] of Florida, the first African American governor elected in the [[Deep South]], the third African American governor elected in the [[Southern United States]], and the first elected African American Republican governor.{{Efn|[[P. B. S. Pinchback]], the first Black governor of a state, was also the first black Republican to serve as Governor of a U.S. state, when he briefly served as [[Governor of Louisiana]] during [[Reconstruction era|Reconstruction]]. However, Pinchback was never elected governor, as he was appointed to the position after the previous Governor, [[Henry Clay Warmoth]], was removed from office.}} This is the second consecutive Florida gubernatorial election in which the Democratic nominee is a former Republican.

== Background ==
A heavily populated [[South Atlantic states|South Atlantic state]] with a large and increasingly conservative [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latino American]] population and the northern parts lying in the [[Bible Belt]], Florida is considered to be a moderately to strongly [[red states and blue states|red state]], having not elected a Democratic governor since 1994 nor a Democrat for president since [[2012 United States presidential election|2012]] and having moved significantly rightward in the last decade.<ref name="NYTANA">{{cite web |last1=Mazzei |first1=Patricia |date=October 29, 2024 |title=Florida Stopped Being a Swing State Slowly, Then All at Once |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/29/us/florida-trump-republicans-swing-state.html |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=The New York Times}}</ref> In [[2022 Florida gubernatorial election|2022]], incumbent governor [[Ron DeSantis]] was re-elected by a 19.4% margin, a considerable improvement from his 0.4-point victory four years earlier in the [[2018 Florida gubernatorial election|gubernatorial election]] during the [[2018 blue wave]].<ref name="PartyS"/>

This was followed in 2024 by Republican [[Donald Trump]] winning his adoptive home state by a 13% margin as he won a second non-consecutive presidential term, improving his 3.4% margin of victory in [[2020 United States presidential election in Florida|2020]] and seemingly diminishing Florida's longtime [[swing state|swing-state]] and [[Florida bellwether|bellwether]] status. Republicans also control all statewide offices, a large majority of the state's U.S. House delegation, both U.S. Senate seats, and supermajorities in both houses of the [[Florida Legislature]].<ref name="PartyS">{{cite web |title=Party control of Florida state government |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Florida_state_government |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Ballotpedia |language=en}}</ref>

=== Candidate eligibility and requirements ===
Article IV, Section 5(b) of the [[Constitution of Florida|Florida Constitution]] states that, for a person to serve as governor, they must:<ref>{{Cite web |title=Article IV, Florida Constitution |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Article_IV,_Florida_Constitution |access-date=May 13, 2023 |website=[[Ballotpedia]]}}</ref>
* Be at least thirty years old;
* Be a permanent resident of Florida for at least seven years;
* Not have served as governor for six years or more of the two prior terms.

==== Cancelled debates ====
In June 2026, the [[Republican Party of Florida]] announced that they would not be hosting a gubernatorial debate, as originally planned, later that month. The party stated that they had made the decision to cancel the debate after no candidate except Donalds met its qualifications.<ref name="Cancelled"/> The party's minimum requirements for a candidate to participate included:

* At least 10% support in a Republican party-sponsored primary voter poll
* A minimum $10 million in raised contributions
* Over 10,000 unique individual campaign donors

The announcement drew criticism from gubernatorial candidates Collins, Fishback, and Renner, as well as incumbent Governor [[Ron DeSantis]].<ref name="Cancelled"/> DeSantis attacked the party for trying to "engineer the outcome" of the primary election and acting against "the best interest of Republican voters."<ref name="Cancelled"/> DeSantis additionally noted that he himself would not have qualified under the set criteria during his [[Ron DeSantis#2018 candidacy|2018 primary run]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Ellenbogen |first=Romy |date=June 12, 2026 |title=DeSantis hits Florida GOP over Republican primary debate |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/06/12/florida-desantis-gop-republican-debate-donalds-fishback/ |work=Tampa Bay Times}}</ref> The ''[[Miami Herald]]'' also panned the decision, calling for a primary debate to take place.<ref>{{cite news |author=Miami-Herald Editorial Board |date=June 23, 2026 |title=Florida GOP canceled the debate, but the real story is why they did it - Opinion |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/opinion/editorials/article316224360.html |work=[[Miami Herald]]}}</ref>

On June 24, [[WJAX-TV]] announced that the planned CBS debate would be cancelled, after "a majority of the Republican candidates didn’t agree to participate." Only Fishback and Renner agreed to debate, with Collins stating that he would only accept if Donalds showed as well. Donalds refused to participate in any debate, leading Fishback labeling Donalds a "coward".<ref name="Jax">{{cite news |last=Stofan |first=Jake |date=June 24, 2026 |title=With 2 candidates refusing to commit, Action News Jax will not host GOP Gubernatorial Primary debate |url=https://www.actionnewsjax.com/news/local/with-2-candidates-refusing-commit-action-news-jax-will-not-host-gop-gubernatorial-primary-debate/3FI5T5XLNBGGRJ2YQHC5IX6TWI/ |work=Action News Jax}}</ref>

On June 25, Renner announced on X that the planned Fox 13 debate, set for July 21, had been cancelled.<ref name="Fox Cancels">{{cite tweet |number=2070193010164318251 |user=Paul_Renner |title=I just learned that the proposed Fox 13 debate in Tampa on July 21st has been canceled. That's why I called on Fox News and Newsmax to host a statewide debate. With so many voters... |author-link=Paul Renner (politician) |last=Renner |first=Paul}}</ref>

{{Elections in Georgia (U.S. state) sidebar}}
The '''2026 Georgia gubernatorial election''' will take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Georgia]]. Incumbent [[Georgia Republican Party|Republican]] governor [[Brian Kemp]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. 

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2026, with a primary runoff held on June 16. Businessman [[Rick Jackson (businessman)|Rick Jackson]] and incumbent Lieutenant Governor [[Burt Jones]] received the most votes in the first round of the Republican primary, but failed to reach the 50% threshold, causing a runoff which Jackson won. Jackson's campaign was predominantly self-funded, managing to overcome an endorsement for Jones from President [[Donald Trump]] and Kemp. Former [[Mayor of Atlanta|Atlanta Mayor]] [[Keisha Lance Bottoms]] won the Democratic nomination without a runoff against six other candidates.

The 2026 gubernatorial primary was the first time that Democratic turnout exceeded that of Republicans since [[2006 Georgia gubernatorial election|2006]].

If Lance Bottoms is elected, she would be the first female and first African-American governor of Georgia and could be the first female African-American governor in United States history. If Jackson is elected, he would be the oldest elected governor of Georgia at the age of 72 surpassing [[Lamartine Griffin Hardman]].

== Background ==
Georgia is considered a [[swing state]] at the federal level, but the state has maintained a Republican lean at the state level, with Republicans holding all statewide executive offices in the [[2022 Georgia elections|2022 midterms]], where incumbent governor Brian Kemp was [[2022 Georgia gubernatorial election|re-elected]] in a rematch against [[Democratic Party of Georgia|Democrat]] [[Stacey Abrams]] by a 7.5 percent margin.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bluestein |first=Greg |title=Abrams says she will 'likely run again.' That doesn't excite some Democrats |language=English |work=[[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]] |url=https://www.ajc.com/politics/abrams-says-she-will-likely-run-again-that-doesnt-excite-some-democrats/23WS3YRCB5E5FEVI5DPK6PU6LA/ |access-date=2023-05-13 |issn=1539-7459 |date=March 16, 2023}}</ref> Republicans also control both the [[Georgia State Senate|state senate]] and [[Georgia House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], together with Kemp's governorship establishing a [[government trifecta]], alongside an all but one Republican pick on the [[Supreme Court of Georgia (U.S. state)|state's supreme court]]. A year prior to the 2026 elections, the [[2025 Georgia Public Service Commission special election]] resulted in two Democrats being elected to the Commission, both by landslide victories, and marking the first time that Democrats won any seats on the PSC since the [[2000 Georgia state elections|2000 elections]] or any state-wide non-federal offices since the [[2006 Georgia state elections|2006 elections]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vakil |first=Caroline |date=November 4, 2025 |title=Democrats win key Georgia special elections seen as midterm bellwethers |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/5589670-gop-incumbents-lose-seats/ |access-date=November 12, 2025 |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Emily |date=2025-11-06 |title=What Georgia Democrats' PSC wins could mean for power bills and the midterm elections |url=https://www.wabe.org/what-democrats-psc-wins-could-mean-for-power-bills-and-the-midterm-elections/ |access-date=2025-11-12 |website=WABE |language=en-US}}</ref> Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Georgia since [[1998 Georgia gubernatorial election|1998]].

== Republican primary ==

=== Candidates ===
With Kemp term-limited, speculation mounted about Lieutenant Governor [[Burt Jones]], Secretary of State [[Brad Raffensperger]], and Attorney General [[Chris Carr (politician)|Chris Carr]]. Carr and Raffensperger sought to associate themselves with Kemp, drawing on his relative popularity.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Timotija |first1=Filip |title=Georgia attorney general launches bid in 2026 governor’s race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5003295-georgia-chris-carr-governor-race/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |date=November 21, 2024}}</ref> Jones sought to ally himself with Trump, who endorsed him in August 2025. 

Rick Jackson, a healthcare CEO, announced his campaign in February 2026. Previously unknown in the political realm, Jackson quickly consolidated support from right-wing primary voters, in part due to his significant personal financial resources. Jackson spent more than $83 million in personal funds during the primary. Jackson's campaign emphasized his success as a self-made billionaire, highlighting his impoverished childhood. Jackson also sought to tie himself to Trump, claiming he would be "Trump's favorite governor" and "just like Trump, but with a Southern tone."<ref name="Trumps favorite governor">{{cite news |title=Burt Jones was the inevitable Republican nominee for Georgia governor. Then Rick Jackson showed up |url=https://apnews.com/article/rick-jackson-georgia-governor-burt-jones-trump-4c1789c599857e220180068e26de9199 |access-date=October 7, 2026 |agency=Associated Press |date=March 14, 2026}}</ref> An aggressive television ad campaign allowed Jackson to take a small polling lead by spring 2026. Jackson's self-funding represented the largest amount any candidate had ever spent in a primary race for Georgia governor.<ref name="Trumps favorite governor"></ref>

Jones's campaign focused primarily on rural connections, Trump, and support from Republican allies in the General Assembly. Jones accused Jackson of "made his fortune recruiting for [[Planned Parenthood]]" and funding [[Transgender surgery]] for minors.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bynum |first1=Zachary |title=Georgia GOP governor candidates Rick Jackson and Burt Jones clash over defamation lawsuit as the race heats up |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/atlanta/news/georgia-gop-governors-race-turns-messy-as-burt-jones-and-rick-jackson-clash-over-money-smears-and-campaign-tactics/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |agency=CBS News |date=March 10, 2026}}</ref> Jackson denied these accusations and filed for [[defamation]] against Jones, a lawsuit he later dropped.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rick Jackson drops lawsuits against Burt Jones as he seeks rival’s endorsement |url=https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/09/gop-candidate-for-governor-rick-jackson-drops-lawsuits-against-burt-jones/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |agency=Atlanta Journal-Constitution |date=September 22, 2026}}</ref>

Jackson won the runoff by a 5-point margin, despite Kemp endorsing Jones two days before the vote. With the Democratic primary already over, focus shifted to the candidates' ability to counter Keisha Lance Bottoms. Jackson had consistently attacked Bottoms's record as mayor since he launched his campaign.

In the previous two occasions ([[2018 Georgia gubernatorial election|2018]] and [[2010 Georgia gubernatorial election|2010]]) where the Republican primary did not feature an incumbent governor, the plurality-winner in the primary went on to lose the primary runoff. This trend repeated itself in 2026.

The '''2026 Iowa gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Iowa]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman Zach Lahn and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state auditor [[Rob Sand]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Kim Reynolds]] is not seeking a third term.

[[Primary elections]] were held on June 2, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 1, 2025|title=State of Iowa Election Calendar 2026|url=https://sos.iowa.gov/elections/pdf/cal3yr.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260521023253/https://sos.iowa.gov/elections/pdf/cal3yr.pdf|archive-date=May 21, 2026|access-date=April 18, 2025|publisher=[[Secretary of State of Iowa]]}}</ref> In the Republican primary, congressman [[Randy Feenstra]] emerged as the frontrunner after being endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], but Lahn won the nomination in an [[Upset (competition)|upset]] with 37.65% of the vote. Sand was the only candidate to qualify for the ballot in the Democratic primary.

This is the first open gubernatorial election in Iowa since [[2006 Iowa gubernatorial election|2006]] and the first to be held at the same time as the [[2026 United States Senate election in Iowa|open Senate election]] since [[1968 Iowa gubernatorial election|1968]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Could Iowa Democrats Win 2026's Gubernatorial and US Senate Races? |url=https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2026/06/03/could-iowa-democrats-win-2026s-gubernatorial-and-us-senate-races/ |work=Smart Politics |date=June 3, 2026 |accessdate=June 6, 2026}}</ref> The 2006 gubernatorial election is the most recent won by Democrats in Iowa.

== Background ==
[[Iowa]] is considered to be a moderate-to-strong [[Red states and blue states|red state]], with both chambers of its state legislature controlled by the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]]. However, in [[2025 Iowa elections#State legislative|special elections in 2025]], Iowa Republicans lost their supermajority in the [[Iowa Senate]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Democrat Renee Hardman wins Iowa state Senate seat, blocking GOP from reclaiming supermajority |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/amp/politics/democrat-renee-hardman-wins-iowa-state-senate-seat-blocking-gop-from-reclaiming-supermajority |access-date=October 7, 2026 |publisher=PBS |date=December 31, 2025}}</ref> Republicans still maintain their supermajority in the [[Iowa House of Representatives]] that they won in [[2024 Iowa House of Representatives election|2024]].<ref>{{cite news |title=GOP at risk of significant state legislative losses, Post analysis finds |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/06/its-not-just-congress-how-midterms-can-reshape-state-by-state-power/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |publisher=Washington Post |date=October 6, 2026}}</ref> The last time the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] won a gubernatorial election in Iowa was in [[2006 Iowa gubernatorial election|2006]]. All 4 members of the [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House of Representatives]] from Iowa have been Republicans since [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Iowa|2022]] and Republicans have won all [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] elections in Iowa since 2010, making Iowa's congressional delegation entirely Republican. Iowa has voted for Republican presidents since [[2016 United States presidential election in Iowa|2016]], trending in favor of the Republican Party increasingly since then.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McCue |first=Dan |title=Des Moines Register Poll Reconfirms Iowa’s Shift From Swing to Red State |url=https://www.thewellnews.com/opinion-polls/des-moines-register-poll-reconfirms-iowas-shift-from-swing-to-red-state/ |access-date=July 27, 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref> Sand, a Democratic, won statewide election in [[2022 Iowa elections|2022]] as   [[2022_Iowa_State_Auditor_election|state auditor]] by just 2,893 votes.<ref>{{cite news |title=Democrat Rob Sand wins state auditor’s race, Todd Halbur concedes |url=https://dailyiowan.com/2022/11/19/democrat-rob-sand-wins-state-auditors-race-todd-halbur-concedes/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |publisher=Daily Iowan |date=November 19, 2022}}</ref>
