== General election ==

=== Campaign ===
Though originally from Iowa, Zach Lahn faced scrutiny following reporting by ''[[The Des Moines Register]]'' that he lived in [[Kansas]] until 2023, when he allegedly returned to Iowa.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Henderson |first=O. Kay |date=June 5, 2026 |title=Sand suggests Lahn should have run for governor in another state - Radio Iowa |url=https://www.radioiowa.com/2026/06/05/sand-suggests-lahn-should-have-run-for-governor-in-another-state/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260607080158/https://www.radioiowa.com/2026/06/05/sand-suggests-lahn-should-have-run-for-governor-in-another-state/ |archive-date=June 7, 2026 |access-date=July 2, 2026 |work=Radio Iowa |language=en-US |url-status=live}}</ref> Lahn registered to vote in [[Iowa]] on October 17, 2024, ahead of the 2024 election.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carpenter |first=Tim |date=May 29, 2026 |title=Co-founder of Wichita private school contending for Iowa GOP's gubernatorial nomination • Kansas Reflector |url=https://kansasreflector.com/2026/05/29/co-founder-of-wichita-private-school-contending-for-iowa-gops-gubernatorial-nomination/ |access-date=July 7, 2026 |website=Kansas Reflector |language=en-US}}</ref> The newspaper later reported that flight records indicated Lahn spent 75 nights in [[Wichita, Kansas]] between October 2025 and spring 2026, frequently traveling there by private plane.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Larson |first=Luke |date=June 19, 2026 |title=Lahn defends Iowa residency amid campaign criticism |url=https://who13.com/news/politics/iowa-politics/lahn-defends-iowa-residency-amid-campaign-criticism/ |website=WHO13 Des Moines}}</ref> Lahn said the trips were related to custody arrangements involving his children, who live in Kansas. 

Rob Sand criticized Lahn as a "part-time Iowan" and a [[Carpetbagger (politics)|carpetbagger]], arguing that his frequent travel to Kansas conflicted with his "Iowa First" campaign message. Sand, meanwhile, has faced criticism from Governor Kim Reynolds and other state Republicans, who have accused him of using high-profile audits and allegations of fraud to bolster his political profile.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Luu |first=Isabella |date=January 6, 2026 |title=State Auditor Rob Sand lays out legislative priorities for 2026 session |url=https://www.iowapublicradio.org/state-government-news/2026-01-06/state-auditor-rob-sand-priorities-2026-legislative-session |access-date=August 12, 2026 |website=Iowa Public Radio |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Henderson |first=O. Kay |date=February 18, 2025 |title=Auditor, governor quarrel over access to E.S.A. information - Radio Iowa |url=https://www.radioiowa.com/2025/02/18/auditor-governor-quarrell-over-access-to-e-s-a-information/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250724203522/https://www.radioiowa.com/2025/02/18/auditor-governor-quarrell-over-access-to-e-s-a-information/ |archive-date=July 24, 2025 |access-date=August 12, 2026 |work=Radio Iowa |language=en-US |url-status=live}}</ref> 

In early September, ''[[The Des Moines Register]]'' reported that the [[Black Hawk County, Iowa|Black Hawk County]] Sheriff's Office was investigating Lahn's running mate, Wulf, for theft and fraud in relation to accusations that Wulf had misled lenders and business associates about his finances.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lenders, farmers accuse Lt. Gov candidate Derek Wulf of theft, fraud|url=https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/09/04/republican-derek-wulf-finances-fraud-iowa-election-zach-lahn/91251482007/|first=Tyler|last=Jett|date=September 4, 2026|access-date=September 4, 2026|website=[[The Des Moines Register]]}}</ref>

{{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2025}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Illinois gubernatorial election | country = Illinois | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2022 Illinois gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Illinois gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = JB Pritzker 2026 (cropped 3x4).jpg | nominee1 = [[JB Pritzker]] | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = [[Christian Mitchell]] | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = Darren Bailey at a 2022 Campaign Event (cropped2).jpg | nominee2 = [[Darren Bailey]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = Aaron Del Mar | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | map_image = | map_caption = | title = [[Governor of Illinois|governor]] | before_election = [[JB Pritzker]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsIL}} The '''2026 Illinois gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Illinois]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[JB Pritzker]] is seeking a third term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former nominee [[Darren Bailey]]. [[Primary elections]] were held on March 17, 2026.{{Cite web |last=Illinois State Board of Elections |title=Schedule of Future Elections |url=https://www.elections.il.gov/agencyforms/1%20SCHEDULE%20OF%20FUTURE%20ELECTIONS/Schedule%20of%20Elections%20-%20Revised.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260221135507/https://www.elections.il.gov/agencyforms/1%20SCHEDULE%20OF%20FUTURE%20ELECTIONS/Schedule%20of%20Elections%20-%20Revised.pdf |archive-date=February 21, 2026 |access-date=2025-07-21 |website=www.elections.il.gov}} Pritzker secured the Democratic nomination unopposed, while [[Darren Bailey]] secured the Republican nomination with 54% of the vote.{{cite web |title=Illinois Governor Primary Results 2026 |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/illinois-governor-results |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260411230100/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/illinois-governor-results |archive-date=April 11, 2026 |access-date=April 19, 2026 |website=[[NBC News]]}} Pritzker selected [[Christian Mitchell]] as his running mate, as incumbent lieutenant governor [[Julianna Stratton]] is the Democratic nominee for [[2026 United States Senate election in Illinois|U.S. Senate]]. This is the first gubernatorial rematch in Illinois since [[1986 Illinois gubernatorial election|1986]]. == Background == A moderately to strongly [[blue state]], Illinois has a reputation for being both the most populous and the most left-leaning state in the Midwest, traits vastly owed to the progressive and diverse [[Chicago metropolitan area]]. Though the state has historically favored Republicans for [[Governor of Illinois|governor]], Democrats have won all but one gubernatorial race in Illinois since [[2002 Illinois gubernatorial election|2002]], the exception being [[Bruce Rauner]]'s narrow victory in [[2014 Illinois gubernatorial election|2014]].{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2014 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2014&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250404104935/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2014&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2025-04-04 |access-date=2025-04-09 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} In addition, Democrats have won Illinois by double-digit margins in every presidential race since [[1992 United States presidential election in Illinois|1992]]; and consistently occupied all of its statewide offices since [[2018 Illinois elections|2019]]. Incumbent governor [[JB Pritzker]], a member of the Democratic Party, has comfortably won in the past two elections, having first been elected with a 15.6% lead in [[2018 Illinois gubernatorial election|2018]]{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2018 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2018&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520050528/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2018&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2024-05-20 |access-date=2025-04-09 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} and won re-election by 12.5% in [[2022 Illinois gubernatorial election|2022]].{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2022 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2022&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240419033643/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2022&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2024-04-19 |access-date=2025-04-09 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} Despite the state's strong Democratic lean, Republicans are comfortably favored in most of rural Illinois, especially in much of [[Forgottonia|West Central]] and [[Southern Illinois]]. Illinois is one of 16 states that do not have gubernatorial term limits. {{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2026}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Kansas gubernatorial election | country = Kansas | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2022 Kansas gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Kansas gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = Cindy 2 cropped.jpg | nominee1 = [[Cindy Holscher]] | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = [[KC Ohaebosim]] | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = TY mASTERSON (cropped).jpg | image_size = 150x150px | nominee2 = [[Ty Masterson]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = [[Jeff Klemp]] | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | map_image = | map_caption = | title = [[Governor of Kansas|Governor]] | before_election = [[Laura Kelly]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = | turnout = }} {{ElectionsKS}} The '''2026 Kansas gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[List of governors of Kansas|governor of Kansas]]. The primary elections took place on August 4, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|publisher=NCSL |access-date=August 5, 2025}} Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Laura Kelly]] is term-limited and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. This will be one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]] and the only one of those states that Trump won by a double-digit margin. ==Background== Kansas has a long tradition of ticket-splitting at the gubernatorial level: despite the state's consistent support for Republican presidential nominees, Democratic candidates have won the governor's office for the majority of years since the late 1960s, reflecting a pattern of voters distinguishing between state executive and federal races. This competitive tradition continued in the [[2018 Kansas gubernatorial election|2018 election]], when Laura Kelly won the open seat in a favorable national environment during the [[2018 United States elections|2018 midterms]] and benefited from widespread dissatisfaction with the outgoing administration of [[Sam Brownback]], who had departed mid-term after being nominated by President [[Donald Trump]] to serve as [[United States Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom]] in 2017.{{Cite news |last=Paul |first=Kari |date=November 7, 2018 |title=Kansas sees its own blue wave: 'If you can flip it here, you can flip it anywhere' |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/kansas-sees-its-own-blue-wave-if-you-can-flip-it-here-you-can-flip-it-anywhere-2018-11-07 |access-date=September 29, 2024 |work=[[MarketWatch]]}} Kelly won re-election in [[2022 Kansas gubernatorial election|2022]] on the strength of her own personal popularity, with the negative reaction to the [[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization|overturning of ''Roe v. Wade'']] providing additional tailwind, amplified by the presence of an [[2022 Kansas abortion referendum|abortion referendum]] on the ballot a few months prior.{{Cite web |last=Bahl |first=Andrew |title=National poll: More than half of residents approve of Gov. Laura Kelly's job performance |url=https://www.cjonline.com/story/news/politics/elections/2021/11/18/kansas-governor-laura-kelly-approval-rating-ahead-reelection-run-poll/8665879002/ |access-date=September 29, 2024 |website=[[The Topeka Capital-Journal]] |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Hanna |first=John |date=November 9, 2022 |title=Abortion rights support helps Kansas Gov. Kelly win 2nd term |url=https://apnews.com/article/2022-midterm-elections-biden-donald-trump-kansas-topeka-39afdff811fd2f30a212036d5ec6e3fa |access-date=September 29, 2024 |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |language=en}} Since her re-election, Kelly has seen a continued rise in personal popularity, and as of 2024 ranks among the ten most popular governors in the country, which some commentators have attributed to her frequent use of her veto powers and extensive travel across the state.{{Cite web |date=April 23, 2024 |title=Report: Kansas gov. is one of the top 10 most popular in the nation |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/report-kansas-gov-one-top-203024475.html |access-date=September 29, 2024 |website=[[Yahoo News]] |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |author=A. O. L. Staff |date=May 4, 2024 |title=Are Gov. Laura Kelly's rising approval numbers because of her frequent use of veto powers? |url=https://www.aol.com/gov-laura-kellys-rising-approval-090237691.html |access-date=September 29, 2024 |via=AOL news |language=en-US}} While Democratic candidates have remained competitive at the gubernatorial level, the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] has historically dominated Kansas in federal and legislative politics. The '''2026 Maryland gubernatorial election''' will take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Maryland]]. The primary elections took place on June 23, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=August 5, 2025}}</ref> Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Wes Moore]] is running for a second term.<ref name="Moore" /> Moore will face off against his [[2022 Maryland gubernatorial election|2022 opponent]] [[Dan Cox]], making this the first gubernatorial rematch in Maryland since [[2010 Maryland gubernatorial election|2010]]. The winner is scheduled to serve a four-year term beginning on January 20, 2027.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Maryland Constitution – Article II, Section 1 |url=https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/43const/html/02art2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260708215204/https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/43const/html/02art2.html |archive-date=July 8, 2026 |access-date=July 8, 2026 |website=msa.maryland.gov}}</ref>

== Background ==
At the federal and state level, Maryland is a solid [[blue state]] and one of the most consistently Democratic states in the nation, with [[Kamala Harris]] carrying it by 29 points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Maryland|2024 presidential election]]. Elections in Maryland are dominated by the [[Baltimore metropolitan area]] and the [[Washington metropolitan area|D.C. suburbs]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Barker |first1=Jeff |title=Is Maryland growing even more blue politically? Democrats are showing gains in battleground counties. |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/12/09/is-maryland-growing-even-more-blue-politically-democrats-are-showing-gains-in-battleground-counties/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=December 9, 2020}}</ref> Going into this election, Democrats occupy all [[Government of Maryland#Executive branch|statewide offices]] and hold supermajorities in both houses of the [[Maryland General Assembly|state legislature]], as well as all but one seat in the state's congressional delegation.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schouten |first1=Fredreka |title=Wes Moore targets Maryland's only GOP congressman with redistricting, but a powerful Democrat stands in his way |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/01/20/politics/maryland-redistricting-wes-moore |access-date=January 20, 2026 |work=[[CNN]] |date=January 20, 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

== Democratic primary ==
=== Campaign ===
Moore has maintained positive [[Governorship of Wes Moore#Approval ratings|approval ratings]] throughout his first term, though his numbers have steadily declined.<ref name="LaunchesBS">{{cite news |last1=Janesch |first1=Sam |title=Gov. Wes Moore formally launches bid for second term |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2025/09/09/gov-wes-moore-formally-launches-bid-for-second-term/ |access-date=September 9, 2025 |work=The Baltimore Sun |date=September 9, 2025}}</ref> Mileah Kromer, the director of the [[University of Maryland, Baltimore County]]'s Institute of Politics, has associated the downward trend in Moore's approval rating with voter frustration over affordability issues and a distrust of local, state, and federal government.<ref name="UMBC Approval Apr2026" /> An incumbent Democratic governor has not lost re-election in Maryland since [[1950 Maryland gubernatorial election|1950]], when [[William Preston Lane Jr.]] failed to win a second term.

Moore faced token opposition in the Democratic primary.<ref name="MoorePrepares" /><ref name="UMBC Approval Apr2026" />

== Republican primary ==
[[File:Ed Hale Sr. (26579635541).jpg|x170px|thumb|Businessman [[Ed Hale (businessman)|Ed Hale]] finished second in the primary.]]
=== Campaign ===
During the Republican primary, candidates campaigned against Moore's handling of economic issues, especially toward tax reforms and increases to vehicle registration fees in the state during his first term.<ref name="MoorePrepares">{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=Gov. Wes Moore prepares to make case to Maryland voters for another 4 years in office |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-wes-moore-session-analysis-re-election-primary-W366Z6Q74ZG4JNMVD63GVX2OM4/ |access-date=April 15, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=April 15, 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan P. |title=Trio of GOP candidates for governor — out of nine total — meet in debate |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2026/05/20/trio-of-gop-candidates-for-governor-out-of-nine-total-meet-in-debate/ |access-date=May 20, 2026 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=May 20, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Gaskill |first1=Hannah |title=9 GOP MD governor candidates a stark contrast to party in Larry Hogan's day |url=https://thedailyrecord.com/2026/05/20/republican-governor-candidates-larry-hogan/ |access-date=May 20, 2026 |work=[[Daily Record (Maryland)|The Daily Record]] |date=May 20, 2026}}</ref>

Much of the speculation as to which Republicans may challenge Moore in the 2026 election revolved around former governor [[Larry Hogan]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan |title=Hogan lays out five-point economic agenda for Senate race that echoes positions as governor |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2024/06/26/hogan-lays-out-five-point-economic-agenda-for-senate-race-that-echoes-positions-as-governor/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=June 27, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wintrode |first1=Brenda |title=Poll: Marylanders favor Moore over Hogan in 2026, oppose new taxes |url=https://www.thebaltimorebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/gonzales-poll-moore-hogan-taxes-O6NY7HLASZGQHCGOSERYA4X5RU/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=January 7, 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Janesch |first1=Sam |title=Mysterious 'No Moore' campaign launches Maryland's next gubernatorial race as Republicans, Larry Hogan battle Wes Moore |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2025/02/24/no-moore-maryland-governor-race-moore-hogan/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=February 24, 2025}}</ref> Hogan's entry would have given Republicans a high-profile candidate, potentially making the race more competitive.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Crane |first1=Steve |last2=Sears |first2=Bryan P. |title=Banker, Blast owner Ed Hale preparing a 2026 challenge to Wes Moore |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2025/05/02/banker-blast-owner-ed-hale-preparing-a-2026-challenge-to-wes-moore/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=May 2, 2025}}</ref> However, he announced in an op-ed to ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]'' in January 2026 that he would not run for a third term as governor in 2026,<ref name="HoganOped" /> after which speculation turned to [[Steve Hershey]], the minority leader of the [[Maryland Senate]] who had formed an exploratory committee into a potential gubernatorial campaign.<ref name="Regroups">{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=With Larry Hogan out of the Maryland governor's race, the GOP regroups |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/01/21/with-larry-hogan-out-of-the-maryland-governors-race-the-gop-regroups/ |access-date=February 21, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=January 21, 2026}}</ref> Hershey filed to [[2026 Maryland Senate election#District 36|run for re-election]] in February 2026,<ref name="Hershey" /> leaving the Republican Party without a formidable opponent against Moore.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=How Republicans are fighting to have a greater say in Maryland politics |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/02/21/how-republicans-are-fighting-to-have-a-louder-say-in-maryland-politics/ |access-date=February 21, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=February 21, 2026}}</ref>

Republican challengers to Moore face an uphill battle against him,<ref name="LaunchesBS" /> especially as public frustration with President [[Donald Trump]] continues to boost Democratic officeholders in deep blue states.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wes Moore touts progress, but uncertainties abound |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/02/11/moore-touts-progress-editorial/ |access-date=February 11, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=February 11, 2026}}</ref> As of May 2026, Republican candidates in the race have struggled to raise funds for their campaigns,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=Wes Moore has $70 to spend on reelection for every $1 any GOP candidate has |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-governor-race-campaign-fundraising-republican-wes-moore-5KV7EPXRPNFWTIG5EEIBA2O42E/ |access-date=May 20, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=May 20, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> lack experience in running a statewide campaign, and hold positions in line with Trump.<ref name="UMBC Approval Apr2026">{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan P. |title=Moore job approval falls below 50% for the first time |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2026/04/01/moore-job-approval-falls-below-50-for-the-first-time/ |access-date=April 1, 2026 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=April 1, 2026}}</ref> Media outlets described Cox and Hale as the frontrunners of the Republican primary.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=A party-switcher and a MAGA loyalist are the GOP's top options to take on Moore |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-republican-governor-cox-hale-AEH7YRQPWNHA7CRVY4LFVKOTXI/ |access-date=June 17, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=June 17, 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="MooreLaunch" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Crawford |first1=Ian |title=Moore officially launches reelection bid with Baltimore, Prince George's events |url=https://marylandmatters.org/briefs/moore-officially-launches-reelection-bid-with-baltimore-prince-georges-events/ |access-date=May 4, 2026 |work=[[WTOP-FM]] |publisher=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=May 3, 2026}}</ref>

As the primaries approached, some of the [[Maryland Republican Party]]'s establishment appeared to begin coalescing around Hale, believing him to be more electable than Cox. However, Cox still enjoyed name recognition from his previous gubernatorial campaign as well as solid voter bases in Trump-leaning regions of the state.<ref name="GOPestablishment" /> In June 2026, the [[Maryland Democratic Party]] and Governor Moore began airing advertisements and sending out mailers promoting Cox over Hale.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Epstein |first1=Reid J. |title=Democrats Keep Helping Out This Far-Right Maryland Republican |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/16/us/politics/wes-moore-dan-cox-maryland.html |access-date=June 16, 2026 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 16, 2026}}</ref> Cox won the Republican primary on June 23, 2026, defeating Hale.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan P. |last2=Will |first2=Hammann |title=Cox tops Hale in GOP primary, heads to rematch with Moore for governor |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2026/06/23/moore-cruises-to-renomination-as-republicans-duke-it-out/ |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=June 23, 2026}}</ref>

==General election==
===Campaign===
Moore is widely expected to win re-election to a second term and enters the general election with a substantial fundraising advantage over Cox.<ref name="HaleConcedes">{{cite news |last1=Ibrahim |first1=Mennatalla |title=Ed Hale concedes to Dan Cox in Maryland GOP governor primary race |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/06/23/early-returns-show-hale-cox-locked-in-tight-maryland-gop-governor-race/ |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=June 23, 2026}}</ref> 

Moore is expected to campaign on his efforts to address affordability issues, expand opportunities, and protect the state from the [[second Trump administration]], whose actions have led to increased prices and caused the state to lose jobs and federal funding.<ref name="MoorePrepares" /> Moore's campaign will also seek to tie Cox to President [[Donald Trump]], who endorsed Cox in [[2022 Maryland gubernatorial election|2022]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=Governor rematch: Democrat Moore will face GOP's Cox again |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/maryland-governor-primary-election-2026-BBC7RVV2FBAMBBNS6UZR2I27WM/ |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=June 23, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Following the primary elections, the [[Maryland Democratic Party]] launched a website intended to remind voters about Cox's association with Trump as well as his past opposition to abortion rights, gun safety, and former President [[Joe Biden]]'s victory in the [[2020 United States presidential election]].<ref name="GOPLeaders" /> Cox pushed back against attempts to tie him to Trump, saying that he would not be seeking the president's endorsement and would be focusing his campaign on local issues.<ref>{{cite news |title=Republican nominee Dan Cox bites back at Gov. Moore on Maryland redistricting |url=https://wtop.com/maryland/2026/07/republican-nominee-dan-cox-bites-back-at-gov-moore-on-maryland-redistricting/ |access-date=July 1, 2026 |work=[[WTOP-FM]] |date=July 1, 2026}}</ref>

Cox is expected to campaign against Moore's handling of economic issues.<ref name="CoxAffordability"/> Following the Republican primary, the [[Maryland Republican Party]] and its leaders embraced Cox,<ref name="Ehrlich" /><ref name="CoxAffordability">{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=Dan Cox says Maryland affordability crisis gives GOP new opening in 2026 |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/07/08/dan-cox-says-maryland-affordability-crisis-gives-gop-new-opening-in-2026/ |access-date=July 8, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=July 8, 2026}}</ref> with [[Maryland Senate]] minority leader [[Steve Hershey]] and [[Maryland House of Delegates|House of Delegates]] minority leader [[Jason C. Buckel]] telling ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]'' that they believed Cox could defeat Moore with an affordability-focused campaign as opposed to 2022 campaign platform, which highlighted far-right policy stances and baseless conspiracy theories. At the same time, Republican legislative leaders stated that their path to competing against Moore would rely less on defending Cox and more on persuading voters to focus on affordability and fiscal issues.<ref name="GOPLeaders">{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=Maryland GOP leaders: Cox must address voter concerns, Moore's record |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/06/25/maryland-gop-leaders-cox-must-center-voter-concerns-moores-broken-promises/ |access-date=June 25, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=June 25, 2026}}</ref>

{{ElectionsME}}

The '''2026 Maine gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Maine]]. Incumbent [[Maine Democratic Party|Democratic]] governor [[Janet Mills]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. Although Maine has adopted [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]], it is only used for primary elections and federal general elections. Therefore, the primary was conducted with ranked-choice voting, and the general election will be conducted with the traditional [[Plurality voting|plurality voting]] system. [[Primary elections]] were held on June 9, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2025-05-23 |website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref>

Democrat [[Hannah Pingree]] and Republican [[Robert B. Charles|Bobby Charles]] won their respective primaries, and will be joined on the ballot by independent [[Rick Bennett (Maine politician)|Rick Bennett]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2026-06-19 |title=Hannah Pingree wins ranked-choice runoff in Democratic primary for governor |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/06/19/hannah-pingree-wins-ranked-choice-runoff-in-democratic-primary-for-governor/ |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Background ==
Incumbent Democratic governor [[Janet Mills]] was re-elected with 55.69% of the vote in [[2022 Maine gubernatorial election|2022]] over Republican former governor [[Paul LePage]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mistler |first=Steve |date=2022-11-09 |title=Maine Gov. Janet Mills wins second term, defeating former GOP Gov. Paul LePage |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/11/09/1134198072/maine-election-results-governor-paul-lepage-janet-mills |access-date=2026-01-20 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref> She is term-limited and not eligible to run for a third consecutive term.

A sparsely populated state in [[New England]], Maine is one of the most [[Rural areas in the United States|rural]] states in the nation and is considered to be moderately [[Red states and blue states|blue]]. Both houses of the [[Maine Legislature]] were controlled by the Maine Democratic Party in the prior session. A Republican has not received 50% or more of the vote in a gubernatorial election since [[1962 Maine gubernatorial election|1962]], when incumbent Republican [[John H. Reed]] received 50.08% of the vote.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Maine Election Returns |url=https://www.maine.gov/legis/lawlib/lldl/elections/electionshome.html |access-date=2026-01-20 |website=www.maine.gov}}</ref>

==Democratic primary==
[[Shenna Bellows]], [[Troy Jackson]], and [[Hannah Pingree]] announced an "alliance" on May 22, 2026, in which they would rank each other ahead of their opponents [[Angus King III]] and [[Nirav D. Shah|Nirav Shah]]; Shah was leading in most public polls.<ref name="PingreeJacksonBellowsAlliance">{{Cite web |last=Brodey |first=Sam |date=May 28, 2026 |title=It has famous names, wildcards, and a COVID doctor: How Maine's governor race became the primary to watch - The Boston Globe |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/05/28/nation/maine-janet-mills-governor-race-graham-platner/ |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=BostonGlobe.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Shah received the most first-preference votes, with 26.8%, followed by Pingree with 23.3%, Jackson with 21.0%, Bellows with 20.7%, and King with 8.2%. As a result of finishing last, King was eliminated and his voters' second preferences were redistributed to the remaining four candidates. Pingree was ultimately nominated after four rounds of ranked-choice tabulation, defeating Shah in the final round by a 56%–44% margin.<ref name=":7" />

Following his loss in the gubernatorial primary, [[Troy Jackson]] became the Democratic nominee in the [[2026 United States Senate election in Maine|2026 United States Senate election]] after former nominee [[Graham Platner]] withdrew from the race.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=Emma |date=2026-07-25 |title=Troy Jackson officially clinches Maine Democratic U.S. Senate nomination • Maine Morning Star |url=https://mainemorningstar.com/2026/07/25/troy-jackson-officially-clinches-maine-democratic-u-s-senate-nomination/ |access-date=2026-09-23 |website=Maine Morning Star |language=en-US}}</ref>

The Maine gubernatorial election uses [[instant-runoff voting]] as its algorithm: in each round, the candidate with the fewest [[first-preference vote]]s among the remaining candidates is eliminated, and each ballot which was formerly voting for that candidate is transferred to its new first preference.  This necessarily results in a number of rounds equal to 1 less than the number of candidates.

==Republican primary==
All Republican candidates said that they opposed ranked choice voting. [[Robert B. Charles|Robert Charles]] was particularly critical of ranked choice voting and encouraged Republican primary voters to rank him across the ballot and not rank other candidates. Charles criticized what he called "back room deals" among other candidates to encourage their supporters to rank another candidate second, claiming other candidates could not be trusted to work to repeal ranked choice voting while encouraging its use.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mistler |first=Steve |date=2026-05-15 |title=Looking to topple Bobby Charles, Maine's GOP primary candidates are turning to an unlikely tool |url=https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2026-05-15/looking-to-topple-bobby-charles-maines-gop-primary-candidates-are-turning-to-an-unlikely-tool|access-date=2025-05-19 |website=[[MPBN]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Miller |first=Kevin |date=2026-05-08 |title=Some, but not all, GOP gubernatorial candidates are embracing ranked-choice voting |url=https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2026-05-08/some-but-not-all-gop-gubernatorial-candidates-are-embracing-ranked-choice-voting|access-date=2025-05-19 |website=[[MPBN]] |language=en-US}}</ref> The candidates who endorsed a second choice were Robert Wessels, who endorsed [[Jonathan S. Bush|Jonathan Bush]] as his second choice, Ben Midgley, who endorsed David Jones as his second choice, and David Jones, who endorsed Midgley as his second choice.

Charles would win 37.7% of the vote, with Midgley and Bush finishing with 20.1% and 19.8% respectively, and every other candidate some distance behind them. State senator [[James D. Libby|James Libby]], who had suspended his campaign in April but did not formally withdrawn from the race, finished in last.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=2026-06-10 |title=What to watch for as Maine races head to ranked-choice runoffs |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/06/10/what-to-watch-for-as-maine-races-head-to-ranked-choice-runoffs/ |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}}</ref> After seven rounds of ranked-choice voting tabulation, Charles was declared the winner.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-06-19 |title=Bobby Charles holds lead to win Republican primary for governor after RCV runoff |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/06/19/bobby-charles-holds-lead-to-win-republican-primary-for-governor-after-rcv-runoff/ |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Convention vote ===
On April 25, 2026, the Maine Republican Party announced the results of a straw poll by delegates to the Maine Republican Convention. {{ElectionsMI}}
The '''2026 Michigan gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Michigan]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state secretary of state [[Jocelyn Benson]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] congressman [[John James (Michigan politician)|John James]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Democratic incumbent [[Gretchen Whitmer]] is ineligible to seek a third term.

[[Primary elections]] were held on August 4. Benson won the Democratic nomination with 83.2% of the vote over Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson. Endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], James won the Republican nomination with 50.1% of the vote over businessman [[Perry Johnson (businessman)|Perry Johnson]].

Republicans have not won a gubernatorial election in Michigan since [[2014 Michigan gubernatorial election|2014]].

{{toclimit|3}}

==Background==
Michigan is a [[Swing state|purple]] state in the heart of the [[Great Lakes]] and [[Rust Belt]] which consistently elected [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] for president since [[1992 United States presidential election in Michigan|1992]] until [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee [[Donald Trump]] narrowly flipped the state in [[2016 United States presidential election in Michigan|2016]]. In [[2020 United States presidential election in Michigan|2020]], Democratic nominee [[Joe Biden]] won Michigan by 2.78%. In the [[2024 United States presidential election in Michigan|2024 presidential election]], Donald Trump won Michigan by 1.42%, which was attributed to [[Joe Biden|President Biden]]'s unpopularity and rightward shifts in working-class and [[Arab Americans|Arab American]] voters.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Michigan Presidential Election Voting History - 270toWin |url=https://www.270towin.com/states/michigan |access-date=2025-09-07 |website=270toWin.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Shalal |first=Andrea |date=November 10, 2024 |title=Kamala Harris' Michigan loss highlights Democrats' weak spots |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/harris-michigan-loss-highlights-democrats-many-weak-spots-2024-11-10/ |access-date=January 1, 2026 |work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref>

Since the [[2018 Michigan elections]], Democrats occupied all statewide offices in Michigan. Since [[2022 Michigan Senate election|2022]], Democrats held a narrow majority in the [[Michigan Senate|State Senate]] while Republicans held a narrow majority in the [[Michigan House of Representatives]] since [[2024 Michigan House of Representatives election|2024]]. According to the [[Morning Consult]], which measures the popularity of governors across the country, Democratic governor [[Gretchen Whitmer]] has a net +26 approval rating in Michigan as of September 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 2, 2026 |title=Tracking the Approval Ratings of All 50 U.S. Governors |url=https://pro.morningconsult.com/trackers/governor-approval-ratings |access-date=September 24, 2026 |website=[[Morning Consult]]}}</ref>

In [[2018 Michigan gubernatorial election|2018]], Gretchen Whitmer and her running mate [[Garlin Gilchrist]] won by 9.56%. In [[2022 Michigan gubernatorial election|2022]], Whitmer and Gilchrist won by 10.53%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2018 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Michigan |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2018&fips=26&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250218051919/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2018&fips=26&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2025-02-18 |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=uselectionatlas.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2022 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Michigan |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2022&fips=26&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204065112/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=26&year=2022&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=2024-12-04 |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=uselectionatlas.org}}</ref>

== General election ==

=== Campaign ===
In September 2026, the [[Libertarian Party of Michigan]] formally disavowed connections and support to Anthony Hudson, their gubernatorial nominee. The party stated that Hudson's campaign was promoting positions that contradicted their purpose as a party, while Hudson responded and said that he was comfortable with their disavowal. Given that this happened after the withdrawal deadline had passed, Hudson's name will still appear listed as the party's nominee on the election ballot.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dailey |first=Katherine |date=September 29, 2026 |title=Michigan Libertarian Party disavows its own gubernatorial nominee |url=https://michiganadvance.com/2026/09/29/michigan-libertarian-party-disavows-its-own-gubernatorial-nominee/ |access-date=September 30, 2026 |website=[[Michigan Advance]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Also in September 2026, it was revealed that Hudson's running mate, Beau Parmenter, had been arrested that month and charged with felony larceny by conversion for an incident from May 2025.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Evans |first1=Jordan Willow |title=Libertarian Candidate for Michigan Lt. Governor Arrested, Charged With Felony Larceny |url=https://independentpoliticalreport.com/2026/09/libertarian-candidate-for-michigan-lt-governor-arrested-charged-with-felony-larceny/ |access-date=October 3, 2026 |work=[[Independent Political Report]] |date=September 18, 2026}}</ref>

{{ElectionsMN}}
The '''2026 Minnesota gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Minnesota|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Minnesota|lieutenant governor]] of [[Minnesota]]. [[Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party|Democratic]] senator [[Amy Klobuchar]] and [[Republican Party of Minnesota|Republican]] state House speaker [[Lisa Demuth]] are the nominees for their respective parties.

Democratic incumbent [[Tim Walz]] ran for a third term, but withdrew in January following a [[2020s Minnesota fraud scandals|scandal over fraud in state funded-social services]]. Following Walz's withdrawal, Klobuchar entered the Democratic primary and won the nomination with 89.7% of the vote against minimal opposition. In the Republican primary, Demuth defeated businessman [[Mike Lindell]], who was endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], and healthcare technology executive Kendall Qualls, who was endorsed by the state party, with 43.4% of the vote.

The winner of this election will be the first female governor of Minnesota.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Akaolisa |first=Tom |date=2026-08-17 |title=MINNEAPOLIMEDIA EDITORIAL {{!}} Minnesota Will Elect Its First Woman Governor. The Harder Task Is Governing a Fractured State {{!}} MinneapoliMedia |url=https://minneapolimedia.town.news/g/coon-rapids-mn/n/384781/minneapolimedia-editorial-minnesota-will-elect-its-first-woman-governor |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=minneapolimedia.town.news |language=en}}</ref> Republicans have not won a gubernatorial election in Minnesota since [[2006 Minnesota gubernatorial election|2006]].

== Democratic–Farmer–Labor primary ==
After Walz announced his withdrawal from the race, [[United States Senate|U.S. Senator]] [[Amy Klobuchar]] launched a campaign for the governor's office on January 29, 2026.<ref>{{cite news| last1=Griffith| first1= Michelle| title= Sen. Klobuchar launches campaign for Minnesota governor| url= https://minnesotareformer.com/2026/01/29/sen-klobuchar-launches-campaign-for-minnesota-governor/| access-date= June 4, 2026| work= [[Minnesota Reformer]]| date= January 29, 2026}}</ref> Six other [[Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party|Democratic-Farmer-Labor]] (DFL) candidates filed, none of whom have previously held elected office. Community organizer Kobey Layne challenged Klobuchar for the DFL's endorsement on May 30, 2026, but Klobuchar was endorsed on the first ballot alongside her running mate, [[Ben Schierer]].<ref name= "LayneMN">{{cite news| last1=Griffith| first1=Michelle| title=Klobuchar fights off challenge from left, wins DFL convention nod in bid for governor| url= https://minnesotareformer.com/2026/05/30/klobuchar-fights-off-challenge-from-left-wins-dfl-convention-nod-in-bid-for-governor/ |access-date= June 3, 2026| work= Minnesota Reformer| date= May 30, 2026}}</ref>

{{Elections in Nebraska}}
The '''2026 Nebraska gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Nebraska]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Jim Pillen]] is running for re-election to a second term. 

[[Primary elections]] took place on May 12, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|website=way[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]|access-date=August 5, 2025}}</ref> Pillen secured his party's nomination with 76% of the vote, while [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former state senator [[Lynne Walz]] secured her party's nomination with 91% of the vote. Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Nebraska since [[1994 Nebraska gubernatorial election|1994]].

{{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=November 2024}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Nevada gubernatorial election | country = Nevada | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2022 Nevada gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Nevada gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = Joe Lombardo (55512471876) (cropped).jpg | nominee1 = [[Joe Lombardo]] | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate1 = | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford addresses the United Nations Human Rights Committee, October 17-18, 2023 1 (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Aaron Ford (Nevada politician)|Aaron Ford]] | running_mate2 = | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | title = [[Governor of Nevada|Governor]] | before_election = [[Joe Lombardo]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsNV}} The '''2026 Nevada gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Nevada]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Joe Lombardo]] is seeking a second term. He is being challenged by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] attorney general [[Aaron Ford (Nevada politician)|Aaron Ford]]. [[Primary elections]] took place on June 9, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]|access-date=August 5, 2025}} Lombardo won the Republican nomination with 91.0% of the vote. Ford won the Democratic nomination with 63.8% over Washoe commission chair [[Alexis Hill (Nevada politician)|Alexis Hill]]. == Background == Nevada is considered to be a purple to slightly blue state at the federal and state levels, with neither party having [[Government trifecta|control of all three]] branches of government. Apart from the governor, Nevada's [[Lieutenant Governor of Nevada|lieutenant governor]] and [[Nevada State Controller|state controller]] are Republicans. Nevada's [[Nevada Attorney General|attorney general]], [[Nevada State Treasurer|treasurer]], and [[Secretary of State of Nevada|state secretary of state]] are Democrats.{{cn|date=March 2026}} [[Donald Trump]] won the state in [[2024 United States presidential election|2024]], becoming the first Republican presidential nominee to win the state since [[2004 United States presidential election in Nevada|2004]].{{cite news |title=Trump turns Nevada red in presidential race for first time in two decades |url=https://abc3340.com/news/nation-world/trump-turns-nevada-red-in-presidential-race-for-first-time-in-two-decades |access-date=March 6, 2026 |publisher=ABC3340 |date=November 6, 2024}} The [[Nevada Legislature]] is controlled by members of the Democratic Party, with a majority in both the [[Nevada Assembly|state assembly]] and [[Nevada Senate|senate]]. The lieutenant governor, a Republican, serves as the president of the state senate but only votes in the case of a tie. At the federal level, both [[United States Senate|United States Senators]] and three out of four members of the [[United States House of Representatives]] from Nevada are Democrats.{{Cite news |title=Election Results, 2022 |url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/election-results-2022/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221123004555/https://www.reviewjournal.com/election-results-2022/ |archive-date=November 23, 2022 |work=[[Las Vegas Review-Journal]]}}{{Cite news |title=Election Results, 2024 |url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/general-election-results-2024/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241229090710/https://www.reviewjournal.com/general-election-results-2024/ |archive-date=December 29, 2024 |work=[[Las Vegas Review-Journal]]}} With the exception of [[2018 Nevada gubernatorial election|2018]], Republicans have won every gubernatorial election in the state since [[1998 Nevada gubernatorial election|1998]].{{Cite news |last1=Mueller |first1=Tabitha |last2=Golonka |first2=Sean |last3=Solis |first3=Jacob |date=November 11, 2022 |title=Lombardo defeats Sisolak; Democrats win attorney general, secretary of state races |url=https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/lombardo-defeats-sisolak-democrats-win-attorney-general-secretary-of-state-races |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221112031753/https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/lombardo-defeats-sisolak-democrats-win-attorney-general-secretary-of-state-races |archive-date=November 12, 2022 |work=[[The Nevada Independent]]}} == Republican primary == === Candidates === ==== Nominee ==== *[[Joe Lombardo]], incumbent [[Governor of Nevada|governor]] (2023–present){{cite news |title=Joe Lombardo launches re-election bid for Nevada governor |first1=Isabella |last1=Aldrete |first2=Kiara |last2=Adams |first3=Eric |last3=Neugeboren |work=[[The Nevada Independent]] |date=September 15, 2025 |access-date=September 16, 2025 |url=https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/joe-lombardo-launches-re-election-bid-for-nevada-governor}} ==== Eliminated in primary ==== * Donald J. The '''2026 New York gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of New York]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Kathy Hochul]] is running for re-election to a second full term.<ref name="HochulRunning">{{Cite news |last=Parsnow |first=Luke |date=July 2, 2024 |title=Hochul says she's running for another term as New York governor in 2026 |url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2024/07/02/hochul-says-she-s-running-for-another-term-as-governor-in-2026 |access-date=August 20, 2024 |website=[[Spectrum News]] |language=en |archive-date=July 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708215410/https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2024/07/02/hochul-says-she-s-running-for-another-term-as-governor-in-2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Primary elections]] took place on June 23, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260423040741/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=April 23, 2026|access-date=August 5, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures|NCSL]]}}</ref> The gubernatorial candidates selected their running mates, instead of having separate primaries.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cuza|first=Bobby|date=May 8, 2025|title=State lawmakers eliminate lieutenant governor primary|url=https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2025/05/09/albany-lawmakers-eliminate-lieutenant-governor-primary?cid=share_clip|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260105102847/https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2025/05/09/albany-lawmakers-eliminate-lieutenant-governor-primary?cid=share_clip|archive-date=January 5, 2026|work=[[Spectrum News]] |url-status=live}}</ref> 

Hochul will face Nassau County Executive [[Bruce Blakeman]], the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] and [[Conservative Party of New York State|Conservative]] nominee, in the general election. After U.S. representative [[Elise Stefanik]] withdrew from the Republican primary in December 2025, Blakeman was endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]].<ref name=te>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/12/20/trump-new-york-governor-endorsement-bruce-blakeman-00702013|title=Trump endorses in New York governor race the day after Stefanik drops out|date=December 20, 2025|work=Politico|access-date=2026-10-10}}</ref> Republicans have not won a statewide election in New York since [[George Pataki]] was re-elected governor in [[2002 New York gubernatorial election|2002]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://abc7ny.com/post/new-york-rep-elise-stefanik-announce-run-governor-soon-friday/18122558/|title=Rep. Elise Stefanik to announce run for New York governor as soon as Friday|date=November 6, 2025|work=ABC7 New York|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251107000827/https://abc7ny.com/post/new-york-rep-elise-stefanik-announce-run-governor-soon-friday/18122558/|archive-date=2025-11-07|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Background==
Governor [[Kathy Hochul]] took office on August 24, 2021, upon the resignation of her predecessor, [[Andrew Cuomo]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/24/nyregion/kathy-hochul-governor-ny.html|title=Hochul Is Sworn In: 'I Want People to Believe in Their Government Again'|first=Luis|last=Ferré-Sadurní|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=August 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211224074148/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/24/nyregion/kathy-hochul-governor-ny.html|archive-date=2021-12-24|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> Hochul was elected to a full term in [[2022 New York gubernatorial election|2022]] with 53.1% of the vote in the closest New York gubernatorial election since [[1994 New York gubernatorial election|1994]].<ref name="results">{{cite web |title=2022 General Election Governor and Lt. Governor Results |url=https://elections.ny.gov/2022-general-election-governor-and-lt-governor-results |website=[[New York State Board of Elections]]|date=November 8, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.timesunion.com/state/article/Zeldin-concede-17571499.php|title=Zeldin concedes to Hochul in closest governor's race since 1994|first=Brendan J.|last=Lyons|date=November 9, 2022|website=Times Union|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261004233945/https://www.timesunion.com/state/article/Zeldin-concede-17571499.php|archive-date=2026-10-04|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Democratic primary==
Due to low approval ratings, poor Democratic performances in the [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections|2022 midterm elections]] in [[2022 New York state elections|New York]], and controversies surrounding her administration, Hochul was considered vulnerable to a primary challenge in 2026.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Reisman |first=Nick |date=September 5, 2024 |title=Hochul's headwinds become tougher with indictment of alleged foreign agent |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/09/05/linda-sun-arrest-hochul-approval-00177430?nname=new-york-playbook&nid=0000014f-1646-d88f-a1cf-5f46b74f0000&nrid=7fbb50ed-ea1a-4aff-a106-d6b8cc25c14a&nlid=630317 |work=[[Politico]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240923230245/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/09/05/linda-sun-arrest-hochul-approval-00177430|archive-date=2024-09-23|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> 

On June 2, 2025, following months of reports about a strained relationship with the governor's office, [[Antonio Delgado]] launched his campaign for the Democratic nomination.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Mays |first=Jeffery C. |date=June 2, 2025 |title=Antonio Delgado, Hochul's No. 2, Will Challenge Her in Governor's Race |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/02/nyregion/antonio-delgado-governor-hochul.html |access-date=June 2, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250602204431/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/02/nyregion/antonio-delgado-governor-hochul.html|archive-date=2025-06-02|url-status=live}}</ref> On February 4, 2026, he announced nurse, union organizer, and socialist activist [[India Walton]] as his running mate.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/capital-region/politics/2026/02/04/antonio-delgado-governor-election-running-mate|title=Delgado picks India Walton as running mate in governor's race|date=February 4, 2026|work=Spectrum Local News|access-date=2026-10-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260210185600/https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/capital-region/politics/2026/02/04/antonio-delgado-governor-election-running-mate|archive-date=2026-02-10|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Despite early perceptions of vulnerability to a left-wing challenge, Hochul was endorsed in February 2026 by [[Zohran Mamdani]] and [[Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez]], both prominent members of the [[New York City Democratic Socialists of America]]. ''[[Politico]]'' noted that the endorsements "all but crowd out her little-known primary challenger, (Antonio) Delgado," while Democratic strategist Trip Yang called Hochul "the comeback player of the year."<ref name="embrace">{{cite news |title=Why the left decided to embrace, and not fight, Kathy Hochul |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/06/why-the-left-decided-to-embrace-and-not-fight-kathy-hochul-00769785 |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=2026-02-08 |language=en |date=2026-02-06|last=Reisman|first=Nick}}</ref> She was soon endorsed by the [[New York State Democratic Party|New York Democratic Party]] after securing 85% of support from party members at the state convention.<ref>{{cite news |title=Hochul projects 'strength' as she resoundingly wins Democratic backing for a new term |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/06/hochul-projects-strength-as-she-resoundingly-wins-democratic-backing-for-a-new-term-00769561 |work=Politico |access-date=2026-02-13 |language=en |date=2026-02-06}}</ref>  Delgado ended his campaign on February 10, 2026, citing a lack of a viable path forward.<ref name=Sterne>{{Cite news |last1=Sterne |first1=Peter |last2=Lewis |first2=Rebecca |date=February 10, 2026 |title=Antonio Delgado ends his campaign for governor |url=https://www.cityandstateny.com/politics/2026/02/antonio-delgado-ends-his-campaign-governor/411320/ |access-date=2026-02-10 |work=City & State |language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260212094733/https://www.cityandstateny.com/politics/2026/02/antonio-delgado-ends-his-campaign-governor/411320/|archive-date=2026-02-12|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Republican primary==
U.S. representative [[Elise Stefanik]] was considered a potential gubernatorial candidate throughout 2025. She formally announced her candidacy on November 7, 2025.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rep. Elise Stefanik announces run for New York governor, challenging Kathy Hochul in 2026 election - CBS New York |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/elise-stefanik-running-for-new-york-governor/ |website=CBS |access-date=November 7, 2025 |date=November 7, 2025}}</ref> A July 2025 Siena poll showed Stefanik leading two other potential Republican gubernatorial candidates, U.S. representative [[Mike Lawler]] and Nassau County executive [[Bruce Blakeman]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2025/06/30/poll--stefanik-leads-potential-gop-field-for-n-y--governor|title=Poll: Stefanik leads potential GOP field for N.Y. governor; Hochul leads all 3|work=Spectrum Local News|last=Parsnow|first=Luke}}</ref> In May 2025, President [[Donald Trump]] endorsed Lawler and Blakeman for re-election to their current posts "in a not-so-subtle attempt to clear the field for upstate Congresswoman Elise Stefanik to get the GOP nomination".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/trump-bruce-blakeman-mike-lawler-endorsements/|title=Ahead of N.Y. governor's race, President Trump's endorsements send "loud message" |last=Kramer|first=Marcia|date=May 7, 2025|website=CBS News|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305092233/https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/trump-bruce-blakeman-mike-lawler-endorsements/|archive-date=2026-03-05|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> On July 23, 2025, Mike Lawler announced that he would run for re-election to Congress.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Anderson |first1=Renee |last2=Kramer |first2=Marcia |last3=Woodall |first3=Hunter |date=July 23, 2025 |title=Mike Lawler to sit out New York governor's race and run for reelection in House district |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/mike-lawler-reelection-new-york-governor-race-elise-stefanik-republicans/ |access-date=2026-10-10 |work=[[CBS News]] |language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305092233/https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/trump-bruce-blakeman-mike-lawler-endorsements/|archive-date=2026-03-05|url-status=live}}</ref>

Bruce Blakeman was re-elected to the post of Nassau County executive by a double-digit margin in November 2025.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://gothamist.com/news/blakeman-reelected-as-nassau-county-exec-and-gop-hopes-for-a-bulwark-against-mamdani|title=Blakeman reelected as Nassau County exec and GOP hopes for a bulwark against Mamdani|first=Jimmy|last=Vielkind|date=November 5, 2025|website=Gothamist|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260206133736/https://gothamist.com/news/blakeman-reelected-as-nassau-county-exec-and-gop-hopes-for-a-bulwark-against-mamdani|archive-date=2026-02-06|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> When asked about Blakeman's potential gubernatorial candidacy, Trump stated that Blakeman and Stefanik were "both great people".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://abcnews.com/Politics/county-gop-leader-bruce-blakeman-announces-run-new/story?id=128244979|title=County GOP leader Bruce Blakeman announces run for New York governor, taking on fellow Trump ally Elise Stefanik|first=Oren|last=Oppenheim|website=ABC News|date=December 9, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260206133736/https://gothamist.com/news/blakeman-reelected-as-nassau-county-exec-and-gop-hopes-for-a-bulwark-against-mamdani|archive-date=2026-02-06|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> On December 9, 2025, Blakeman launched his campaign for the 2026 Republican gubernatorial nomination.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kramer |first=Marcia |last2=Capellini |first2=Jeff |last3=Westbrook |first3=Elijah |date=2025-12-09 |title=Bruce Blakeman announces run for New York governor, to challenge Elise Stefanik in Republican primary |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/bruce-blakeman-running-for-new-york-governor-2026/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251209152008/https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/bruce-blakeman-running-for-new-york-governor-2026/ |archive-date=2025-12-09 |access-date=2026-10-10 |work=CBS News}}</ref> According to ''[[The New York Times]]'', Trump's decision to remain neutral and not to attempt to clear the field for Stefanik "sent shock waves through Republican circles".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/10/nyregion/blakeman-trump-stefanik.html|title=Trump Didn't Clear a Path for Stefanik in the N.Y. Governor's Race|first=Grace|last=Ashford|work=The New York Times |date=December 10, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251212101329/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/10/nyregion/blakeman-trump-stefanik.html|archive-date=2025-12-12|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref> On December 19, Stefanik announced she was withdrawing her candidacy.<ref name="sq">{{Cite news |last=Jacobs |first=Ben |date=December 19, 2025 |title=Stefanik Quits Governor's Race, Will Not Run for Reelection |url=https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/elise-stefanik-new-york-governor-interview.html |access-date=December 19, 2025 |work=[[New York (magazine)|New York]]|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251212101329/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/10/nyregion/blakeman-trump-stefanik.html|archive-date=2025-12-12|url-status=live}}</ref> President Trump endorsed Blakeman's candidacy on December 20.<ref name=te/>

In February 2026, Libertarian nominee Larry Sharpe announced his intention to petition his way onto the Republican primary ballot.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cityandstateny.com/politics/2026/02/state-gop-formally-designates-blakeman-nominee-governor/411361/|title=State GOP formally designates Blakeman as nominee for governor|first=Rebecca C.|last=Lewis|date=February 11, 2026|work=City & State|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260909194922/https://www.cityandstateny.com/politics/2026/02/state-gop-formally-designates-blakeman-nominee-governor/411361/|archive-date=2026-09-09|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Conservative convention==
The [[New York State Conservative Party]] held its annual conference and nominating convention in Albany in February 2026, officially endorsing Blakeman for governor. Because New York utilizes a fusion voting system, Blakeman accepted the third-party ballot line to run concurrently on both the Republican and Conservative lines.<ref name="ConservativeLine">{{cite news |title=Bruce Blakeman receives nomination for governor from NY State Conservative Party |url=https://longisland.news12.com/bruce-blakeman-receives-nomination-for-governor-from-ny-state-conservative-party |work=News 12 |access-date=2026-02-15}}</ref>
===Candidates===
====Nominee====
*[[Bruce Blakeman]], [[Nassau County Executive|Nassau County executive]] (2021–present)<ref name="ConservativeLine"/>
**Running mate: Todd Hood, [[Madison County, New York|Madison County]] sheriff (2018–present)<ref name="HoodLtGov"/>

==Working Families convention==
The [[Working Families Party|New York Working Families Party]] declined to nominate Hochul or Delgado, instead opting for a "placeholder candidate" to appear on their ballot line. The party has stated that the placeholder candidate will later be replaced by the Democratic nominee.<ref name="Placeholder"/> A convention attendee told ''[[City & State]]'' that Delgado won 41% of the weighted party committee vote to Hochul's 3%, while "placeholder candidate" won 56% of the vote. State party leaders Jasmine Gripper and [[Ana María Archila]] disputed the claim, but did not share the exact vote totals.<ref name="Placeholder"/>

On August 21, the Working Families Party nominated Hochul and Adams.<ref name="WFPLine"/>

{{ElectionsOH}}

The '''2026 Ohio gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Ohio]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] entrepreneur [[Vivek Ramaswamy]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former state health director [[Amy Acton]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent governor [[Mike DeWine]] is ineligible to seek a third consecutive term.

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 5, with Ramaswamy defeating minimal opposition for the Republican nomination and Acton running unopposed for the Democratic nomination. If elected, Ramaswamy would become the first [[Indian American]] governor of Ohio and the first [[Hindus|Hindu]] governor in the United States.{{Efn|[[Bobby Jindal]] was born Hindu but converted to Christianity as a teenager.}} Acton would be Ohio's first elected female{{Efn|[[Nancy Hollister]] served as governor, albeit for only 11 days, following [[George Voinovich]]'s resignation to take his seat in the [[U.S. Senate]].}} and first Jewish governor if elected.

The campaign has been described as "ugly" and heavily reliant on [[negative campaigning]]. Ramaswamy has focused on Acton's background to portray her as dishonest and [[Mental disorder|mentally ill]], while Acton has portrayed Ramaswamy as an out-of-touch [[Plutocracy|plutocrat]] and [[Scam|con artist]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Contrera |first=Jessica |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Attack Ad Featuring Candidate's Mother Turns Ohio Governor's Race Even Uglier |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/ramaswamy-campaign-ad-acton-estranged-mother-donna-arthur.html |access-date=October 21, 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> 

Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Ohio since [[2006 Ohio gubernatorial election|2006]]. The winner of the election will be inaugurated on January 11, 2027.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Muhammad |first1=Mariyam |title=Can Mike DeWine run for Ohio governor in 2026? What to know about term limits |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/2024/11/08/mike-dewine-run-ohio-governor-2026-state-law-says/76111304007/ |website=[[The Columbus Dispatch]] |access-date=February 5, 2025}}</ref>

== General election ==

=== Campaign ===
On September 2, Ramaswamy accepted invitations to participate in gubernatorial debates hosted by [[CNN]] and [[WLWT]] and called on Acton to join him. Acton's campaign subsequently declined, citing what it characterized as inaccurate and personal attacks in Ramaswamy's campaign advertising. As a result, no debates between the two major-party nominees have been scheduled.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bischoff |first1=Laura A. |title=Amy Acton refuses to debate Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio governor's race |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/state/2026/09/02/ohio-governor-candidates-may-not-debate-find-out-why/91585349007/ |website=[[The Columbus Dispatch]] |date=September 2, 2026 |access-date=September 4, 2026}}</ref> 

==== Canfield Fair incident ====
On September 6, Acton was attacked at a campaign event at the [[Canfield, Ohio|Canfield]] Fair. An armed individual lunged at her and was apprehended by local authorities. Several campaign volunteers suffered minor injuries.<ref name="wlwysept6">{{Cite web |last=Knue |first=Kurt |date=September 6, 2026 |title=Amy Acton attacked at campaign event near Youngstown; multiple people reportedly injured |url=https://www.wlwt.com/article/amy-acton-attacked-at-campaign-event-near-youngstown/73625988 |access-date=September 6, 2026 |website=WLWT |language=en}}</ref> The suspect, Patrick Havas, was charged with "two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct."<ref name="tiosept6">{{cite web |last1=Ziegler |first1=Jen |title=Armed man arrested after pushing toward Amy Acton is brother of Ramaswamy donor who quit Husted campaign |url=https://tiffinohio.net/posts/patrick-havas-arrested-acton-attack-brother-ramaswamy-donor/ |website=TiffinOhio.net |date=September 6, 2026 |access-date=September 25, 2026}}</ref>

==== Attacks on Amy Acton's upbringing & ad controversy ====
The Ramaswamy campaign has been described as "ugly" and heavily focused upon [[negative campaigning]].<ref name="nytoct20">{{Cite news |last=Contrera |first=Jessica |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Attack Ad Featuring Candidate's Mother Turns Ohio Governor's Race Even Uglier |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/ramaswamy-campaign-ad-acton-estranged-mother-donna-arthur.html |access-date=October 20, 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

[[Attack ad|Attack ads]] by the Vivek Ramaswamy campaign focused on Acton's background to portray her as dishonest and [[Mental disorder|mentally ill]],<ref name="apoct21">{{Cite web |last=Carr Smyth |first=Julie |date=October 21, 2026 |title=Ramaswamy takes responsibility for ad with Amy Acton's mother and will spend millions to promote it |url=https://apnews.com/article/election-2026-ohio-governor-acton-mother-ramaswamy-dc59bd5f0c47f9e06f37022e2ba2cce5 |access-date=October 21, 2026 |website=[[Associated Press]] |quote=Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's team confirmed late Tuesday that it produced a controversial advertisement featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, and the campaign said it will spend $4 million to broadcast it despite facing bipartisan rebuke for dredging up the painful childhood of his Democratic opponent in Ohio's governor's race. Acton, who has made no secret of facing homelessness and sexual abuse as a child, had spent the day pushing back forcefully against the content of the video, whose origins were initially murky. In it, her birth mother Donna Arthur calls her "a liar" and insinuates she has mental health issues.}}</ref><ref name="nroct20">{{Cite web |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Amy Acton's Mom Claims Candidate Lied About Childhood in Attack Ad — Despite Extensive Record of Abuse |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/news/amy-actons-mom-claims-candidate-lied-about-childhood-in-attack-ad-despite-extensive-record-of-abuse/ |access-date=October 20, 2026 |website=National Review |language=en-US}}</ref> claiming that she had "lied" and "exaggerated" about being abused, despite evidence that she had undergone [[Child sexual abuse|childhood rape]], other types of [[sexual abuse]], [[Homelessness in the United States|homelessness]], [[poverty]], and [[Neglect|parental neglect]].<ref name="apoct21" /><ref name="nroct20" /><ref name="wapooct20">{{Cite news |last=Tumulty |first=Karen |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Ohio governor's race in uproar over video featuring Democrat's estranged mother |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/20/ohio-governors-race-uproar-over-video-featuring-democrats-estranged-mother/ |access-date=October 21, 2026 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

An [[attack ad]] featuring Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, denouncing her received nationwide attention. Arthur has been estranged from Acton since Acton was [[Child protective services|removed]] from her stepfather's and her mother's home at the age of 12; the [[stepfather]] was charged with [[Rape|raping]] her.<ref name="nytoct20"/><ref name="nroct20"/><ref name="wapooct20"/> The ad was initially only shared on social media and lacked a "paid for by" television disclosure; the Ramaswamy campaign later took credit for creating it.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 21, 2026 |title=Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign confirms it made the viral attack ad rattling Ohio’s race for governor |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/amy-acton-attack-ad-ohio-governors-race-rcna604601 |access-date=October 21, 2026 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref> Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy’s campaign, said the ad will "air both online and on TV in the closing days of the campaign". On October 21, 2026, the Ramaswamy campaign said it would broadcast the ad, despite the $4 million price tag and bipartisan condemnation.<ref name="apoct21" /> Ohio Republicans, including U.S. Senator [[Jon Husted]] and [[Ohio Secretary of State|Secretary of State]] [[Frank LaRose]], publicly criticized the ad.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Svitek|first1=Patrick |last2=Fox|first2=Lauren|date=October 20, 2026 |title=Key Ohio Republicans criticize Ramaswamy’s ad with Acton’s estranged mother, even as Vance warned them not to |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/20/politics/amy-acton-mother-video |access-date=October 21, 2026 |work=CNN |language=en}}</ref> Two days later, Governor [[Mike DeWine]] called for the ad to be pulled.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Balmert |first=Jessie |title=Gov. Mike DeWine condemns Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's estranged mom |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/22/gov-mike-dewine-condemns-ramaswamy-ad-featuring-actons-estranged-mom/92377815007/ |access-date=October 22, 2026 |website=The Columbus Dispatch |language=en-US}}</ref> President Trump expressed support for the ad, encouraging Ramaswamy to keep running it, and criticized DeWine for his opposition.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hazard |first=Charlotte |title=Trump praises Ramaswamy attack ad against Acton, says it shouldn't be taken down |url=https://fox17.com/news/nation-world/trump-praises-ramaswamy-attack-ad-against-acton-says-it-shouldnt-be-taken-down-ohio-mike-dewine |access-date=October 22, 2026 |website=WZTV |language=en-US}}</ref> Vice President Vance also expressed support for the ad.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Kyle Kondik and J. Miles Coleman |title=The Governors: Ohio to Leans Democratic Among Other Changes as Dems Eye Gubernatorial Majority |url=https://centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/the-governors-ohio-to-leans-democratic-among-other-changes-as-dems-eye-gubernatorial-majority/ |access-date=October 24, 2026 |website=Sabato's Crystal Ball |language=en-US}}</ref>

The [[Associated Press]] reported that Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, "said the two were removed from their mother Donna Arthur’s custody as children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Acton has not seen Arthur, whose last known address was in Pennsylvania, since they were in a courtroom together in 1978. According to police and court documents obtained by the Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported his alleged conduct to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died."<ref name="apoct21" />
