{{pp|small=yes}} {{short description|none}}{{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Oklahoma gubernatorial election | country = Oklahoma | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2022 Oklahoma gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Oklahoma gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = Mike Mazzei OK Senate Headshot.jpg | nominee1 = [[Mike Mazzei]] | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate1 = | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = Cyndi Munson.jpg | nominee2 = [[Cyndi Munson]] | running_mate2 = | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | title = [[Governor of Oklahoma|Governor]] | before_election = [[Kevin Stitt]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsOK}} The '''2026 Oklahoma gubernatorial election''' will take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[governor of Oklahoma]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former state senator [[Mike Mazzei]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state representative [[Cyndi Munson]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Kevin Stitt]] is [[Term limits in the United States|term-limited]] and ineligible to seek a third term. Primary elections were held on June 16, 2026, and in races where no candidate receives over 50% of the vote, runoff elections took place on August 25, 2026. Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Oklahoma since [[2006 Oklahoma gubernatorial election|2006]]. ==Republican primary== ===Campaign=== In August 2023, [[KOSU]] noted that Attorney General [[Gentner Drummond]] had raised significantly more than other statewide elected officials in 2023, fueling rumors of a gubernatorial run.{{cite news |last1=Nissley |first1=Isabel |title=Oklahoma Attorney General raises $225K, topping state officials' campaign contributions |url=https://www.kosu.org/politics/2023-08-08/oklahoma-attorney-general-raises-225k-topping-state-officials-campaign-contributions |access-date=25 August 2023 |work=[[KOSU]] |date=August 8, 2023}} The same month, ''[[The Black Wall Street Times]]'' reported State Superintendent of Public Instruction [[Ryan Walters (American politician)|Ryan Walters]] was preparing for a 2026 gubernatorial campaign.{{cite news |title=Sources: Ryan Walters mulls bid for governor amid attacks on TPS |url=https://theblackwallsttimes.com/2023/08/07/sources-ryan-walters-mulls-bid-for-governor-amid-attacks-on-tps/ |access-date=25 August 2023 |work=[[The Black Wall Street Times]] |date=August 7, 2023}} U.S. Representative [[Kevin Hern]] was the first major contender to public acknowledge he was considering a campaign in August 2024, but ruled out a run that December after House Republicans won a narrow majority in the [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections|2024 elections]].{{cite news |last1=Krehbiel |first1=Randy |title=Could Congressman Kevin Hern be Oklahoma's next governor? |url=https://tulsaworld.com/news/state-regional/government-politics/could-congressman-kevin-hern-be-oklahomas-next-governor/article_dfbf99fe-6585-11ef-a997-3319440d32fb.html |access-date=August 30, 2024 |work=[[Tulsa World]] |date=August 29, 2024 |language=en}} In early January 2025, former state senator [[Mike Mazzei]] posted a gubernatorial campaign logo to [[Facebook]].{{Cite news |first1= Reese |last1=Gorman |last2=Luetkemeyer |first2=Em |date=January 12, 2025 |title=Oklahoma Attorney General Prepares to Jump in Governor's Race |url=https://www.notus.org/oklahoma/oklahoma-attorney-general-prepares-governor-race |access-date=January 12, 2025 |work=NOTUS |language=en-US}} On January 13, 2025, Drummond announced his campaign for governor. He was the first major candidate to enter the race and the second overall after Leisa Mitchell Haynes. On February 18, former Oklahoma House Speaker [[Charles McCall]] officially announced his campaign. Mazzei officially launched his campaign on April 3. In May, former state senator [[Jake A. Merrick|Jake Merrick]] entered the race followed by businessman Kenneth Sturgell. The '''2026 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Pennsylvania]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Josh Shapiro]] is seeking a second term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state treasurer [[Stacy Garrity]].

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 26, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|access-date=September 27, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref> Shapiro and Garrity secured their nominations unopposed. This is one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. If elected, Garrity would be the first female governor of Pennsylvania.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Tannenbaum|first=Michael|date=August 15, 2025|title=Pa. Treasurer Stacy Garrity to run for governor against Josh Shapiro|url=https://www.phillyvoice.com/stacy-garrity-pennsylvania-governor-2026-republican-shapiro/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250818172457/https://www.phillyvoice.com/stacy-garrity-pennsylvania-governor-2026-republican-shapiro/|archive-date=August 18, 2025|access-date=May 25, 2026|work=Philly Voice}}</ref>

== Background ==
[[Pennsylvania]] is a [[purple state]] located in the [[Northeastern United States]]. A part of the [[Rust Belt]], it was narrowly won by Republican [[Donald Trump]] in [[2024 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|his non-consecutive second victory in 2024]] after similarly narrow victories by Democrat [[Joe Biden]] in [[2020 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2020]] and Trump in his first election in [[2016 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2016]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/revisit-pennsylvania-election-results/|title=Revisit Pennsylvania election results from 2020 and 2016 ahead of Election Day 2024 - CBS News|date=November 4, 2024|website=www.cbsnews.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The 2024 presidential election was close, not a landslide |url=https://abcnews.go.com/538/2024-presidential-election-close-landslide/story?id=116240898 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126224157/https://abcnews.go.com/538/2024-presidential-election-close-landslide/story?id=116240898 |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 26, 2024 |website=ABC News}}</ref>

The state has a Democratic and Republican senator, making it one of only three states to have a split Senate delegation,{{efn|The other two are [[Maine]], with an independent who caucuses with the Democrats and a Republican, and [[Wisconsin]], with a Democrat and a Republican.<ref>[https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2024/11/19/119th-congress-smashes-record-low-for-number-of-split-us-senate-delegations/ 119th Congress Smashes Record Low for Number of Split US Senate Delegations], Smart Politics, November 19, 2024. Retrieved January 31, 2026</ref>}} while Republicans hold a majority in the state's House delegation, with ten seats to the Democrats' seven.<ref>{{cite news |title=119th Congress Smashes Record Low for Number of Split US Senate Delegations |url=https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2024/11/19/119th-congress-smashes-record-low-for-number-of-split-us-senate-delegations/ |access-date=September 4, 2025 |issue=Smart Politics |date=November 19, 2024}}</ref> Democrats also control the [[Pennsylvania House of Representatives]] while Republicans control the [[Pennsylvania Senate]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Democrats will again control Pennsylvania House after holding on to one-seat majority |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/11/pennsylvania-election-results-2024-state-house-democratic-republican-control/ |access-date=September 4, 2025 |publisher=Spotlight PA |date=November 8, 2024}}</ref> 

Republicans have not won a Pennsylvania gubernatorial election since [[2010 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|2010]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Josh Shapiro]] was first elected with 56.5% of the vote in  [[2022 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|2022]], succeeding term-limited Democrat [[Tom Wolf]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://penncapital-star.com/campaigns-elections/inside-josh-shapiros-2022-landslide-and-what-it-means-for-2024-analysis/|title=Inside Josh Shapiro's 2022 landslide -- and what it means for 2024 | Analysis • Pennsylvania Capital-Star|first=Nick|last=Field|date=May 21, 2023}}</ref>

==General election==
===Campaign===
A major issue in the general election has been the growing [[opposition to AI data centers]], similarly experienced throughout the country. Shapiro, despite having previously supported the construction of two [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] data center campuses estimated at $20 million the previous year and being quoted as saying Pennsylvania was "all in on AI",<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cityandstatepa.com/policy/2026/05/gov-josh-shapiros-new-data-center-standards-reflect-new-reality/413789/|title=Gov. Josh Shapiro's new data center standards reflect new reality|first1=Justin|last1=Sweitzer|first2=Harrison|last2=Cann|website=[[City & State]]|date=May 27, 2026|access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref> signed an executive order in August 2026 that implemented new regulations on them and eliminated fast-tracking of approvals to build them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://whyy.org/articles/shapiro-data-centers-executive-order-pennsylvania/|title=Pennsylvania Gov. Shapiro signs wide-ranging executive order reining in data center development|first=Susan|last=Phillips|publisher=[[WHYY-TV]]|date=August 19, 2026|access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref> Garrity has criticized Shapiro for this, claiming he "sold us out" for his prior support of Amazon's $20 million data center projects, although Garrity has similarly made comments supportive of AI data centers in the past and to which Shapiro has also capitalized on.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6055856-shapiro-garrity-pennsylvania-data-center-ads/|title=Shapiro, Garrity accuse each other of supporting data centers|first=Mira|last=Bhakta|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=August 27, 2026|access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref>

The '''2026 Rhode Island gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Rhode Island]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Dan McKee]] ran for re-election to a second full term but was defeated in the primary by [[Helena Buonanno Foulkes|Helena Foulkes]]. [[Primary elections]] took place on September 9, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 26, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|url-status=live|access-date=September 27, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref> 

Republicans have not won a statewide election in Rhode Island since [[2006 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2006]]. While Rhode Island is generally a safely Democratic state, the Democratic primary was predicted to be competitive due to McKee's high unpopularity<ref name="politico-20260808" />. The election has also been noted as not following national trends of progressives versus moderates, with both Democrats being relatively moderate and the primary instead largely boiling down to anger over the longtime closure of the [[Washington Bridge (Providence, Rhode Island)|Washington Bridge]].<ref name="politico-20260808">{{Cite web |last1=Okun |first1=Eli |date=August 8, 2026 |title=Why Rhode Island may oust a sitting governor over a bridge |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/08/rhode-island-governor-bridge-01030024 |access-date=2026-08-12 |website=Politico |language=en}}</ref>

This is the first election since [[2014 Hawaii gubernatorial election|2014]] in which an elected state governor lost renomination.{{efn|Governor [[Jeff Colyer]] of Kansas, who had taken office after the resignation of [[Sam Brownback]], was defeated by [[Kris Kobach]] in the [[2018 Kansas gubernatorial election|2018]] Republican primary election.}} It is also the first time since [[1994 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1994]] in which an incumbent governor of Rhode Island lost renomination.

==Republican primary==
2022 lieutenant governor nominee Aaron Guckian defeated actress Elaine Pelino for the Republican nomination. Pelino requested a recount, which was approved by the Rhode Island Board of Elections, however it did not change the outcome.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NEWS |first=NBC 10 |date=2026-09-15 |title=Recount does not change outcome of Republican primary in governor's race |url=https://turnto10.com/news/local/officials-begin-recount-of-republican-primary-for-rhode-island-governor-sept-15-2026 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=WJAR |language=en}}</ref>

The '''2026 South Carolina gubernatorial election''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[governor of South Carolina]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state attorney general [[Alan Wilson (politician)|Alan Wilson]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state representative [[Jermaine Johnson (politician)|Jermaine Johnson]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Henry McMaster]] is ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. 

In the Republican primary on June 9, Lieutenant Governor [[Pamela Evette]] emerged as the top vote-getter with the help of an endorsement from President [[Donald Trump]], but did not secure a majority needed to win the nomination, triggering a June 23 runoff between her and Wilson. After Trump announced his support for both Wilson and Evette, Wilson was nominated in the runoff with 68.6% of the vote. Johnson won the Democratic nomination in the June 9 primary with 59.7% of the vote against Billy Webster, the chief of staff for former governor [[Richard Riley]].

Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in South Carolina since [[1998 South Carolina gubernatorial election|1998]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Holdman |first=Jessica |date=October 28, 2025 |title=SC Democratic Rep. Jermaine Johnson announces campaign for governor |url=https://scdailygazette.com/2025/10/28/sc-democratic-rep-jermaine-johnson-announces-campaign-for-governor/ |access-date=June 16, 2026 |website=SC Daily Gazette |language=en-US}}</ref>

The '''2026 Wisconsin gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Wisconsin]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Milwaukee County executive [[David Crowley (Wisconsin politician)|David Crowley]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] U.S. representative [[Tom Tiffany]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Incumbent Democratic governor [[Tony Evers]] declined to seek re-election to a third term.

[[Primary elections]] were held on August 11, 2026. Tiffany won the Republican nomination without serious challenge.<ref name=KremerWPR /> Crowley, despite having temporarily withdrawn his candidacy, won the Democratic nomination in an [[upset victory]] over state representative [[Francesca Hong]], receiving 39.8% of the vote.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mueller |first=Julia |title=Crowley defeats democratic socialist Hong to face Tiffany in Wisconsin governor's race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6023019-crowley-wins-wisconsin-governor-primary/ |access-date=August 12, 2026 |website=The Hill |date=August 12, 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref>

This is the first Wisconsin gubernatorial election since [[2010 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2010]] in which the incumbent is not seeking re-election,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beck |first=Molly |title=Wisconsin's Democratic Gov. Tony Evers won't seek a third term in 2026 |url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/politics/2025/07/24/wisconsin-democratic-gov-tony-evers-wont-seek-re-election-in-2026/84246291007/ |access-date=February 4, 2026 |website=Journal Sentinel |language=en-US}}</ref> along with being one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state won by [[Donald Trump]] in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]].<ref name="Gilbert 2024">{{Cite web |last=Gilbert |first=Craig |title=Gilbert: How small voting shifts made Wisconsin the closest state in the nation |url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/25/gilbert-small-voting-shifts-made-wisconsin-2024s-closest-state/76461074007/ |website=[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]] |language=en-US |date=November 25, 2024 |access-date=November 26, 2024}}</ref>

If elected, Crowley would be the first African-American governor of Wisconsin.

== Background ==
Wisconsin is considered to be a [[purple state]] at the federal and state levels with a uniquely competitive track record (presidential races decided by less than a point in [[2016 United States presidential election in Wisconsin|2016]], [[2020 United States presidential election in Wisconsin|2020]], and [[2024 United States presidential election in Wisconsin|2024]]; Senate races decided by roughly a point in [[2022 United States Senate election in Wisconsin|2022]] and [[2024 United States Senate election in Wisconsin|2024]]; and a governor's race decided by a point in [[2018 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2018]]).<ref name="Gilbert 2024" /> The past two federal election cycles in Wisconsin featured split outcomes, with Democrats winning for governor and Republicans for Senate in [[2022 Wisconsin elections|2022]] and Democrats winning for Senate and Republicans for president in [[2024 Wisconsin elections|2024]]. Wisconsin has voted with the winner of the last five presidential elections, and in 2024 it had the second-highest voter turnout in the country (behind [[Minnesota]]) and one of the biggest turnout increases in the country.<ref name="Gilbert 2024" /> Both parties have seen success in the state in recent years. Republicans narrowly control both chambers of the [[Wisconsin Legislature]] and hold a majority in Wisconsin's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] delegation. However, Democrats control most statewide executive offices and have won the last two gubernatorial races.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Unger |first=Nancy C. |title=How Wisconsin Became the Ultimate Purple State |url=https://time.com/7093734/wisconsin-purple-state-history/ |website=[[TIME Magazine]] |language=en |date=October 28, 2024 |access-date=May 28, 2025}}</ref>

Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Tony Evers]] was first elected in [[2018 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2018]], narrowly defeating incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gowen |first=Annie |title=How the Democrats finally defeated Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/how-the-democrats-finally-defeated-wisconsin-gov-scott-walker/2018/11/07/3377ed17-9cbe-4537-8b2a-acd0c37a8d35_story.html |url-access=registration |date=November 7, 2018 |access-date=May 28, 2025 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> He was re-elected by a slightly larger margin in [[2022 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2022]], defeating Republican businessman Tim Michels.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bosman |first=Julie |date=November 9, 2022 |title=Tony Evers and Ron Johnson Keep Their Seats in Wisconsin |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/09/us/politics/wisconsin-tony-evers-ron-johnson.html |access-date=May 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> In July 2025, Evers announced he would not seek re-election to a third term. The race is widely seen as a tossup due to Evers's retirement and the state's even partisan lean.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cavalli |first=Samantha |date=July 25, 2025 |title=Political analysts call governor's seat 'a toss-up' after Evers decides to not run for a 3rd term |url=https://www.wbay.com/2025/07/25/political-analysts-call-governors-seat-toss-up-after-evers-decides-not-run-3rd-term/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250730005208/https://www.wbay.com/2025/07/25/political-analysts-call-governors-seat-toss-up-after-evers-decides-not-run-3rd-term/ |archive-date=July 30, 2025 |access-date=March 5, 2026 |website=WBAY.com}}</ref>

==Democratic primary==
=== Governor ===
Tony Evers's decision not to seek re-election triggered a competitive Democratic primary.<ref name=BauerAP /> The Associated Press described the process leading up to the August 11 primary as chaotic.<ref name=BauerAP>{{cite web | title=Wisconsin's 2026 primary election arrives with high-profile races for governor, two congressional seats | url=https://pbswisconsin.org/news-item/wisconsins-2026-primary-election-arrives-with-high-profile-races-for-governor-two-congressional-seats/ }}</ref> Lieutenant Governor Sara Rodriguez amassed support as a centrist candidate until she dropped out in mid-July, prompting Milwaukee County executive David Crowley to re-enter the race ten days after withdrawing.<ref name=BauerAP /> The race became a showdown between Crowley, who was endorsed by Evers and other establishment figures, and state representative Francesca Hong, a [[democratic socialist]].<ref name=BauerAP /> Crowley narrowly won the Democratic nomination in an [[upset victory]] over Hong, as polls showed him trailing Hong by nearly 20 points just a week earlier.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Wagner |first1=Bayliss |last2=Igielnik |first2=Ruth |date=2026-08-12 |title=Why Were Polls So Wrong in the Wisconsin Governor's Race? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/12/us/politics/crowley-hong-wisconsin-governor-primary-polls.html |access-date=2026-08-12 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Republican primary ==

Tom Tiffany, a member of the [[House Freedom Caucus]], was expected to obtain the nomination without meaningful challenge.<ref>{{cite web | title=Wisconsin's Democratic showdown between Francesca Hong and David Crowley and more races to watch today - CBS News | website=[[CBS News]] | date=August 11, 2026 | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/wisconsin-governor-democratic-primary-francesca-hong-david-crowley-minnesota-graham/ }}</ref> Tiffany received an endorsement from Donald Trump, who Tiffany believes may have won the 2020 presidential election.<ref name=KremerWPR>{{cite web | title=As the Democratic primary heats up, Republican Tom Tiffany has campaigned for governor on his own terms | date=July 20, 2026 | url=https://www.wpr.org/news/republican-tom-tiffany-campaign-wisconsin-governor-primary-2026 }}</ref> As a member of the federal House, Tiffany objected to the certification of Pennsylvania's and Arizona's electoral results on January 6, 2021, and was prevented from objecting to Wisconsin's electoral results because the [[January 6 attack|Capitol building was stormed by pro-Trump insurgents]].<ref name=KremerWPR /> He has kept mention of Trump to a minimum during his primary campaign.<ref name=KremerWPR />

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Alaska''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Alaska]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Dan Sullivan (U.S. senator)|Dan S. Sullivan]] is seeking a third term. He is being challenged by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former congresswoman [[Mary Peltola]]. The election will be conducted under [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]].

A [[nonpartisan primary]] election was held on August 18 to determine the four candidates in the general election. Peltola and Sullivan were the first to advance with 49.5% and 41.4% of the vote respectively, followed by Republican former U.S. Forest Service employee Daniel J. Sullivan and Republican perennial candidate Gerald Heikes.

Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy has drawn allegations of being a [[spoiler candidacy|spoiler]] due to having the same name as the incumbent, but was allowed to remain on the ballot by the state Supreme Court and listed as unaffiliated to help avoid confusion. The [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]] filed a [[United States v. Alaska|lawsuit]] to block the election results if Dan S. Sullivan loses by a small margin, arguing this outcome could result from him sharing a name with another candidate.<ref>{{cite news |last = Barrett, Devlin; Browning, Kellen |first = |title = On Trump's Order, Justice Dept. Seeks to Block Alaska Vote if Republican Loses |newspaper = The New York Times |date = October 23, 2026 |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/justice-dept-alaska-senate-race-sullivan.html?smid=url-share |accessdate = October 24, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last = Timms, Mariah; Radnofsky, Louise; Wise, Lindsay |first =  |title = Trump Says He Directed Justice Department to Sue Alaska Over Senate Race |newspaper = The Wall Street Journal  |date = October 23, 2026 |url = https://www.wsj.com/politics/elections/justice-department-sues-to-block-alaska-senate-results-if-gop-candidate-loses-c2597f6c |accessdate = October 24, 2026}}</ref>

Democrats have not won a Senate election in Alaska since [[2008 United States Senate election in Alaska|2008]].

==Primary election==
Under Alaska's voting system, all candidates, regardless of party, run on the same primary ballot. The top four candidates in the primary advance to the general election, which is then conducted using [[ranked-choice voting]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Top-four primary |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Top-four_primary |website=Ballotpedia |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Background ===
Incumbent Republican [[Dan Sullivan (U.S. senator)|Dan Sullivan]] announced his run for re-election in early 2025. He was first elected in [[2014 United States Senate election in Alaska|2014]], defeating [[Mark Begich]], the most recent Democrat to represent Alaska in the [[U.S. Senate]]. He was last re-elected in [[2020 United States Senate election in Alaska|2020]], prior to the implementation of Alaska's ranked-choice voting system.<ref name=":0" /> Facing few obvious swing state targets to regain the Senate majority in [[2026 United States Senate elections|2026]], Democrats began looking towards more Republican-leaning states, such as [[2026 United States Senate special election in Ohio|Ohio]] and [[2026 United States Senate election in Texas|Texas]], as potential targets.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Neukam |first=Stephen |date=2025-08-06 |title=Senate Democrats' top remaining targets for the 2026 midterms |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/08/06/senate-democrats-2026-elections-candidates |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Axios |language=en}}</ref> Among these states was Alaska, where Senate Democratic leader [[Chuck Schumer]] heavily courted former U.S. Representative [[Mary Peltola]], the last Democrat to win any statewide election in Alaska, to run for Senate.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nichols |first=Hans |last2=Neukam |first2=Stephen |date=2025-08-13 |title=Scoop: Schumer courts Peltola for Alaska Senate race |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/08/13/alaska-senate-peltola-schumer-sullivan |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Axios |language=en}}</ref> Peltola narrowly lost her congressional seat in 2024, and had considered running for either Senate or [[2026 Alaska gubernatorial election|governor]], but she ultimately decided to enter the Senate race in early 2026, setting up the race between her and Sullivan.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Herz |first=Nathaniel |date=2025-07-15 |title=Dems are 'salivating' over a Peltola bid for Senate, but Alaska governor race could be ‘wide open' |url=https://alaskabeacon.com/2025/07/15/dems-are-salivating-over-a-peltola-bid-for-senate-but-alaska-governor-race-could-be-wide-open/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Alaska Beacon |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Thiessen |first=Mark |date=2026-01-12 |title=Democrat Mary Peltola, barrier-breaking ex-Alaska congresswoman, is challenging Republican Dan Sullivan in Senate race |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrat-mary-peltola-barrier-breaking-ex-alaska-congresswoman-is-challenging-republican-dan-sullivan-in-senate-race |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=PBS News |language=en-us}}</ref>

====Daniel James Sullivan====
'''Daniel James Sullivan Jr.''' (born June 1957)<ref name=Bohrer2026a>{{Cite web |last=Bohrer |first=Becky |date=2026-06-09 |title=The other Dan Sullivan in Alaska's US Senate race says candidacy was ‘my choice,' not a sham |url=https://apnews.com/article/alaska-senate-dan-sullivan-peltola-68ca38749253c6bf52d13051fda01251 |access-date=2026-06-27 |website=AP News |language=en|quote=}}</ref> is a retired teacher and [[United States Forest Service]] employee from [[Petersburg, Alaska]], who filed to run as a Republican three days before the filing deadline.<ref name=SullivanPressRelease>{{Cite press release |title=Dan Sullivan Challenges Dan Sullivan for U.S. Senate Seat: Urges Alaskans to defeat incumbent, elect a Sullivan who Stands up for Alaska |date=2026-05-29 |publisher=Sullivan for Senate |url=https://www.sullivanforsenate.com/press |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260529204149/https://www.sullivanforsenate.com/press |archive-date=2026-05-29}}</ref> In an interview with the ''[[Petersburg Pilot]]'', Sullivan stated that he had been considering running against the incumbent U.S. senator for 12 years, and remarked that he finally decided to run after the Senator's lack of opposition to the [[Anti-Weaponization Fund]].<ref name=Morrow2026a /> Senator Sullivan said this was "an effort to confuse Alaskans" and "dirty politics" by Democrats, calling Dan J. Sullivan a "sham candidate".  This was denied by Dan J. Sullivan, who called himself a "pragmatic Republican centrist". It was also denied by Mary Peltola's campaign, the Alaska Democratic Party, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Senator Sullivan threatened legal action if the [[Lieutenant Governor of Alaska]] did not remove Dan J. Sullivan from the ballot.<ref name="cnn dan sullivan">{{Cite web |last1=Raju |first1=Ranu |last2=Fayez |first2=Aleena |date=2026-06-07 |title=GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan is raising alarms about an eleventh-hour challenger: Dan J. Sullivan |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/06/07/politics/dan-sullivan-alaska-senate-ballot |access-date=2026-06-07 |website=CNN |language=en-us}}</ref>

Dan J. Sullivan grew up in the [[Chicago metropolitan area]], and has lived in [[Southeast Alaska]] since 1980. He worked for the [[United States Forest Service]] in his early career before beginning a career as an elementary school teacher.<ref name=Bohrer2026a /> Sullivan taught in elementary schools for over 20 years before retiring.<ref name=Heckart2026a>{{Cite web |last=Heckart |first=Taylor |date=2026-06-04 |title=It's no joke: A second Dan Sullivan says he really does want to be Alaska's next senator |url=https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-06-04/its-no-joke-a-second-dan-sullivan-says-he-really-does-want-to-be-alaskas-next-senator |access-date=2026-06-27 |work=Alaska Public Media}}</ref> He was appointed to the city of Petersburg's Public Safety Advisory Board in December 2021.<ref name=Heckart2026a /> He served in that position until October 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dan Sullivan |url=https://www.petersburgak.gov/directory-listing/dan-sullivan |access-date=2026-06-27 |website=Petersburg, Alaska |language=en}}</ref> He stated that he was a member of the [[Alaskan Independence Party]] from when he moved to Alaska in 1980 until the party's dissolution in late 2025.<ref name=Heckart2026a /><ref name=Morrow2026a>{{Cite web |last=Morrow |first=Caleb |date=2026-06-04 |title=Petersburg's Dan Sullivan challenges Senator Dan Sullivan |url=HTTPS://www.petersburgpilot.com/story/2026/06/04/news/petersburgs-dan-sullivan-challenges-senator-dan-sullivan/15854.html |access-date=2026-06-27 |work=Petersburg Pilot}}</ref> 

Sullivan's initial campaign announcement stated that he was "focused on unseating the incumbent, putting Alaska first, and restoring accountability, common sense, and public service to Washington, D.C."<ref name=SullivanPressRelease /> He later described his political philosophy as "a pragmatic Republican centrist" similar to [[Lisa Murkowski]], with influence from [[Rand Paul]].<ref name=Bohrer2026a /> Incumbent U.S. Senator Daniel Scott Sullivan argued in an early June 2026 interview with [[CNN]] that "[Daniel James Sullivan's] whole purpose of running is to confuse Alaskans, to make him, make them think – Alaskan voters – that somehow he's me, so they could rig the vote in favor of [[Mary Peltola]]."<ref name="cnn dan sullivan"/> An analysis of [[Federal Election Commission]] records by [[KTUU-TV]] showed that he had donated to Peltola's previous campaigns, including $100 in 2022 and $30 in 2024. KTUU reported that "That financial history is the extent of the documented link between the Petersburg Sullivan and the Peltola campaign."<ref name=CourtneySimon2026>{{Cite web |last1=Courtney |first1=Wil |last2=Simon |first2=Matthew |date=2026-06-13 |title=Two Dan Sullivans: Petersburg candidate poised for removal from ballot by state |url=https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/06/13/two-dan-sullivans-petersburg-candidate-poised-removal-ballot-by-state/ |access-date=2026-06-27 |work=KTUU-TV}}</ref> His initial press release and website design were supported by political strategist Amber Lee, who has previously worked with Democratic campaigns in Alaska.<ref name=Courtney2026a>{{Cite web |last=Courtney |first=Wil |date=2026-06-04 |title=Sullivan vs. Sullivan: Senator accuses Peltola of ‘rigging' election — but evidence of her involvement is unclear |url=https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/06/04/sullivan-vs-sullivan-senator-accuses-peltola-rigging-election-evidence-her-involvement-is-unclear/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |work=KTUU-TV}}</ref> Lee has publicly spoken in favor of Peltola's candidacy, including in a January 2026 interview with [[The Hill (newspaper)|''The Hill'']].<ref name=Courtney2026a /><ref name=ElissaSlotkin>{{Cite web |last=Mueller |first=Julia |date=2026-01-15 |title=Peltola's entrance in Alaska Senate race gives Democrats hope |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5689076-alaska-senate-race-democrats/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |work=The Hill}}</ref>

''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' reported that weeks before the election, polls showed that approximately one third of voters likely to vote in the primary election could not distinguish the two candidates.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Epstein |first=Reid J. |date=2014-08-13 |title=Alaska Election Offers Two Chances to Vote for Dan Sullivan |url=http://online.wsj.com/articles/alaska-election-offers-two-chances-to-vote-for-dan-sullivan-1407897002 |access-date=2026-06-27 |work=Wall Street Journal |issn=0099-9660}}</ref> Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy was the subject of legal debate, which {{As of|2026|6|27|df=US|lc=y}} advanced to the [[Alaska Supreme Court]].<ref name=Ruskin2026a>{{Cite web |last=Ruskin |first=Liz |date=2026-06-27 |title=Judge puts 2nd Dan Sullivan back on ballot in Alaska's U.S. Senate race |url=https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/2026-06-26/judge-puts-2nd-dan-sullivan-back-on-ballot-in-alaskas-u-s-senate-race |access-date=2026-06-27 |work=Alaska Public Media}}</ref> In its initial response to Sullivan's candidacy filing, the Alaska Division of Elections stated that Sullivan's name would appear on the ballot as "Sullivan, Dan J. (Registered Republican)."<ref name=Hanson2026a>{{Cite web |last=Hanson |first=Lars |date=2026-06-27 |title=Judge orders Petersburg's Dan J. Sullivan onto Alaska U.S. Senate primary ballot |url=https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/06/27/judge-orders-petersburgs-dan-j-sullivan-onto-alaska-us-senate-primary-ballot/ |access-date=2026-06-27 |work=[[KTUU-TV]]}}</ref>

An Alaskan election official ordered Sullivan's name removed from the ballot, as his candidacy "was not filed in order to declare an actual good-faith candidacy for the office of United States Senator, but was instead filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ruskin |first=Liz |date=2026-06-15 |title=Alaska Elections Division makes it official, says Dan J. Sullivan can't run against Sen. Dan S. Sullivan |url=https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/2026-06-15/alaska-elections-division-makes-it-official-says-dan-j-sullivan-cant-run-against-sen-dan-s-sullivan |access-date=2026-06-29 |work=Alaska Public Media}}</ref> a decision he appealed.<ref> https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5936869-dan-sullivan-ballot-challenge</ref> Anchorage Superior Court judge Thomas A. Matthews reversed the Division of Elections' decision to exclude Sullivan from the primary ballot on June 26. Matthews' decision ruled that the "good-faith" standard for ballot access was not supported by Alaska law, the Division of Elections' regulations, or [[Article One of the United States Constitution#Section 3: Senate|Article One, Section 3 of the United States Constitution]].<ref name=Hanson2026a /><ref name=Ruskin2026a /><ref name=DeMarban2026a>{{Cite web |last=DeMarban |first=Alex |date=2026-06-27 |title=Judge allows namesake challenger to Sen. Dan Sullivan to appear on Alaska ballot |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/06/26/superior-court-judge-rules-in-favor-of-namesake-challenger-to-sen-dan-sullivan/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |work=Anchorage Daily News}}</ref> On July 2 the [[Alaska Supreme Court]] affirmed the decision, ordering Sullivan's name to be listed on the August 18th primary ballot.<ref name="adn supreme court">{{Cite web |last=DeMarban |first=Alex |title=Alaska Supreme Court allows namesake challenger to U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan to appear on the ballot |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/06/29/alaska-supreme-court-rules-that-dan-j-sullivan-can-appear-on-the-ballot-against-sen-dan-sullivan/ |access-date=2026-07-02 |website=Anchorage Daily News}}</ref> The Division of Elections released a sample ballot that will distinguish between the two Sullivans by listing Dan J. Sullivan as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." and no party affiliation (despite Sullivan filing as a Republican) and identifying Dan S. Sullivan as the incumbent, which the DoE had not done for any other incumbent for at least 10 years.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/06/30/election-officials-sample-ballot-shows-how-they-seek-to-distinguish-two-dan-sullivans-in-us-senate-race/|title=Election officials' sample ballot shows how they seek to distinguish two Dan Sullivans in U.S. Senate race|first=Alex|last=DeMarban|date=July 1, 2026|work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}}</ref>

Daniel James Sullivan and Daniel Scott Sullivan are unrelated to each other, and are unrelated to former [[List of mayors of Anchorage, Alaska|Anchorage mayor]] [[Dan Sullivan (Anchorage mayor)|Daniel Albert Sullivan]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=DeMarban |first=Alex |title=Namesake challenger to Sen. Dan Sullivan remains defiant despite state investigation |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/06/10/namesake-challenger-to-sen-dan-sullivan-remains-defiant-despite-state-investigation/ |access-date=2026-06-27 |website=Anchorage Daily News|date=2026-06-10|quote=}}</ref>

=== Campaign ===
Peltola's entry into the race immediately made the race competitive, according to most predictors.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kondik |first=Kyle |date=2026-01-13 |title=Alaska Senate Race Comes Onto the Competitive Board with Peltola's Entry |url=https://centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/alaska-senate-race-comes-onto-the-competitive-board-with-peltolas-entry/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Sabato's Crystal Ball |language=en-US}}</ref> She still faces significant hurdles, such as Sullivan's incumbency and lack of a prominent Republican challenger, the unpopularity of the national Democratic Party in Alaska, and a reduction in cross-party support. [[Lisa Murkowski]], Alaska's other U.S. Senator and a noted [[moderate]] Republican, had endorsed Peltola in her [[2022 United States House of Representatives election in Alaska|2022]] and [[2024 United States House of Representatives election in Alaska|2024]] bids for U.S. House, but she endorsed Sullivan in this race instead.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-12 |title=Former Rep. Mary Peltola jumps into Alaska Senate race |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/peltola-alaska-senate-2026-midterms-00721596 |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}</ref> However, as Trump's unpopularity grew, especially amidst the [[2026 Iran war]], Peltola's chances of flipping the Senate seat grew.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beacon |first=Alaska |date=2026-06-18 |title=Alaska among 9 states to decide if Dems flip US Senate |url=https://www.juneauindependent.com/post/alaska-among-9-states-to-decide-if-dems-flip-us-senate |access-date=2026-08-11 |website=Juneau Independent |language=en}}</ref>

Over the course of the primary campaign, a [[super PAC]] called Fair Deal Alaska registered to a [[virtual office]] address in [[Wasilla, Alaska|Wasilla]] spent around $770,000 promoting Green Party candidate [[Richard Grayson (writer)|Richard Grayson]] and Democrat [[Carol Hafner]] in what the ''[[Alaska Beacon]]'' and the ''[[Anchorage Daily News]]'' described as an apparent attempt to dilute support for Peltola in the general election.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite news |last=Samuels |first=Iris |date=August 13, 2026 |title=Millions pour into Alaska to boost fringe U.S. Senate candidates |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/13/millions-pour-into-alaska-to-boost-fringe-us-senate-candidates/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260814003724/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/13/millions-pour-into-alaska-to-boost-fringe-us-senate-candidates/ |archive-date=August 14, 2026 |access-date=August 13, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}}</ref> Another PAC called American Democracy Project spent over $240,000 to promote Democrat David Leslie.<ref name=":5" /> A similar group called Right for Alaska spent $1.2 million promoting Republican Gerald Heikes and [[Alaskan Party]] candidate Earl "Skip" Southworth, who were considered more likely to draw support from Dan S. Sullivan.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Herz |first=Nathaniel |date=August 3, 2026 |title=As Alaska's U.S. Senate campaign heats up, super PACs boost out-of-state candidates |url=https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/03/as-alaskas-u-s-senate-campaign-heats-up-super-pacs-boost-out-of-state-candidates/ |work=[[Alaska Beacon]]}}</ref><ref name=":5" />

Both Grayson and Leslie expressed concern about the outside spending on their behalf to the ''Anchorage Daily News''. Grayson—a [[satirical candidate]] living in Arizona—said that he supported Peltola and pledged to withdraw if he advanced to the general election.<ref name=":5" />

== General election ==
===Campaign===
Democratic candidate David Leslie placed fourth in the primary. Leslie, a [[democratic socialism|democratic socialist]] who had criticized Peltola's stances on the [[Gaza genocide]], environmental protection, and actions by [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE), initially said he would not withdraw but later reversed course, citing "pressure from not just the Alaska Democratic leadership, but many different institutions of power".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Herz |first1=Nathaniel |title=This Democratic Socialist could cost Mary Peltola votes in November. But he says he'd actually boost her. |url=https://anchoragepress.com/this-democratic-socialist-could-cost-mary-peltola-votes-in-november-but-he-says-hed-actually-boost-her/ |access-date=September 27, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Press]] |date=August 21, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260903140950/https://anchoragepress.com/this-democratic-socialist-could-cost-mary-peltola-votes-in-november-but-he-says-hed-actually-boost-her/ |archive-date=September 3, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="DropsOut">{{cite news |last1=DeMarban |first1=Alex |title=Alaska's 4th-place U.S. Senate finisher drops out, elevating GOP candidate to ballot |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/01/alaskas-4th-place-us-senate-finisher-drops-out-elevating-gop-candidate-to-ballot/ |access-date=September 27, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 1, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260922113331/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/01/alaskas-4th-place-us-senate-finisher-drops-out-elevating-gop-candidate-to-ballot/ |archive-date=September 22, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Leslie's withdrawal allowed Republican [[perennial candidate]] Gerald Heikes to advance to the general election.<ref name="DropsOut"/>

On September 23, ''[[The New York Times]]'' published allegations from anonymous aides who had worked for Peltola's congressional office and Senate campaign. The report included text messages showing that Peltola had used an ableist slur and expressed hope that a board member of a local [[Planned Parenthood]] chapter "dies of a botched abortion". The anonymous aides also claimed that Peltola had used a homophobic slur, shoved a congressional aide, and ordered congressional aides to feed crickets to her family's pet chameleon. The Peltola campaign claimed that some of the allegations were false or exaggerated, and said that many of the alleged outbursts could be attributed to stress from the death of Peltola's husband and mother while she was serving in Congress.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Browning |first1=Kellen |title=Angry Outbursts, Slurs, and Firings: Tumult Rocks a Key Senate Campaign |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/politics/mary-peltola-alaska-senate-race.html |access-date=September 27, 2026 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 23, 2026}}</ref> The [[Alaska Democratic Party]] and Republican senator [[Lisa Murkowski]] also defended Peltola, while Senator Sullivan and the [[Alaska Republican Party]] condemned her. Alaskan political analysts and operatives interviewed by the ''[[Anchorage Daily News]]'' did not believe the allegations would have a major impact on the election.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kanagy |first1=Mary |title=How ex-staffers' allegations of hostile behavior by Peltola might affect Alaska's key U.S. Senate race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/26/how-ex-staffers-allegations-of-hostile-behavior-by-peltola-might-affect-alaskas-key-us-senate-race/ |access-date=September 27, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 26, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260926191309/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/26/how-ex-staffers-allegations-of-hostile-behavior-by-peltola-might-affect-alaskas-key-us-senate-race/ |archive-date=September 26, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In late October, a suit was filed by the Trump administration attempting to block certification of the election if Dan S. Sullivan loses in the election. A professor of law has suggested that the suit seems to lack merit and stated that the "statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification" and that the "lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month".<ref>Riccardi, Nicholas, ''[https://apnews.com/article/alaska-senate-race-sullivan-name-lawsuit-certification-d8f4a3c7b5247cc427a05f796d7c0d82 Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaska Senate race]'',  The Associated Press, October 23, 2026 </ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Barrett |first=Devlin |date=2026-10-23 |title=The Justice Department argues that confusion over the Alaska race's two Dan Sullivans could taint a narrow result. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/23/us/midterm-elections-trump |access-date=2026-10-23 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> [[Vanita Gupta]], a former [[United States Associate Attorney General|associate US attorney general]], had similar views on the lack of merit, basing it on the power granted to states to determine their own elections.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tierney Sneed, Ethan Cohen |date=2026-10-23 |title=Trump DOJ sues to block Alaska US Senate results if Republican incumbent loses {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/23/politics/doj-sues-alaska-dan-sullivan-us-senate |access-date=2026-10-23 |work=CNN |language=en}}</ref>

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Alabama''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Alabama]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Congressman [[Barry Moore (American politician)|Barry Moore]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] attorney Everett Wess are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Tommy Tuberville]] is not seeking a second term in order to [[2026 Alabama gubernatorial election|run for governor]].<ref name="Tuberville" />

[[Primary election]]s were held on May 19, which were followed by [[Two round system|runoffs]] for both parties on June 16 after no candidates received a majority.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cason |first1=Mike |title=The date of Alabama's landmark 2026 primary elections has changed: Here's why |url=https://www.al.com/politics/2025/05/the-date-of-alabamas-landmark-2026-primary-elections-has-changed-heres-why.html |website=AL.com |date=May 12, 2025 |access-date=1 August 2025}}</ref> Moore won the Republican runoff with 55.8% of the vote over businessman Jared Hudson and Wess won the Democratic runoff with 54.6% of the vote over businessman Dakarai Larriett.

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Colorado''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Colorado]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[John Hickenlooper]] is seeking a second term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state senator [[Mark Baisley]].

[[Primary elections]] were held on June 30. In the Democratic primary, Hickenlooper won the nomination with 52.8% of the vote over state senator [[Julie Gonzales]]. Baisley was the only candidate to receive at least 30% support from the Republican State Assembly, allowing him to advance to the primary unopposed.

== Background ==
While Colorado was once considered a swing state, it has shifted significantly to the left over the past decade and is now regarded as solidly Democratic at both the federal and state levels. Democrats currently hold all statewide offices, both U.S. Senate seats, and strong majorities in both chambers of the [[Colorado General Assembly]], while the state's U.S. House delegation is evenly split. In [[2014 United States Senate election in Colorado|2014]], Republican [[Cory Gardner]] narrowly defeated Democratic incumbent [[Mark Udall]] for the U.S. Senate. As the state continued trending Democratic, Gardner—then the only Republican holding major statewide office—lost his [[2020 United States Senate election in Colorado|2020 re-election]] bid to Democrat John Hickenlooper by a significant margin.<ref>{{cite news |last=Frank |first=John |date=November 4, 2020 |title=John Hickenlooper easily defeats Cory Gardner in Colorado's U.S. Senate race |url=https://coloradosun.com/2020/11/03/cory-gardner-john-hickenlooper-colorado-results/ |access-date=March 12, 2026 |website=The Colorado Sun |language=en-US}}</ref> In late 2024, Hickenlooper announced he would seek re-election but indicated that the campaign would be his final run for the Senate.<ref name="CBS-22A">{{cite news |last1=Sarles |first1=Jesse |title=Sen. John Hickenlooper says his re-election bid in two years will be his last campaign for Senate |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/colorado/news/john-hickenlooper-run-senate-again-2026-final-term/ |publisher=[[CBS News]] |access-date=December 6, 2024 |date=August 22, 2024}}</ref>

== Democratic primary ==
=== Candidates ===
To move forward to the primary, candidates had to petition onto the ballot or achieve 30% or more at the [[Colorado Democratic Party]] State Assembly. John Hickenlooper was the only candidate to petition onto the primary ballot. All other candidates went through the State Assembly process. [[Julie Gonzales]] was the only candidate to achieve 30% or more.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=[[Colorado Democratic Party]] |access-date=March 28, 2026 |url=https://www.coloradodems.org/press/colorado-democratic-party-concludes-2026-state-assembly-announces-results |title=Colorado Democratic Party Concludes 2026 State Assembly, Announces Results}}</ref>

{{Elections in Florida}}
The '''2026 United States Senate special election in Florida''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Florida]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] appointee [[Ashley Moody]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] State Representative [[Angie Nixon]] are the nominees for their respective parties. The winner will complete the term won in [[2022 United States Senate election in Florida|2022]] by [[Marco Rubio]], who resigned in 2025 to become [[United States Secretary of State|secretary of state]].

After being appointed to the seat, Moody won the Republican nomination against minimal opposition. [[Alex Vindman]], the former director of European Affairs for the [[United States National Security Council|National Security Council]], was considered the Democratic frontrunner and held a significant fundraising advantage during the August 18 primary, but Nixon won the nomination with 56.1% of the vote in a major upset.

Democrats have not won a Senate race in Florida since [[2012 United States Senate election in Florida|2012]].

== Democratic primary ==
===Campaign===
[[Angie Nixon]], a [[Democratic Party (United States)#Progressives|progressive Democrat]] and a member of the [[Democratic Socialists of America]], won the nomination over [[Alex Vindman]], despite Vindman having amassed $16.3 million in campaign funding compared to Nixon's $975,000.<ref name="NBC Dixon 2026-08-18">{{cite news|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/angie-nixon-winner-florida-senate-primary-democrat-alex-vindman-moody-rcna593255|title=Democratic socialist Angie Nixon upsets Alex Vindman in Florida's Democratic Senate primary|publisher=NBC News|date=2026-08-18}}</ref><ref name="Guardian Luscombe 2026-08-18">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/18/angie-nixon-alex-vindman-florida-results|title=Democratic socialist Angie Nixon clinches surprise primary win in Florida US Senate race|work=The Guardian|date=2026-08-18}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Peters |first=Cameron |date=2026-09-06 |title=Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026? |url=https://www.vox.com/america-actually/502027/angie-nixon-florida-democratic-senate-nominee-progressive |access-date=2026-09-19 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Mazzei |first=Patricia |date=2026-09-13 |title=She’s Been Fighting for 20 Years. Has Angie Nixon’s Moment Come? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/us/politics/angie-nixon-florida-senate.html |access-date=2026-09-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Nixon campaigned on [[universal healthcare]], free [[childcare]], and a national [[rent freeze]].<ref name="Bloomberg Smith 2026-08-18">{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-19/progressive-nixon-downs-vindman-in-florida-senate-primary-race|title=Progressive Nixon Downs Vindman in Florida Senate Primary Race|work=Bloomberg|date=2026-08-18}}</ref> Nixon had criticized Vindman for having only recently moved to Florida; Vindman ignored her and attacked the Republican candidate, Moody.<ref name="NBC Dixon 2026-08-18" /> The result was considered a major upset.<ref name="NBC Dixon 2026-08-18" /><ref name="Guardian Luscombe 2026-08-18" />

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Georgia''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Jon Ossoff]] is seeking a second term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] congressman [[Mike Collins (politician)|Mike Collins]]. A [[two-round system|runoff election]] is scheduled for December 1 if no candidate gets a majority.<ref>{{cite news|last=Bluestein|first=Greg|title=Libertarians won't be on the ballot in Georgia, meaning likely no runoffs|newspaper=[[Atlanta Journal-Constitution]]|date=July 11, 2026|url=https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/07/libertarians-wont-be-on-the-ballot-in-georgia-meaning-likely-no-runoffs/|url-access=subscription|access-date=September 15, 2026}}</ref>

[[Primary election]]s were held on May 19, with Ossoff running unopposed for the Democratic nomination. No candidate obtained a majority in the first round of the Republican primary between Collins, former football coach [[Derek Dooley (American football)|Derek Dooley]], and congressman [[Buddy Carter]], leading to a runoff between Collins and Dooley on June 16. After receiving an endorsement from President [[Donald Trump]], Collins was nominated with 55.5% of the vote.

This is one of two Democratic-held Senate seats up for election in 2026 in a state won by Trump in [[2024 United States presidential election|2024]], along with [[2026 United States Senate election in Michigan|Michigan]].
{{TOC limit|3}}

== Background ==
Georgia is considered to be a [[Purple state|purple or swing state]] at the federal level. It was a top battleground state in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Georgia|2020]] and [[2024 United States presidential election in Georgia|2024]] presidential elections.<ref>{{cite news |title=The 2024 Swing States: Why Georgia Could Sway the Presidential Election |url=https://www.usnews.com/news/elections/articles/the-2024-swing-states-why-georgia-could-sway-the-presidential-election |access-date=February 7, 2026 |publisher=US News |date=November 5, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Georgia emerges as a major 2020 battleground state |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/07/23/georgia-2020-democrats-bottoms-stacey-abrams-biden-379372 |access-date=February 7, 2026 |publisher=Politico |date=July 23, 2020}}</ref>

Both parties have seen success in the state in recent years. The state backed Joe Biden by 0.24% and Donald Trump by 2.2%, respectively, in 2020 and 2024. Democrats hold both of Georgia's [[List of United States senators from Georgia|U.S. Senate seats]]. Republicans control all statewide executive offices,{{efn|While Democrats did flip 2 seats in the [[2025 Georgia Public Service Commission special election]], Republicans still hold a 3–2 majority.}} control both chambers of the legislature, and hold a majority in Georgia's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] delegation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-06 |title=2 Republican incumbents lose in Georgia House, but overall Democratic gains are limited |url=https://apnews.com/article/georgia-house-senate-legislature-democrats-republicans-296a4233e0b360ec60f1adc2f4174925 |access-date=2024-12-07 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

As one of only two seats up held by a Democrat in a state that voted for Trump in 2024, the race is expected to be competitive.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Democrats Rush to Regroup in the Southern Battlegrounds |website=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 25, 2024 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/25/us/politics/democrats-georgia-north-carolina-trump-harris-campaign.html}}</ref>

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Iowa''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Iowa]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] congresswoman [[Ashley Hinson]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state representative [[Josh Turek]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Joni Ernst]] is not seeking a third term.<ref name="ErnstRetire"/>

[[Primary elections]] were held on June 2. Endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], Hinson won the Republican nomination with 73.9% of the vote over former state senator [[Jim Carlin (politician)|Jim Carlin]]. Turek won the Democratic nomination with 62.6% of the vote over state senator [[Zach Wahls]].

Democrats have not won a Senate election in Iowa since [[2008 United States Senate election in Iowa|2008]]. This is Iowa's first open Senate election to be held concurrently with an [[2026 Iowa gubernatorial election|open gubernatorial election]] since [[1968 United States Senate election in Iowa|1968]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Could Iowa Democrats Win 2026's Gubernatorial and US Senate Races? |url=https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2026/06/03/could-iowa-democrats-win-2026s-gubernatorial-and-us-senate-races/ |work=Smart Politics |date=June 3, 2026 |access-date=June 6, 2026}}</ref>

== Background ==
Since voting for President [[Barack Obama]] in both [[2008 United States presidential election in Iowa|2008]] and [[2012 United States presidential election in Iowa|2012]], Iowa has trended increasingly Republican and is now considered a moderately to strongly [[red state]] at the federal and state level. Republican nominee [[Donald Trump]] won Iowa in [[2020 United States presidential election in Iowa|2020]] by 8 percentage points, and in [[2024 United States presidential election in Iowa|2024]] grew his margin to 13 percentage points. Republicans control every statewide executive office (except the [[Iowa Auditor of State|state auditor's office]]), majorities in both chambers of the [[Iowa State Legislature|state legislature]], and the entire congressional delegation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ta |first=Linh |date=2024-11-06 |title=Iowa remains solidly Republican |url=https://www.axios.com/local/des-moines/2024/11/06/iowa-remains-red-despite-iowa-poll-republicans |access-date=2024-12-13 |website=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |language=en}}</ref>  Incumbent Senator Joni Ernst was [[2014 United States Senate election in Iowa|first elected]] as part of the [[2014 United States Senate elections|2014]] [[Wave elections in the United States|red wave]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barrett |first=Ted |date=2014-11-05 |title=Joni Ernst wins Iowa Senate race |url=https://www.cnn.com/2014/11/05/politics/iowa-senate-digital/index.html |access-date=2024-12-13 |website=[[CNN]] |language=en}}</ref> and was reelected in [[2020 United States Senate election in Iowa|2020]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pfannenstiel |first=Brianne |title='Six more years!': Republican U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst wins reelection, beating Democrat Theresa Greenfield |url=https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/news/politics/2020/11/02/iowa-election-results-us-senate-theresa-greenfield-joni-ernst/5997461002/ |access-date=December 13, 2024 |date=November 2, 2020 |website=[[The Des Moines Register]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

In the latter half of her second term, Ernst came under increasing pressure.  In December 2024, she faced pushback from Republicans for her skepticism of [[Pete Hegseth]]'s nomination for [[United States Secretary of Defense|Secretary of Defense]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Copp |first1=Tara |title=Sen. Joni Ernst wants to hear from Hegseth on sex assault in the military and women in combat |url=https://apnews.com/article/ernst-hegseth-nominee-trump-vetting-assault-pentagon-138c79c9199c8525d43b77417674d81e |access-date=17 October 2026 |agency=Associated Press |date=December 7, 2024}}</ref>  She later sparked controversy for replying "we are all going to die" when a constituent confronted her for deaths that could be caused by cuts to [[Medicaid]] and [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program|SNAP]], which she supported as part of the [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=MSN |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/were-all-going-to-die-gop-fumbles-defense-of-medicaid-cuts/ar-AA1FXvi2 |access-date=2025-06-03 |website=www.msn.com}}</ref> 

In September 2025, Ernst announced that she would not seek reelection, officially citing family obligations, although her decision was interpreted in light of previous controversies.  The resulting open seat was expected to make the race more competitive.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Opsahl |first1=Robin |title=U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst announces she will not seek reelection |url=https://iowacapitaldispatch.com/2025/09/02/u-s-sen-joni-ernst-announces-she-will-not-seek-reelection/ |access-date=17 October 2026 |work=Iowa Capital Dispatch |agency=Iowa Capital Dispatch |date=2 September 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=The Associated Press |title=Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa confirms she will not run for reelection in 2026 |url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2025/09/02/sen-joni-ernst-of-iowa-confirms-she-will-not-run-for-reelection-in-2026 |website=MPR News |access-date=17 October 2026 |language=en |date=2 September 2025}}</ref>

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Idaho''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Idaho]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Jim Risch]] is seeking a fourth term. Former state representative [[Todd Achilles]] is running as an [[Independent politician|independent]]. 

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 19.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 26, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|url-status=live|access-date=September 27, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref> Risch won the Republican nomination with 67.3% of the vote, facing minimal opposition. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nomination was won by realtor David Roth, who was the nominee in [[2022 United States Senate election in Idaho|2022]], but after Achilles entered the race in July with the support of Democratic leaders, Roth withdrew near the end of the month.<ref name="Roth">{{cite web|url=https://idahocapitalsun.com/2026/07/28/idaho-democrat-david-roth-ends-campaign-for-us-senate-seat-held-by-risch/|title=Idaho Democrat David Roth ends campaign for US Senate seat held by Risch|last=Guido|first=Laura|date=July 28, 2026|access-date=July 28, 2026|website=[[States Newsroom|Idaho Capital Sun]]}}</ref>

Idaho is considered a [[red state]].<ref>{{cite web |last = |first = |title = The Road To Red: How One Political Party Came To Dominate Idaho |website = NPR/Bosie State Public Radio |date = |url = https://www.boisestatepublicradio.org/the-road-to-red-how-one-political-party-came-to-dominate-idaho |accessdate = October 21, 2026}}</ref> It is one of three states (along with [[2026 United States Senate election in Nebraska|Nebraska]] and [[2026 United States Senate election in South Dakota|South Dakota]]) in the [[2026 United States Senate elections|2026 Senate election cycle]] where the Democratic nominee has withdrawn from the race.<ref>{{cite news |last = Shane Goldmacher |first = Shane Goldmacher |title = Democrat Quits Senate Race in South Dakota, Clearing Way for Independent |newspaper = The New York Times |date = August 4, 2026 |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/04/us/politics/julian-beaudion-drops-out-south-dakota.html |accessdate = October 12, 2026}}</ref> Republicans have not lost a Senate race in Idaho since [[1974 United States Senate election in Idaho|1974]].<ref name="IdahoSenators">{{cite web |title=Idaho Senators |url=https://www.senate.gov/states/ID/senators.htm |website=[[United States Senate]] |access-date=October 24, 2026}}</ref><ref name="DemocraticPropsects">{{cite web |last1=Gonzales |first1=Nathan |title=Idaho Senate: Democratic Prospects Still Slim |url=https://insideelections.com/idaho-senate-democratic-prospects-still-slim/ |website=[[Inside Elections]] |access-date=October 24, 2026 |date=August 27, 2007 |quote= The last Democrat to win a U.S. Senate race was legendary Sen. Frank Church (D) in 1974. But he lost reelection six years later.}}</ref>

== General election ==
=== Campaign ===
On July 8, 2026, the Ada County Democratic Central Committee sent Roth a letter giving him until August 12 to prove that his campaign "has turned a corner" by raising $50,000 and producing a campaign plan, or the committee would consider endorsing independent candidate Todd Achilles instead. The committee said it was concerned that Roth's campaign was "not positioned to meet the moment” and argued that "we can't afford to let this moment slip away in the best political environment Idaho has seen in decades." Roth called the demands "completely ridiculous" and said he had no intention of complying, while accusing local Democratic leaders of trying to force him out of the race in favor of Achilles.<ref>{{cite news |last=Donovan Smith |first=Orion |title=Idaho They think Jim Risch could be beaten, but they aren't sure they want a Democrat to run for Senate |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/jul/18/idaho-democrats-think-jim-risch-could-be-beaten-bu/ |access-date=July 25, 2026 |work=[[The Spokesman-Review]] |date=July 18, 2026}}</ref> On July 28, Roth announced he would drop out of the race.<ref name="Roth"/>

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Illinois''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Illinois]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] lieutenant governor [[Juliana Stratton]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former state party chair [[Don Tracy]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Democratic incumbent [[Dick Durbin]] is not seeking a sixth term.

Primary elections were held on March 17. Supported by Governor [[JB Pritzker]], Stratton won the Democratic nomination with 40.4% of the vote over Congressman [[Raja Krishnamoorthi]] and Congresswoman [[Robin Kelly]]. Tracy won the Republican nomination with 40% of the vote over attorney Jeannie Evans.

This will be the first open Senate election in Illinois since [[2010 United States Senate elections in Illinois|2010]]. Republicans have not won a Senate election in Illinois since that race.

== Democratic primary ==
On April 23, 2025, incumbent Senator [[Dick Durbin]], who has held the seat since 1997, announced he would not seek re-election.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 23, 2025|last=Pecorin |first=Allison |title=Sen. Dick Durbin announces retirement after decades in Congress |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/sen-dick-durbin-announces-retirement-after-decades-congress/story?id=121089205 |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=ABC News |language=en}}</ref> The following day, [[Lieutenant Governor of Illinois|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Juliana Stratton]] launched her campaign with the immediate endorsement of [[Governor of Illinois|Governor]] [[JB Pritzker]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Juliana Stratton Launches Campaign for U.S. Senate, Promising to Center 'Middle Class' |url=https://news.wttw.com/2025/04/24/juliana-stratton-launches-campaign-us-senate-promising-center-middle-class |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=WTTW News}}</ref>

[[File:Dick Durbin 117th Congress portrait (1) (crop).jpeg|left|thumb|211x211px|Incumbent Senator [[Dick Durbin]]]]

Reports soon emerged that Pritzker and his allies were attempting to discourage other prominent Democrats from entering the race, particularly [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. Representatives]] [[Raja Krishnamoorthi]], [[Robin Kelly]], and [[Lauren Underwood]],<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ahern |first1=Mary Ann |last2=Schmidt|first2=Rose |date=2025-05-01 |title=Sources: Pritzker team calls congresswoman 'damaged goods,' seeking to stop potential Senate run |url=https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/chicago-politics/sources-pritzker-calls-congresswoman-damaged-goods-senate/3735712/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=NBC Chicago |language=en-US}}</ref> though Pritzker denied the claims.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kapos |first=Shia |date=2025-05-02 |title=Senate race's sharp elbows |url=https://www.politico.com/newsletters/illinois-playbook/2025/05/02/senate-races-sharp-elbows-00323163 |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=Politico |language=en}}</ref> Kelly announced her candidacy on May 6,<ref name=":0" /> followed by Krishnamoorthi the next day,<ref name=":1" /> while Underwood declined to run and instead sought re-election to the House.<ref name=":3" />

By July, Krishnamoorthi led the field in fundraising with roughly $21 million. Each of the top candidates secured significant endorsements: Stratton from suburban Democrats, state legislative leaders, and Senator [[Tammy Duckworth]]; Krishnamoorthi from local suburban officials; and Kelly from members of the [[Congressional Black Caucus]] and [[LGBTQ people|LGBT]] advocacy groups.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ahern |first1=Mary Ann |last2=Schmidt |first2=Rose |date=2025-07-14 |title=In heated race, who has the advantage in seeking Sen. Dick Durbin's seat |url=https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/who-has-the-advantage-in-the-race-for-dick-durbins-senate-seat/3789209/ |access-date=2025-07-16 |website=[[WMAQ-TV]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

Krishnamoorthi emphasized his experience on the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] and focused on foreign policy and economic mobility,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Szalinski |first=Ben |date=2025-07-14 |title=Economic mobility top priority of Krishnamoorthi's Senate campaign |url=https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/economic-mobility-top-priority-of-krishnamoorthis-senate-campaign/ |access-date=2025-07-18 |website=Capitol News Illinois |language=en-US}}</ref> while Stratton benefited from substantial financial backing from Pritzker and [[Pritzker family|his family.]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Szalinski |first=Ben |date=2025-07-16 |title=Who is contributing to Illinois' U.S. Senate candidates? |url=https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/who-is-contributing-to-illinois-u-s-senate-candidates/ |access-date=2025-07-18 |website=Capitol News Illinois |language=en-US}}</ref> Stratton pledged not to accept corporate PAC donations, although she accepted individual contributions from billionaires, whereas Krishnamoorthi and Kelly accepted corporate PAC support.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Szalinski |first=Ben |date=2025-07-16 |title=Who is contributing to Illinois' U.S. Senate candidates? |url=https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/who-is-contributing-to-illinois-u-s-senate-candidates/ |access-date=2025-07-19 |website=Capitol News Illinois |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ahern |first1=Mary Ann |last2=Schmidt |first2=Rose |date=2025-07-14 |title=In heated race, who has the advantage in seeking Sen. Dick Durbin's seat |url=https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/who-has-the-advantage-in-the-race-for-dick-durbins-senate-seat/3789209/ |access-date=2025-07-19 |website=NBC Chicago |language=en-US}}</ref>

The campaign featured sharp exchanges over ties to [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement|Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)]]. By December 2025, Krishnamoorthi had raised $24 million, including donations linked to associates of [[President of the United States|President]] [[Donald Trump]], [[Palantir]], and [[The Heritage Foundation]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2026-03-10 |title=US Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi raises millions for Illinois Senate bid as fundraising draws scrutiny |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/03/10/raja-krishnamoorthi-fundraising-illinois-senate/ |access-date=2026-03-14 |website=Chicago Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref> Meanwhile, the [[Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association]], which supported Stratton, received funding from [[CoreCivic]], another ICE contractor.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-02-13 |title=2026 U.S. Senate candidate profile: Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton - CBS Chicago |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/senate-candidate-profile-lieutenant-governor-juliana-stratton/ |access-date=2026-03-14 |website=CBS News |language=en-US}}</ref>

Gov. Juliana Stratton wins Democratic primary for US Senate |url=https://apnews.com/article/election-primary-illinois-democrats-senate-house-f9432112c459e87fdbfea0bdbcd4e492 |access-date=2026-03-18 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Petrella |first=Dan |last2=Soglin |first2=Talia |last3=Royal Pratt |first3=Gregory |date=2026-03-18 |title=Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton wins Democratic nomination for US Senate |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/03/17/illinois-us-senate-democratic-primary/ |access-date=2026-03-18 |website=Chicago Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref>

Stratton won with 40.2% of the statewide vote; she secured 47 counties, including [[Cook County, Illinois|Cook]] and [[Will County, Illinois|Will]] counties in the state's northeast. She recorded her best result in [[St. Clair County, Illinois|St. Clair County]], winning 54.3% of the vote. Krishnamoorthi won 53 counties, carrying [[DuPage County, Illinois|DuPage]], [[Lake County, Illinois|Lake]] and [[Kane County, Illinois|Kane]] counties around Chicago. He performed best in [[Mercer County, Illinois|Mercer County]] with 59.0% of the vote. The two leading candidates tied in [[Jasper County, Illinois|Jasper County]], with 32.9% of the vote each. Finally, Kelly placed third in the race; however, she did win [[Kankakee County, Illinois|Kankakee County]] with 38.2% of the vote.<ref>{{cite web |title=Illinois Senate Primary Results 2026 |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/illinois-senate-results#democratic-primary |website=NBC News |access-date=22 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Illinois U.S. Senate Primary Election Results |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/us/elections/results-illinois-us-senate-primary.html |website=New York Times |access-date=22 March 2026}}</ref> Kelly represents a majority of Kankakee residents as congresswoman for [[Illinois's 2nd congressional district]].
