The '''2026 United States Senate election in Kentucky''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Kentucky]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] congressman [[Andy Barr]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former state representative [[Charles Booker (American politician)|Charles Booker]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Mitch McConnell]] is not seeking an eighth term.<ref name="Schreiner">{{Cite news|last1=Schreiner|first1=Bruce|last2=Freking|first2=Kevin|date=February 20, 2025|title=Sen. Mitch McConnell won't seek reelection in 2026, ending long tenure as Republican power broker|url=https://apnews.com/article/mitch-mcconnell-senate-retirement-34c79ef12bf62d14cb71d3c393f23a83|access-date=February 20, 2025|publisher=[[The Associated Press]]}}</ref>

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 19. Endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], Barr won the Republican nomination with 60.5% of the vote over former state attorney general [[Daniel Cameron (American politician)|Daniel Cameron]]. Booker, the Democratic nominee in [[2022 United States Senate election in Kentucky|2022]], was nominated a second time, winning over Marine officer [[Amy McGrath]] (who had narrowly defeated him in the [[2020 United States Senate election in Kentucky#Democratic primary|2020]] primary for this seat).

This will be the first open Senate election in Kentucky since [[2010 United States Senate election in Kentucky|2010]]. Democrats have not won a Senate race in Kentucky since [[1992 United States Senate election in Kentucky|1992]].

== Background ==
Kentucky, a Southern state in the [[Bible Belt]], is generally considered to be a [[Red states and blue states|Republican stronghold]], having not elected a [[Kentucky Democratic Party|Democrat]] to the U.S. Senate since [[1992 United States Senate election in Kentucky|1992]]. [[Republican Party of Kentucky|Republicans]] control both U.S. Senate seats, all but two statewide executive offices, supermajorities in both houses of the [[Kentucky General Assembly]], and all but one seat in Kentucky's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] [[Kentucky's congressional delegations|delegation]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Kentucky House and Senate Republicans maintain supermajority|url=https://kaco.org/articles/kentucky-house-and-senate-republicans-maintain-supermajority/|access-date=December 5, 2024|publisher=KACO}}</ref> Democrats control both the [[Governor of Kentucky|governorship]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky|lieutenant-governorship]], which flipped from Republican control in [[2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election|2019]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Golshan|first=Tara|date=November 6, 2019|title=Democrat Andy Beshear just unseated Kentucky's Trump-loving governor|url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2019/11/5/20949770/kentucky-governor-election-results-andy-beshear|access-date=December 5, 2024|website=Vox|language=en-US}}</ref>

McConnell was first elected in [[1984 United States Senate election in Kentucky|1984]], defeating then-incumbent [[Walter Dee Huddleston]], and was re-elected in six subsequent elections.<ref>{{Cite news|last=McCausland|first=Phil|date=November 4, 2020|title=Sen. Mitch McConnell wins another term in Kentucky, NBC News projects|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/sen-mitch-mcconnell-wins-another-term-kentucky-nbc-news-projects-n1246037|access-date=December 5, 2024|publisher=[[NBC News]]|language=en}}</ref>

{{Elections in Louisiana sidebar}}

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Louisiana''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Louisiana]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] congresswoman [[Julia Letlow]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Tensas Parish police juror Jamie Davis are the nominees for their respective parties. The winner will succeed two-term Republican incumbent [[Bill Cassidy]], who was defeated in the primary.

Considered vulnerable to a Republican challenger after he voted to convict President [[Donald Trump]] in [[second impeachment trial of Donald Trump|his second impeachment trial]], Cassidy received 24.8% of the vote in the May 16 primary behind Letlow's 44.8% and state treasurer [[John Fleming (Louisiana politician)|John Fleming]]'s 28.3%.<ref name=CassidyRunning>{{cite news |title=Bill Cassidy discusses reelection plans while blistering Louisiana closed party primary law |last=Hilburn |first=Greg |work=[[The Times (Shreveport, Louisiana)|The Times]] |location=[[Shreveport, Louisiana|Shreveport]] |date=January 30, 2024 |access-date=March 31, 2024 |url=https://www.shreveporttimes.com/story/news/2024/01/30/will-louisiana-senator-bill-cassidy-run-for-reelection-under-new-closed-party-primary-law-he-hates/72405214007/}}</ref> Letlow, endorsed by Trump, advanced to a runoff against Fleming on June 27 and won the nomination with 56.9% of the vote.  

Jamie Davis defeated Gary Crockett in the Democratic runoff, receiving 79.9% of the vote. 

With the enactment of House Bill 17 in 2024, the race is the first U.S. Senate election in Louisiana to utilize party primaries instead of a single [[Nonpartisan blanket primary|blanket primary]] since [[2010 United States Senate election in Louisiana|2010]].<ref name="NoOpenPrimaries"/><ref name="Uphill"/> Democrats have not won a Senate election in Louisiana since [[2008 United States Senate election in Louisiana|2008]].

==Background==

===Change of electoral system===
In January 2024, governor [[Jeff Landry]] signed House Bill 17, sponsored by representative [[Julie Emerson]], which eliminated the top-two [[Louisiana primary]] system in favor of partisan primaries in elections for [[United States Congress|Congress]], the [[Louisiana Board of Elementary and Secondary Education|Board of Elementary and Secondary Education]], the [[Louisiana Public Service Commission|Public Service Commission]], and the [[Louisiana Supreme Court|state's Supreme Court]]. Unaffiliated voters may vote in the primaries, but not members of other parties, including the [[Independent Party of Louisiana]]. The bill also indicated the use of [[two-round system|runoff elections]] if no candidate receives a majority in their respective primary. The law will take effect beginning with the 2026 elections, making this election the first in which Louisiana will elect a U.S. senator using this system since [[2010 United States Senate election in Louisiana|2010]]; the top-two primary was first implemented in congressional elections in [[1978 United States Senate election in Louisiana|1978]].<ref name=NoOpenPrimaries>{{cite news |title=Gov. Landry, lawmakers disrupt how Louisiana has voted for nearly 50 years |last=Muller |first=Wesley |work=[[States Newsroom|Louisiana Illuminator]] |date=January 19, 2024 |access-date=March 31, 2024 |url=https://lailluminator.com/2024/01/19/closed-primaries-2/}}</ref>

===Primary challenge to Cassidy===
Senator [[Bill Cassidy]], who has held this seat since 2015, gained notoriety within the Republican Party for his vocal criticism of [[President of the United States|President]] [[Donald Trump]]. Cassidy denounced the [[January 6 United States Capitol attack|January 6 U.S. Capitol attack]], accused participants of [[sedition]], and voted to certify the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 election]] results.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Atoms |first1=Greg |title=Senator Bill Cassidy Says Pro-Trump Rioters Committed Sedition |url=https://710keel.com/senator-bill-cassidy-says-pro-trump-rioters-committed-sedition/ |access-date=January 10, 2021 |work=[[KEEL]] |date=January 8, 2021 |language=en}}</ref> He was one of seven Senate Republicans who voted to convict Trump for [[incitement]] of [[insurrection]] during [[second impeachment trial of Donald Trump|his second impeachment trial]], prompting the [[Republican Party of Louisiana]] to [[censure]] him.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mena |first1=Kelly |last2=Merica |first2=Dan |title=Louisiana Republican Party censures Cassidy following vote to convict Trump |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/02/13/politics/bill-cassidy-louisiana-republican-party-censure/index.html |access-date=February 14, 2021 |work=[[CNN]] |date=February 13, 2021}}</ref> During [[Donald Trump 2024 presidential campaign|Trump's 2024 campaign]], Cassidy publicly opposed his candidacy, citing Trump's [[indictments against Donald Trump|four criminal indictments]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Republican Bill Cassidy derides Trump and calls 2024 race 'sorry state of affairs' |last=Yang |first=Maya |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=March 17, 2024 |access-date=March 31, 2024 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2024/mar/17/republican-bill-cassidy-donald-trump-interview}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy says Trump should drop out of the 2024 presidential race|last=Concepcion |first=Summer |work=[[NBC News]] |date=August 20, 2023 |access-date=August 20, 2023|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/gop-senator-says-trump-drop-2024-presidential-race-rcna100878}}</ref>

Cassidy's stance led analysts to view him as vulnerable to a [[Trumpism|pro-Trump]] [[primary challenge]]. Early speculation in 2024 included Congressman [[Clay Higgins]], a supporter of Trump, who ultimately declined to run.<ref name=Uphill>{{cite news |title=Bill Cassidy faces uphill battle to win reelection but independents can still vote for him |last=Bridges |first=Tyler |work=[[The Times-Picayune/The New Orleans Advocate]] |date=January 28, 2024 |access-date=March 31, 2024 |url=https://www.nola.com/news/politics/bill-cassidy-faces-uphill-battle-to-win-reelection/article_5e2c6d4c-bca5-11ee-b87d-f3e1204248de.html}}</ref><ref name=":0"/> On January 18, 2026, Trump endorsed Julia Letlow, who officially entered the race two days later.<ref name="Trump/Letlow">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Meredith Lee |last2=Carney |first2=Jordain |title=Louisiana's Letlow prepares Senate bid after Trump endorsement |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/18/louisianas-letlow-prepares-senate-bid-00735697 |publisher=Politico |access-date=19 January 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Beaumont |first1=Thomas |last2=Barrow |first2=Bill |title=Rep. Julia Letlow launches primary against Sen. Bill Cassidy in Louisiana |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/wireStory/after-trump-endorsement-rep-julia-letlow-launches-primary-129385190 |website=ABC News |publisher=Associated Press |access-date=21 January 2026}}</ref>

{{Elections in Massachusetts sidebar}}

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Massachusetts''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the [[Commonwealth of Massachusetts]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Ed Markey]] is seeking a third full term. He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] attorney [[John Deaton]].

[[Primary election]]s were held on September 1. Markey won the Democratic nomination over congressman [[Seth Moulton]] with 64.9% of the vote. Deaton, the Republican nominee in [[2024 United States Senate election in Massachusetts|2024]], was nominated a second time after running unopposed in the primary.

Republicans have not won a Senate election in Massachusetts since [[2010 United States Senate special election in Massachusetts|2010]].

{{Short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States Senate elections}} {{Distinguish|2026 Maine State Senate election}} {{Use American English|date=November 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=October 2026}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 United States Senate election in Maine | country = Maine | type = presidential | ongoing = yes | previous_election = 2020 United States Senate election in Maine | previous_year = 2020 | next_election = 2032 United States Senate election in Maine | next_year = ''2032'' | election_date = {{Start date|2026|11|03}} | turnout = | image1 = Susan Collins During Senate Appropriation Homeland Security Subcommittee Hearing 8 May 2025.jpg | nominee1 = [[Susan Collins]] | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = Troy Jackson in the Senate Chamber (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Troy Jackson]] (replacing [[Graham Platner]]) | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | map = | map_caption = County results | title = U.S. senator | before_election = [[Susan Collins]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsME}} The '''2026 United States Senate election in Maine''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Maine]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Susan Collins]] is seeking a sixth term. She is being challenged by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former state Senate president [[Troy Jackson]]. The election will be conducted with [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]]. In the June 9 primaries, Collins was the only candidate to qualify for the Republican nomination. Sullivan harbor master [[Graham Platner]] won the Democratic primary over Governor [[Janet Mills]] with the support of progressive leaders, but withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault accusations and other controversies. Jackson was chosen to replace Platner through a [[Party conference#United States|nominating convention]] on July 25. As Collins is the only Republican senator representing a state that President [[Donald Trump]] did not win in any of his three presidential campaigns, the race is considered to be among the most competitive in 2026. Democrats have not won a Senate election in Maine since [[1988 United States Senate election in Maine|1988]].{{efn|[[Angus King]], who was elected in [[2012 United States Senate election in Maine|2012]] and re-elected in [[2018 United States Senate election in Maine|2018]] and [[2024 United States Senate election in Maine|2024]], is an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, but is not a member of the party.}} == Background == The election will be held on November 3, 2026,{{Cite web|url=https://www.haaretz.com/us-news/2026-05-04/ty-article/.premium/jewish-groups-withhold-support-as-platner-becomes-maine-frontrunner/0000019d-f412-de15-a7df-f67ba8b30000|title=Jewish Political Groups Withhold Support From Graham Platner After He Emerges as Maine Democratic Frontrunner|website=Haaretz.com|last=Nechin|first=Etan|date=May 4, 2026}} coinciding with [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Maine|elections]], a [[2026 Maine gubernatorial election|gubernatorial election]], and other local elections.{{Cite web|url=https://www.mainepublic.org/tags/your-vote-2026|title=Your Vote 2026|website=Maine Public|access-date=May 8, 2026}} Both the primary and general elections will be conducted with [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]].{{cite web |title=Maine elections, 2026 |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Maine_elections,_2026 |website=Ballotpedia |access-date=September 5, 2025}} Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] U.S. senator [[Susan Collins]] is running for re-election to a sixth term.{{Cite web|url=https://www.mainepublic.org/news/2026-02-10/susan-collins-formalizes-reelection-bid-will-seek-sixth-term|title=Susan Collins formalizes reelection bid, will seek sixth term|first=Steve|last=Mistler|date=February 10, 2026|website=Maine Public}} Both primary elections took place on June 9, 2026.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/maine-us-senate-election-polls-2026.html|title=Maine U.S. Senate Election 2026: Latest Polls|work=The New York Times |date=January 16, 2026|via=NYTimes.com}} The northernmost state in [[New England]], [[Maine]] is considered to be a moderately [[Red states and blue states|blue state]]. Maine has voted for every Democratic presidential nominee since [[1992 United States presidential election in Maine|1992]], and Democratic nominee [[Kamala Harris]] defeated Republican nominee [[Donald Trump]] by approximately seven percentage points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Maine]]. Democrats also control the [[Governor of Maine|governorship]], the [[Maine Legislature|state legislature]], and both seats in Maine's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] [[Maine's congressional delegations|congressional delegation]].{{Cite web |last=Cover |first=Susan |title=Maine Democrats say they won enough seats to control state Senate |url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/me/maine/politics/2024/11/06/maine-democrats-say-they-won-enough-seats-to-control-state-senate |date=November 6, 2024 |access-date=December 7, 2024 |website=[[Spectrum News#Spectrum News Maine|Spectrum News]] |language=en}} Since 2018, Collins has been the only Republican representing any New England state in either chamber of Congress.{{Cite web |last=Scanlan|first=Quinn |title=Susan Collins, Congress's last New England Republican, facing toughest reelection yet |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/susan-collins-congresss-england-republican-facing-toughest-reelection/story?id=71716146 |date=July 11, 2020 |access-date=August 1, 2025 |website=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] |language=en}} Collins was first elected in [[1996 United States Senate election in Maine|1996]]. She has been re-elected in four subsequent elections, significantly outperforming other Republicans in the state. In [[2020 United States Senate election in Maine|2020]], despite almost all polls and analysts predicting that she would lose her re-election bid, Collins defeated Democratic nominee [[Sara Gideon]] by a nine-point margin. Democratic presidential nominee [[Joe Biden]] carried Maine by about nine percentage points on the same ballot.{{Cite web |last=Everett |first=Burgess |date=November 4, 2020 |title=Collins wins again in Maine, boosting Senate GOP |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/11/04/maine-senate-election-results-2020-434000 |access-date=December 7, 2024 |website=[[Politico]] |language=en}} This election is expected to be among the most competitive Senate races in 2026.{{Cite news |last1=Sullivan |first1=Andy |last2=Erickson |first2=Bo |date=March 2, 2026 |title=Eight US Senate races to watch in the 2026 midterm elections |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/eight-us-senate-races-watch-2026-midterm-elections-2026-03-02/ |access-date=April 2, 2026 |work=[[Reuters]]}} Collins is the only Republican senator who represents one of the 19 states that [[Donald Trump]] did not win in any of his three presidential campaigns.{{Cite web|url=https://centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/the-end-of-the-line-for-red-state-senate-democrats/|title=The End of the Line for Red State Senate Democrats|access-date=July 9, 2025|date=December 5, 2024|first1=Kyle|last1=Kondik|website=Sabato's Crystal Ball|quote=Collins is now the lone outlier among all 100 senators as someone who continues to hold a Senate seat in a state that hasn't supported her party's presidential nominee in decades. Such outliers were important parts of past recent Democratic Senate majorities, but they will now be all gone.}} With the decline of [[Split-ticket voting|ticket splitting]], Collins is widely viewed as the most vulnerable incumbent Republican senator in 2026.{{cite news |last=Coleman |first=J. Miles |title=The Shocking Decline of Senate Ticket-Splitting |url=https://centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/articles/the-decline-of-senate-ticket-splitting/ |access-date=April 27, 2023 |work=[[Sabato's Crystal Ball]] |date=July 11, 2024}}{{Cite web |last=Stanton |first=Andrew |date=November 14, 2024 |title=Susan Collins' Reelection Plan Throws a Wrench in Democrats' Senate Hopes |url=https://www.newsweek.com/susan-collins-reelection-plans-2026-senate-1986125 |access-date=November 14, 2024 |website=[[Newsweek]]}} Collins is also the only Republican senator facing re-election in a state that [[Kamala Harris]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Maine|2024 presidential election]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/04/17/jordan-wood-challenge-susan-collins-maine-00297115|title=Democrat eyes challenge to Susan Collins in Maine|date=April 17, 2025|website=Politico|last=Mutnick|first=Ally}} Since the [[2024 United States Senate elections]], Collins has been the last senator to represent a non-swing state (in other words, a reliably [[Red states and blue states|Democratic or Republican state]]) that typically supports the opposing party.{{Cite web |url=https://rollcall.com/2025/01/08/senate-democrats-personal-brands-midterm-elections/ |title=How the decline of personal political brands hurts Senate Democrats |last=Gonzales |first=Nathan L. |work=[[Roll Call]] |date=January 8, 2025}} ==Republican primary== Incumbent U.S. senator {{Elections in Michigan}}

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Michigan''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Michigan]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former Wayne County health director [[Abdul El-Sayed]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former congressman [[Mike Rogers (Michigan politician)|Mike Rogers]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Democratic incumbent [[Gary Peters]] is not seeking a third term.

For most of the primary, El-Sayed, congresswoman [[Haley Stevens]], and state senator [[Mallory McMorrow]] sought the Democratic nomination. After McMorrow withdrew in July, El-Sayed and Stevens remained in a tight race, which El-Sayed won on August 4 with 48.5% of the vote. Rogers, the Republican nominee in [[2024 United States Senate election in Michigan|2024]], was the only candidate to qualify for his party's primary ballot.

This is the only open Democratic-held Senate seat up for election in a state won by [[Donald Trump]] in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. Republicans have not won a Senate race in Michigan since [[1994 United States Senate election in Michigan|1994]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 6, 2025 |title=These are the candidates running for Michigan's open Senate seat in 2026 |url=https://michiganindependent.com/politics/candidates-running-for-michigans-open-senate-seat-in-2026/ |access-date=August 4, 2025 |website=The Michigan Independent |language=en-US}}</ref> The election is the most expensive in Michigan history, with over $243 million in spending.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nann Burke |first=Melissa |last2=Schwab |first2=Grant |date=October 9, 2026 |title=Michigan Senate race officially the most expensive in state history |url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/politics/2026/10/09/michigan-senate-race-tv-ad-spending-mike-rogers-abdul-el-sayed/92169289007/ |access-date=October 16, 2026 |website=The Detroit News |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Background ==
Michigan is regarded as a [[battleground state|swing state]]. Most recently in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Michigan|2020]] and [[2024 United States presidential election in Michigan|2024]] presidential elections, it backed [[Joe Biden]] by 2.8% and [[Donald Trump]] by 1.4%, respectively.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 5, 2024 |title=Michigan Presidential Election Results |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-michigan-president.html |access-date=January 29, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Gary Peters was first elected with 54.6% of the vote in [[2014 United States Senate election in Michigan|2014]] and re-elected with 49.9% in [[2020 United States Senate election in Michigan|2020]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mielections.us/election/results/14GEN/|title = 2014 Michigan Official General Election Results - 11/04/2014 |website=Michigan Secretary of State |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240716012120/https://mielections.us/election/results/14GEN/ |archive-date=July 16, 2024|access-date=July 22, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=November 3, 2020 |title=Michigan U.S. Senate Election Results |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/11/03/us/elections/results-michigan-senate.html |access-date=July 22, 2026 |work=[[The New York Times]] |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He announced in January 2025 he was not seeking reelection for a third term.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Howard |first=Andrew |date=January 28, 2025 |title=Gary Peters not running for reelection in battleground Michigan |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/01/28/gary-peters-not-running-for-reelection-in-battleground-michigan-00200925 |access-date=July 22, 2026 |website=Politico}}</ref>

Both parties have had electoral success in Michigan in recent years, though Democrats have performed better in non-presidential races. Democrats currently hold both [[List of United States senators from Michigan|U.S. Senate seats]], all statewide executive offices, and the [[Michigan Senate|state senate]]. Republicans control the [[Michigan House of Representatives]] and hold a majority of the state's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] seats.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 6, 2024 |title=Democrats lose trifecta in Michigan, hobbling Gov. Whitmer's agenda |url=https://apnews.com/article/michigan-house-races-democrats-trifecta-35669bb7d15261abf4219e6f57df7769 |access-date=January 29, 2025 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref> Republicans have not won a U.S. Senate race in Michigan since [[1994 United States Senate election in Michigan|1994]], this Senate seat since [[1972 United States Senate election in Michigan|1972]] or a non-presidential statewide election since [[2014 United States elections|2014]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Spangler |first1=Todd |date=January 28, 2025 |title=Michigan's Gary Peters won't run for US Senate reelection next year |url=https://www.freep.com/story/news/politics/2025/01/28/gary-peters-us-senate-2026/77993125007/ |access-date=January 28, 2025 |work=[[Detroit Free Press]]}}</ref>

As one of two Democratic-held Senate seats in a state won by Donald Trump in 2024, Michigan is considered a key Senate battleground in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gans |first=Jared |date=November 28, 2024 |title=7 most competitive Senate races in 2026 |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/5013277-2026-key-senate-races-watch/ |access-date=January 28, 2025 |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="NBC Retire"/>

==Republican primary==
===Campaign===
Michigan was considered one of the top Republican senate pickup opportunities for the 2026 cycle, and national Republicans quickly coalesced around their [[2024 United States Senate election in Michigan|2024]] senate nominee, former congressman [[Mike Rogers (Michigan politician)|Mike Rogers]], as their preferred candidate. Rogers' only significant opposition was from former co-chair of the [[Michigan Republican Party]] Bernadette Smith, who had vacated this position one week prior to the launch of her candidacy. [[Fox News]] labeled her campaign as a "longshot" due to [[Donald Trump]] having already endorsed Rogers prior to Smith's entrance into the race, and because of her criminal record, which included a [[Nolo contendere|no-contest]] plea of felony [[welfare fraud]] and a guilty conviction for seriously injuring a ten-year-old boy in an automobile accident.<ref name="Clash">{{cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/michigan-gop-leader-signals-senate-bid-sets-up-clash-trump-endorsed-mike-rogers |title=Former Michigan GOP leader signals Senate bid, sets up clash with Trump-endorsed Mike Rogers |website=[[Fox News]] |last1=Steinhauser |first1=Paul |date=November 12, 2025 |access-date=August 10, 2026}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=August 2026}} Smith did not make the primary ballot after being disqualified by the Board of State Canvassers for not submitting the required number of signatures, thus allowing Rogers to win the nomination uncontested.<ref name=BSC/>

{{Elections in Minnesota}}

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Minnesota''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Minnesota]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] lieutenant governor [[Peggy Flanagan]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former journalist [[Michele Tafoya]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Democratic incumbent [[Tina Smith]] is not seeking a second full term.<ref name="buzzing">{{cite news|work=MPR News|access-date=February 13, 2025|last=Bakst|first=Brian|url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2025/02/13/tina-smith-will-not-run-for-reelection-in-senate-in-2026|date=February 13, 2025|title=Sen. Tina Smith won't seek reelection in 2026, putting Minnesota seat up for grabs|archive-date=April 15, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250415045923/https://www.mprnews.org/story/2025/02/13/tina-smith-will-not-run-for-reelection-in-senate-in-2026|url-status=live}}</ref>

After Smith announced she would not run for reelection, Flanagan and congresswoman [[Angie Craig]] sought the Democratic nomination, which Flanagan won on August 11 with 59% of the vote. Tafoya won the Republican nomination with 52.1% of the vote over Navy SEAL Adam Schwarze and former basketball player [[Royce White]].

This will be the first Senate election in Minnesota without an incumbent since [[2006 United States Senate election in Minnesota|2006]].<ref>{{cite news|work=MPR News|access-date=March 1, 2025|last=Masters|first=Clay|url=https://www.albertleatribune.com/2025/02/an-open-minnesota-senate-seat-is-enticing-to-plenty-but-unclear-how-many-will-take-plunge/|date=February 14, 2025|title=An open Minnesota Senate seat is enticing to plenty but unclear how many will take plunge|archive-date=February 14, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250214155430/https://www.albertleatribune.com/2025/02/an-open-minnesota-senate-seat-is-enticing-to-plenty-but-unclear-how-many-will-take-plunge/|url-status=live}}</ref> Republicans have not won a Senate election in Minnesota since [[2002 United States Senate election in Minnesota|2002]].

== Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary ==
=== Background and campaign ===
Former Minnesota House Speaker [[Melissa Hortman]] was reportedly considering running for the seat before [[2025 shootings of Minnesota legislators|her assassination]] in June 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last1= Nir| first1= David| last2= Singer| first2= Jeff| title= Morning Digest: Ron DeSantis uses 'officially nonexistent' clout to tout wife as successor| url= https://www.the-downballot.com/p/morning-digest-ron-desantis-uses| access-date= April 21, 2025| website= The Downballot| language= en| date= February 25, 2025}}</ref>

The Democratic primary election between Flanagan and Craig was widely seen as a part of the national struggle between the Democratic Party's progressive and moderate factions since the [[2024 U.S. The '''2026 United States Senate election in Mississippi''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Mississippi]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=United States Senate election in Mississippi, 2026|url=https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Senate_election_in_Mississippi,_2026|access-date=April 19, 2025|website=[[Ballotpedia]]}}</ref> [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Cindy Hyde-Smith]] is seeking re-election to a second full term. She is being challenged by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Lowndes County district attorney [[Scott Colom]].

[[Primary elections]] were held on March 10. Facing minimal opposition, Hyde-Smith won the Republican nomination with 80.8% of the vote. Colom won the Democratic nomination with 73% of the vote against Marine veteran Albert Littell and Priscilla Williams-Till, a cousin of [[Emmett Till]].<ref name="Colom2">{{cite news |last1=McRae |first1=Emma |date=September 3, 2025 |title=Colom announces Senate run for Hyde-Smith's seat |url=https://cdispatch.com/news/colom-announces-senate-run-for-hyde-smiths-seat/ |access-date=September 3, 2025 |work=[[The Commercial Dispatch]]}}</ref><ref name="WilliamsTill">{{cite news |last1=Harrison |first1=Heather |date=September 9, 2025 |title=Emmett Till's Cousin Is Running for US Senate in Mississippi |url=https://www.mississippifreepress.org/priscilla-williams-till-emmett-tills-cousin-is-running-for-us-senate-in-mississippi/ |access-date=September 9, 2025 |work=Mississippi Free Press}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Meet the US Senate candidates in Mississippi 2026 primary election |url=https://www.clarionledger.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/02/27/united-states-senate-candidates-election-2026-in-mississippi/88839755007/ |access-date=February 27, 2026 |website=Clarion Ledger}}</ref>

Democrats have not won a Senate election in Mississippi since [[1982 United States Senate election in Mississippi|1982]].<ref>https://edition.cnn.com/2026/03/10/politics/cindy-hyde-smith-scott-colom-missisippi-senate-race</ref>

Alme official photo.jpg | nominee1 = [[Kurt Alme]] | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | image2 = Alani Bankhead USAF 2021.png | nominee2 = Alani Bankhead | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | image4 = Seth Bodnar - President at University of Montana (cropped).jpg | colour4 = | nominee4 = [[Seth Bodnar]] | party4 = Independent (US) | image5 = 3x4.svg | nominee5 = Kyle Austin | party5 = Libertarian Party (United States) | map_image = | map_size = | map_caption = County results | title = U.S. senator | before_election = [[Steve Daines]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = | after_party = }} {{ElectionsMT}} The '''2026 United States Senate election in Montana''' will be held on November 3, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Montana]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] U.S. Attorney [[Kurt Alme]], [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Air Force officer Alani Bankhead, and [[Independent politician|independent]] former [[University of Montana]] president [[Seth Bodnar]] are the major candidates. Republican incumbent [[Steve Daines]] is not seeking a third term. In the Republican primary, Daines announced he would seek re-election, but withdrew minutes before the filing deadline and endorsed Alme, who filed to run the same day. As the only major Republican candidate, Alme was nominated with 76.2% of the vote. Bankhead won the Democratic nomination with 43.7% of the vote over former state representative [[Reilly Neill]] and tribal historic preservation officer Michael Black Wolf. Bodnar, supported by former Democratic senator [[Jon Tester]], launched an independent campaign shortly after resigning from the University of Montana. == Background == Montana is considered to be a red state at the federal level, having not voted for a Democratic president since [[Bill Clinton]]'s [[1992 United States presidential election in Montana|plurality victory in 1992]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.270towin.com/states/montana|title=Montana Presidential Election Voting History - 270toWin|website=270toWin.com}} Recently, the state has also been trending red on a statewide level, as Republicans flipped the governorship in [[2020 Montana gubernatorial election|2020]],{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/2020/11/4/21536492/election-results-greg-gianforte-montana-governor-winner|title=Greg Gianforte flips Montana governorship to Republicans|first=Benjamin|last=Rosenberg|date=November 4, 2020|website=Vox}} and the Class I Senate seat in [[2024 United States Senate election in Montana|2024]].https://www.npr.org/2024/11/09/nx-s1-5181908/with-democratic-senator-jon-testers-loss-in-montana-republicans-take-full-control == Republican primary == The filing deadline for participation in primaries was March 5, 2026, at 5:00 p.m.{{Cite web |title = 2026 PRIMARY AND GENERAL ELECTION CALENDAR |publisher = Montana Secretary of State |date = October 2025 |url = https://sosmt.gov/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php?juwpfisadmin=false&action=wpfd&task=file.download&wpfd_category_id=27&wpfd_file_id=72177&token=6f7af6195f33954ee91f868f73055133&preview=1}} At 4:52 p.m. [[Kurt Alme]] filed to run, and 3 minutes later [[Steve Daines]] withdrew. At 5:02 p.m. Daines announced his withdrawal and endorsed Alme. By the end of March, the Democratic field had collectively raised $123,629.43, the vast majority of which was by Reilly Neill, a former state legislator. Neill launched her campaign for Senate immediately following [[Jon Tester]]'s loss to [[Tim Sheehy]] in [[2024 United States Senate election in Montana|2024]], and had run a [[write-in]] campaign in [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Montana|2024]] for the [[Montana's 2nd congressional district|second district]] to the U.S. house, after John Driscoll, the Democratic candidate, refused to spend more than $5,000 on his campaign.{{cite news |last1=Lutey |first1=Tom |title=In Senate race, underfunded Democrats try to fend off a challenge from the middle |url=https://montanafreepress.org/2026/05/08/in-senate-race-underfunded-democrats-try-to-fend-off-a-challenge/ |access-date=June 4, 2026 |work=[[Montana Free Press]] |date=May 8, 2026 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/VsvPj |archive-date=June 4, 2026 |url-status=live}} A poll conducted in late April and early May for the ''[[Montana Free Press]]'' by [[Eagleton Institute of Politics|Eagleton]] suggested that the Democratic candidates for Senate were largely unknown by Montanans.{{cite news |last1=Lutey |first1=Tom |title=Montana U.S. Senate candidates largely unknown to voters, poll finds |url=https://montanafreepress.org/2026/05/19/montana-us-senate-candidates-largely-unknown-to-voters/ |access-date=June 4, 2026 |work=[[Montana Free Press]] |date=May 19, 2026 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/nWF5q |archive-date=June 4, 2026 |url-status=live}} Alani Bankhead, an Air Force veteran based in [[Helena, Montana|Helena]], had raised just over $10,000 by the end of March, leaving her at a heavy financial disadvantage. However, in May, the Progressive Vet PAC ([[political action committee]]) spent $592,000 on mailers in support of Bankhead.{{cite news |last1=Lutey |first1=Tom |title=The mailers fueling speculation in Montana’s Democratic primary for U.S. Senate |url=https://montanafreepress.org/2026/05/15/the-mailers-fueling-speculation-in-montanas-democratic-primary-for-u-s-senate/ |access-date=4 June 2026 |work=[[Montana Free Press]] |date=15 May 2026 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/CjeSf |archive-date=4 June 2026 |url-status=live}} Meanwhile, the More Jobs, Less Government PAC invested in ads attacking Neill as a liberal, and saying that Bankhead would work with [[Donald Trump]].{{cite news |last1=Lutey |first1=Tom |title=The Sheehy-supporting PAC trying to define Montana’s Democratic Senate candidates |url=https://montanafreepress.org/2026/05/26/the-sheehy-supporting-pac-trying-to-define-montanas-democratic-senate-candidates/ |access-date=4 June 2026 |work=[[Montana Free Press]] |date=26 May 2026 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/MT1Lj |archive-date=4 June 2026 |url-status=live}}{{cite news |last1=Everett |first1=Burgess |title=Why groups are spending big in Montana’s Democratic Senate primary |url=https://www.semafor.com/article/06/01/2026/why-groups-are-spending-big-in-montanas-democratic-senate-primary |access-date=4 June 2026 |work=[[Semafor (website)|Semafor]] |date=1 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260604075713/https://www.semafor.com/article/06/01/2026/why-groups-are-spending-big-in-montanas-democratic-senate-primary |archive-date=4 June 2026 |url-status=live}} The Progressive Vet PAC, founded in April 2026, had former Democratic state representative [[Moffie Funk]] as its treasurer, while the More Jobs, Less Government PAC worked to promote the election of Sheehy, a Republican, in 2024. Financial filings by the More Jobs, Less Government PAC declared that their ads were in support of Bankhead, although the Progressive Vet PAC has said that the attack ads are designed to elevate Neill over Bankhead. Brian Miller, a candidate for the U.S. House in the second district, suggested that Progressive Vet's spending was designed to benefit independent candidate [[Seth Bodnar]], in the hopes Bankhead would win the primary and drop out in support of Bodnar. Neill publicly stated she would not drop out of the general election, and when asked by the ''Montana Free Press'' if she would drop out, Bankhead said "not only no, but hell no". Both Neill and Bankhead campaigned in rural areas of Montana. Neill supported expansion of the [[Family Medical Leave Act]], new educational grants, and rural healthcare, while Bankhead advocated for cuts to [[red tape]], greater accountability in government, and protecting children and the elderly.{{cite news |last1=Hansen |first1=Jordan |title=Neill, Bankhead look to court rural voters in Senate primary |url=https://dailymontanan.com/2026/05/28/neill-bankhead-look-to-court-rural-voters-in-senate-primary/ |access-date=June 4, 2026 |work=Daily Montanan |date=May 28, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260604075640/https://dailymontanan.com/2026/05/28/neill-bankhead-look-to-court-rural-voters-in-senate-primary/ |archive-date=June 4, 2026 |url-status=live}} The [[Associated Press]] called the primary for Bankhead at 9:53pm on election night. Preliminary figures showed Bankhead with 44% of the vote to Neill's 33%. colspan="4" |Source: [[Federal Election Commission]] |} == General election == === Campaign === At a June 15 press conference, her first after winning the June 2 primary, Bankhead stated she would remain in the race and called upon Bodnar to drop out, citing a gender discrimination lawsuit filed against the University of Montana (UM) in 2021. A spokesperson for the Bodnar campaign said that he had taken claims of discrimination seriously while being president of UM, and that no wrongdoing had been found as a result of the lawsuit.{{cite news |last1=Thomas |first1=Mariah |title=In Montana Senate Race, Democrat Bankhead Doubles Down on Bid Against Bodnar |url=https://flatheadbeacon.com/2026/06/15/in-montana-senate-race-democrat-bankhead-doubles-down-on-bid-against-bodnar/ |access-date=June 15, 2026 |work=[[Flathead Beacon]] |date=June 15, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260615231703/https://flatheadbeacon.com/2026/06/15/in-montana-senate-race-democrat-bankhead-doubles-down-on-bid-against-bodnar/ |archive-date=June 15, 2026 |url-status=live}} Bodnar also faced criticism from Montana Republicans, who called him an "independent in name only" and portrayed him as a Democrat seeking to avoid the party label.{{cite news |last1=Lutey |first1=Tom |title=Bodnar’s big gamble: Why the independent is pushing for Montana’s nonpartisan era |url=https://montanafreepress.org/2026/06/26/how-seth-bodnar-plans-to-become-montana-first-nonpartisan-u-s-senator/ |access-date=August 31, 2026 |work=[[Montana Free Press]] |date=June 26, 2026}} A Republican-aligned super PAC pointed to Bodnar's registration as a Democrat while he lived in Connecticut in 2012; Montana does not register voters by party. His advisers said that he would not join either the Democratic or Republican caucus if elected, and Bodnar said he rejected the idea that he would have to submit to a party leader. As polls showed Alme likely to win a three-way race, many Democratic leaders called on their nominee, Bankhead, to drop out of the race, believing Bodnar was their best hope to beat Alme.https://flatheadbeacon.com/2026/10/19/u-s-senate-race-bodnar-pitches-independence-as-the-fix-for-a-broken-washington/ Since mid-July, Montana Freedom PAC, a [[political action committee]] supporting Bodnar, has paid for signs and digital advertising suggesting Bankhead should leave the race. As of early August the committee had spent more than $1 million on advertising benefiting Bodnar.{{cite news |last1=Lutey |first1=Tom |title=Scenes from a dropout deadline |url=https://montanafreepress.org/2026/08/06/scenes-from-a-dropout-deadline/ |access-date=August 24, 2026 |work=[[Montana Free Press]] |date=August 6, 2026}}{{cite web |title=Montana Freedom PAC, committee C00943910 |url=https://www.fec.gov/data/committee/C00943910/ |website=fec.gov |publisher=[[Federal Election Commission]] |access-date=August 24, 2026}} On the deadline for candidate withdrawal, August 10, ''[[HuffPost]]'' reported that Bankhead was choosing to stay in the race, keeping it a three-way contest.{{cite news |last1=Blumenthal |first1=Paul |title=Montana Democrat Stays In Senate Race Despite Pressure To Drop Out |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/montana-senate-2026-bankhead-bodnar_n_6a7a1704e4b0a6d70bb2bf90?origin=article-bottom2-nonlife |access-date=August 10, 2026 |work=The Huffington Post |date=August 10, 2026 |url-status=live}}{{bsn|date=August 2026}} Republicans criticized Bodnar over a transgender athlete's participation in women's sports during his presidency of the University of Montana.{{cite news |last=Brown |first=Matthew |title=Montana Republican US Sen. Steve Daines drops reelection bid in surprise move |url=https://apnews.com/article/election-senate-daines-montana-independent-bodnar-3c34598e7d67aadb7cf3dea47bad689a |work=Associated Press |date=March 4, 2026 |access-date=September 23, 2026}}{{cite news |last=Scherer |first=Michael |title=Big Sky Crack-Up |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/04/montana-democrats-intrigue-bodnar/686852/ |work=The Atlantic |date=April 21, 2026 |access-date=September 23, 2026}} Asked about the issue at an August campaign event, Bodnar said he favored fairness in women's sports but believed parents and children should make their own decisions.{{cite news |last=Sakariassen |first=Alex |title=Bodnar wades into deep red Bitterroot water |url=https://thepulp.org/seth-bodnar-ravalli-county-senate-independent/ |work=The Pulp |date=September 4, 2026 |access-date=September 23, 2026}} Alme also criticized diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and accused Bodnar of supporting transgender athletes' participation in girls' sports.{{cite news |last=Plutt |first=J. P. |title=U.S. Senate candidate Alme makes Dillon visit |url=https://www.dillontribune.com/news/u-s-senate-candidate-alme-makes-dillon-visit/article_70282300-2daa-4b1b-a525-4122a3603efc.html |work=Dillon Tribune |date=September 16, 2026 |access-date=September 23, 2026}} On October 12, [[Shannon O'Brien (Montana politician)|Shannon O'Brien]], the Chair of the [[Montana Democratic Party|Montana Democratic Party,]] resigned from her position in order to endorse Bodnar's campaign.{{Cite web |last=Howard |first=Phil |date=2026-10-12 |title=Montana Democratic party chair resigns, endorses Bodnar |url=https://nbcmontana.com/news/local/montana-democratic-party-chair-resigns-endorses-bodnar-10-12-2026 |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=KECI |language=en}} === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style=text-align:center !Source !Ranking !As of |- |align="left"|''[[The Cook Political Report]]''{{Cite web|title=2026 CPR Senate Race Ratings|url=https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings/senate-race-ratings|access-date=October 22, 2026|website=[[Cook Political Report]]}} |{{USRaceRating|Solid|R}} |October 20, 2026 |- |align="left"|[[Decision Desk HQ]]{{cite web|title=2026 Senate Ratings|url=https://votes.decisiondeskhq.com/forecast/2026/senate|url-access=registration|publisher=[[Decision Desk HQ]]|access-date=October 22, 2026}} |{{USRaceRating|Likely|R}} |October 22, 2026 |- |align="left"|''[[The Economist]]''{{Cite web|title=2026 Senate Forecast|url=https://www.economist.com/interactive/2026/us-midterms/prediction-model/senate/|access-date=October 22, 2026|website=[[The Economist]]}}{{efn|''The Economist''{{'}}s prediction model uses unconventional terminology. The '''2026 United States Senate election in North Carolina''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[North Carolina]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former party chair [[Michael Whatley]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former governor [[Roy Cooper]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Thom Tillis]] is not seeking a third term.

Considered vulnerable to a primary challenge due to his moderate positions, Tillis announced he would run for re-election, but withdrew after voting against the [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]]. Whatley, who emerged as the Republican frontrunner after being endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], won the nomination with 64.6% of the vote over author [[Don Brown (author, born 1960)|Don Brown]]. Cooper won the Democratic nomination with 92% of the vote, facing minimal opposition.

Democrats have not won a Senate election in North Carolina since [[2008 United States Senate election in North Carolina|2008]].

== Background ==
A [[swing state]], North Carolina is considered to be a [[Red states and blue states|purple to slightly red]] Southern state at the federal level. It was also a top battleground state in the [[2020 United States presidential election in North Carolina|2020]] and [[2024 United States presidential election in North Carolina|2024]] presidential elections. The state backed [[Donald Trump]] in both elections by 1.3%<ref>{{Cite web|title=November 03, 2020 General Election Results by Contest|url=https://s3.amazonaws.com/dl.ncsbe.gov/State_Board_Meeting_Docs/2020-11-24/Canvass/State%20Composite%20Abstract%20Report%20-%20Contest.pdf|work=North Carolina State Board of Elections}}</ref> and 3.2%,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dl.ncsbe.gov/?prefix=State_Board_Meeting_Docs/2024-11-26/Canvass/ |title=NC - State_Composite_Abstract_Report-Contest.pdf |date=November 26, 2024|access-date=December 30, 2024}}</ref> respectively.

Both parties have seen success in the state in recent years. Republicans control both chambers of the [[North Carolina General Assembly]] and hold a majority in North Carolina's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] delegation,<ref name="2024fedelection">
State Board of Elections. ''[https://er.ncsbe.gov/?election_dt=11/05/2024&county_id=0&office=FED&contest=0 General election results for Federal offices, 2024]''. North Carolina State Board of Elections. Archived at [https://web.archive.org/web/20240724000000/https://er.ncsbe.gov/?election_dt=11/05/2024&county_id=0&office=FED&contest=0 Web Archive].
</ref> as well as both of the state's U.S. Senate seats. In [[2024 North Carolina Council of State elections|2024]], Democrats won half of the state's [[North Carolina Council of State|executive offices]], flipping a net of one seat from Republicans.<ref name=2024generalncsbe>{{Cite web|url=https://er.ncsbe.gov/?election_dt=11/05/2024&county_id=0&office=COS&contest=0|title=NC SBE Contest Results|website=er.ncsbe.gov}}</ref>

Democrats have not won a Senate election in North Carolina since [[Kay Hagan]] defeated [[Elizabeth Dole]] in [[2008 United States Senate election in North Carolina|2008]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/north-carolina-senate-primary-results-midterm-elections-2026/|title=Whatley, Cooper win North Carolina primaries, CBS News projects, teeing up key Senate contest|publisher=CBS News|website=CBS News|access-date=2026-10-14}}</ref>

==Republican primary==
Senator [[Thom Tillis]] was considered vulnerable to a primary challenger from his right. On June 10, 2023, the [[North Carolina Republican Party]] voted to censure Tillis for his support for the [[Respect for Marriage Act]] and immigration reform attempts.<ref>{{cite news |publisher=[[CNN]] |date=June 11, 2023 |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/06/11/politics/thom-tillis-north-carolina-gop-censure/index.html |author1=Berryman, Kim |author2=Pellish, Aaron |title=Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is censured by North Carolina GOP delegates at convention}}</ref><ref name="WRALTillisSpotlight">{{cite news |title=Trump nominations put NC's Thom Tillis, the nation's 'most vulnerable' Republican senator, in the spotlight |url=https://www.wral.com/story/trump-nominations-put-nc-s-thom-tillis-the-nation-s-most-vulnerable-republican-senator-in-the-spotlight/21724608/ |access-date=November 17, 2024 |publisher=[[WRAL-TV]] |author1=Specht, Paul |author2=Doran, Will |date=November 17, 2024 |language=en}}</ref> On June 28, 2025, President [[Donald Trump]] stated he was considering backing a primary challenger after Tillis voted against a motion to consider the [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 29, 2025 |title=Trump threatens Tillis with primary challenge |url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2025/06/28/congress/donald-trump-threatens-thom-tillis-00431472 |access-date=June 29, 2025 |website=[[Politico]] |author=Jacobs, Ben|language=en}}</ref> The following day, Tillis announced that he would not seek re-election.<ref name="Tillis">{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/06/29/thom-tillis-retires-00432045|title=Thom Tillis says he will retire following Trump attacks|last=Carney|first=Jordain|date=June 29, 2025|access-date=June 29, 2025|website=[[Politico]]}}</ref>

==Democratic primary==

[[File:Wiley Nickel endorsing Roy Cooper for Senate.jpg|thumb|Wiley Nickel endorsing Roy Cooper for Senate]]

In 2025, Roy Cooper announced his candidacy for the United States Senate seat in the 2026 election. Shortly after his announcement, former U.S. Representative [[Wiley Nickel]], who had previously entered the race, withdrew his candidacy and endorsed Cooper for the Democratic nomination.<ref>{{cite news |last=Robertson |first=Gary D. |title=Former Congressman Wiley Nickel drops out of 2026 Senate race, endorses Roy Cooper |url=https://abc11.com/post/former-congressman-wiley-nickel-drops-2026-senate-race-endorses-north-carolina-governor-roy-cooper/17348739/
 |work=Associated Press |date=July 29, 2025}}</ref> Nickel cited Cooper's executive experience and electoral strength as reasons for his endorsement.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wiley Nickel exits North Carolina Senate race the day after Roy Cooper announces candidacy |url=https://apnews.com/article/d9da6af3c46da5a96df6c7ba5ada3ae9
 |work=Associated Press |date=July 29, 2025}}</ref>

{{Elections in Nebraska}}

The '''2026 United States Senate election in Nebraska''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[Nebraska]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Pete Ricketts]] is seeking his first full term following a [[2024 United States Senate special election in Nebraska|special election]] in 2024. Former union leader [[Dan Osborn]], who ran in the [[2024 United States Senate election in Nebraska|2024 regular election]], is again running as an [[Political independent|independent]].

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 12, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|title=2026 Election Calendar|url=https://sos.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/doc/elections/2026/2026_Election_Calendar.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260505151000/https://sos.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/doc/elections/2026/2026_Election_Calendar.pdf|archive-date=May 5, 2026|url-status=live|publisher=[[Secretary of State of Nebraska]]}}</ref> Ricketts won the Republican nomination with 81.5% of the vote. Although [[Nebraska Democratic Party|state Democrats]] endorsed Osborn, pastor William Forbes entered the Democratic primary amid accusations of being a [[Spoiler effect|spoiler candidate]]. In response, retired pharmacy technician Cindy Burbank launched a primary candidacy supported by the party and defeated Forbes with 89.2% of the vote before dropping out of the general election in July to support Osborn.

Republicans have not lost a Senate election in Nebraska since [[2006 United States Senate election in Nebraska|2006]] when Ricketts was the party's nominee.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nebraskapublicmedia.org/es/news/news-articles/senate-candidate-dan-osborn-hits-campaign-trail-with-populist-blue-collar-message/|title=Senate candidate Dan Osborn hits campaign trail with populist, blue-collar message|first1=Brian|last1=Beach|publisher=Nebraska Public Media|date=September 23, 2025|access-date=August 14, 2026|quote=Osborn may have lost to Fischer by more than 6 percentage points, but in a state that hasn't elected a non-Republican to the Senate since 2006, the close margin elevated his profile and motivated supporters heading into the next election cycle.}}</ref> The last independent to win a Senate election in Nebraska was progressive [[George W. Norris|George Norris]] in [[1936 United States Senate election in Nebraska|1936]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sainato |first=Michael |date=April 29, 2024 |title=He led a strike at Kellogg's. Now he's aiming for a Nebraska Senate seat |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2024/apr/29/dan-osborn-nebraska-senate-elections |access-date=May 19, 2026 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> This election will be the first in which a state did not have a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] candidate in back-to-back US Senate election cycles.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2025/07/11/will-nebraska-democrats-make-history-in-2026/|title=Will Nebraska Democrats Make History in 2026?|publisher=Smart Politics|date=July 11, 2025|access-date=August 5, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2026/08/05/a-brief-history-of-us-senate-elections-without-democrats-on-the-ballot/|title=A Brief History of US Senate Elections without Democrats on the Ballot|publisher=Smart Politics|date=August 5, 2026|access-date=August 5, 2026}}</ref> Nebraska is one of three states (along with [[2026 United States Senate election in Idaho|Idaho]] and [[2026 United States Senate election in South Dakota|South Dakota]]) where the Democratic nominee has withdrawn from the race, effectively clearing the field for an independent candidate.<ref>{{cite news |last= Goldmacher |first= Shane |title= Democrat Quits Senate Race in South Dakota, Clearing Way for Independent |newspaper= The New York Times |date= August 4, 2026 |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/04/us/politics/julian-beaudion-drops-out-south-dakota.html |access-date = October 12, 2026}}</ref>

== Independent ==
In the [[2024 United States Senate election in Nebraska]], union president [[Dan Osborn]] ran as an [[Independent politician|independent]] against Republican incumbent [[Deb Fischer]], losing by fewer than seven points in one of Nebraska's closest Senate races. Osborn significantly outperformed Democratic nominee [[Preston Love Jr.]], who lost the [[2024 United States Senate special election in Nebraska|concurrent special Senate election]] to Pete Ricketts by more than 24 points.<ref>{{cite news |title=Nebraska U.S. Senate Election Results 2024: Deb Fischer Wins |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-nebraska-us-senate.html |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 5, 2024}}</ref>

In early 2025, Osborn formed an exploratory committee for a potential 2026 run.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/04/03/dan-osborn-nebraska-senate-00268026|title=Dan Osborn makes moves toward another Nebraska Senate run|date=April 3, 2025|website=[[Politico]]}}</ref> In June 2026, he submitted a petition to appear on the general election ballot as an independent,<ref>{{Cite news |title=Dan Osborn submits signatures to challenge Ricketts on Nebraska's November ballot |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/briefs/dan-osborn-submits-signatures-to-challenge-ricketts-on-nebraskas-november-ballot/ |last=Salinas |first=Juan II |work=[[Nebraska Examiner]] |language=en-US |date=June 11, 2026 |access-date=August 7, 2026}}</ref> which was verified the following month.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Nebraska nonpartisan US Senate candidate Dan Osborn qualifies for November ballot |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2026/07/16/nebraska-nonpartisan-us-senate-candidate-dan-osborn-qualifies-for-november-ballot/ |last=Salinas |first=Juan II |work=[[Nebraska Examiner]] |language=en-US |date=July 16, 2026 |access-date=August 7, 2026}}</ref>

Although Osborn is not affiliated with the [[Nebraska Democratic Party]], the party is supporting his candidacy, citing their greater alignment with his platform.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Cottle|first=Michelle|title=He's Not a Democrat. Democrats Love Him Anyway.|publisher=The New York Times|date=August 11, 2026|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/11/opinion/dan-osborn-nebraska-independent-democrats.html|access-date=August 11, 2026}}</ref>

== Democratic primary ==
=== Background ===
[[Jane Kleeb]], the chair of the [[Nebraska Democratic Party]], said the party did not intend to recruit a candidate, similar to the [[2024 United States Senate election in Nebraska#Democratic primary|Nebraska Senate race]] in 2024.<ref name="Downballot">{{cite web|last1=Nir|first1=David|last2=Singer|first2=Jeff|title=Morning Digest: Nebraska independent who spooked GOP launches another Senate bid|url=https://www.the-downballot.com/p/morning-digest-nebraska-independent|website=The Downballot|access-date=July 10, 2025|date=July 9, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/12/us/politics/nebraska-election-takeaways-dan-osborn-ricketts-senate.html |title=Democrat Wins Senate Primary in Nebraska, but Plans to Drop Out |last=Browning |first=Kellen |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 12, 2026 |access-date=May 17, 2026}}</ref> In August 2025, the party endorsed [[Dan Osborn]], an independent candidate.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Coblerobler|first=Ariana Joy|date=August 1, 2025|title=Dan Osborn endorsed by NE Democratic Party for 2026 Senate race|url=https://nebraska.tv/news/local/dan-osborn-endorsed-by-ne-democratic-party-for-2026-senate-race|access-date=November 16, 2025|publisher=NTV}}</ref> 

In March 2026, the party called for Democratic candidate William Forbes to withdraw, with Kleeb accusing him of trying to "trick voters" and opposing abortion access. She urged Democrats to support Osborn instead.<ref name="Slew" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kleeb |first=Jane |author-link=Jane Kleeb |date=March 3, 2026 |title=NDP Press Release - Statement on U.S. Senate Candidate William Forbes |url=https://nebraskademocrats.org/blog/ndp-press-release-statement-on-u-s-senate-candidate-william-forbes/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260318172758/https://nebraskademocrats.org/blog/ndp-press-release-statement-on-u-s-senate-candidate-william-forbes/ |archive-date=March 18, 2026 |access-date=March 18, 2026 |publisher=[[Nebraska Democratic Party]] |language=en-US}}</ref> In an interview with [[CNN]], Forbes acknowledged that he had voted for Donald Trump in multiple elections, but insisted that he was a lifelong Democrat.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kaczynski |first=Andrew |author-link=Andrew Kaczynski |date=March 30, 2026 |title=The Trump-voting pastor Democrats think could cost them a chance at a Nebraska Senate seat |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/03/30/politics/nebraska-senate-trump-pastor |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260330133625/https://edition.cnn.com/2026/03/30/politics/nebraska-senate-trump-pastor |archive-date=March 30, 2026 |access-date=May 20, 2026 |publisher=[[CNN]] |language=en |quote=In an interview with CNN, Forbes said he's voted for President Donald Trump in multiple elections but denied being a Republican plant, insisting that he's a lifelong Democrat. Asked repeatedly to name a Democrat he voted for, Forbes grew frustrated and said the party needed to return to the "morality" it represented under President John F. Kennedy.}}</ref> 

After Forbes entered the race retired pharmacy technician Cindy Burbank launched a primary candidacy endorsed by the state party. On March 17, 2026, [[Secretary of State of Nebraska]] [[Bob Evnen]] removed Burbank from the ballot following a complaint from [[Nebraska Republican Party]] that alleged she was not a good-faith candidate.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Salinas II |first=Juan |date=March 17, 2026 |title=Evnen removes Nebraska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Burbank from ballot |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2026/03/17/evnen-removes-nebraska-democratic-u-s-senate-candidate-burbank-from-ballot/ |access-date=March 23, 2026 |website=[[Nebraska Examiner]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Burbank filed a lawsuit in [[Lancaster County, Nebraska|Lancaster County]] District Court immediately following the removal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nebraska Democratic Senate candidate Burbank sues to get back on the ballot |url=https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/nebraska-democratic-senate-candidate-burbank-sues-get-back-ballot |access-date=March 23, 2026 |website=[[News From The States]] |language=en}}</ref> On March 19, 2026, a District Court judge dismissed Burbank's lawsuit.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Salinas II |first=Juan |date=March 19, 2026 |title=Nebraska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Burbank stays off ballot after lawsuit dismissal — for now |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2026/03/19/nebraska-democratic-u-s-senate-candidate-burbank-stays-off-ballot-after-case-dismissal-for-now/ |access-date=March 23, 2026 |website=[[Nebraska Examiner]] |language=en-US}}</ref> On March 23, 2026, the [[Nebraska Supreme Court]] ruled that Evnen missed a deadline to consider complaints and reinstated Burbank to the ballot.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Salinas II |first=Juan |date=March 23, 2026 |title=Court orders Nebraska candidate back on U.S. Senate ballot, says Evnen acted late |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2026/03/23/nebraska-u-s-senate-candidate-back-on-ballot-state-high-court-rules-sos-acted-too-late/ |access-date=March 23, 2026 |website=[[Nebraska Examiner]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

Burbank stated in April that she would consider leaving the race to "unify the votes" against Ricketts.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.ketv.com/article/nebraskas-primary-democratic-candidates-us-senate/71154257 |title=2 Democratic candidates run for US Senate in Nebraska's primary |last=Carlson |first=Beth |publisher=[[KETV]] |date=April 28, 2026|access-date=July 25, 2026}}</ref> She said in a phone interview a week before the primary that she intended to withdraw from the general election and would support Osborn if there was "no clear path to victory".<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/democrats-nebraska-senate-primary-dan-osborn-pete-ricketts-rcna344474|title=Democrats pick Nebraska Senate nominee who could drop out and back independent Dan Osborn|date=May 13, 2026|publisher=NBC News|last=Bowman |first=Bridget |access-date=July 23, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> She filed to be removed from the ballot on July 17,<ref name="BurbankWithdrawal">{{Cite news |url=https://www.ketv.com/article/nebraska-senate-democrat-candidate-cindy-burbank-ballot-removal/73172106 |title=Cindy Burbank, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Nebraska, asks to be removed from ballot |last=Anderson |first=Jake |work=[[KETV]] |date=July 17, 2026 |access-date=July 17, 2026}}</ref> which was confirmed by Secretary of State Evnen on July 21.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.1011now.com/2026/07/21/nebraska-democrats-must-find-new-senate-candidate-after-burbank-declines-nomination/|title=Nebraska Democrats must find a new Senate candidate after Burbank declines nomination |first=Abigail |last=Carrera|date=July 21, 2026 |website=[[1011now]]}}</ref>

After Burbank's withdrawal, Forbes filed a lawsuit which claimed the Nebraska Democratic Party must have a Senate candidate.<ref>{{Cite website |last=Ashford |first=Molly |title=Arguing that Nebraska Democrats must have a Senate candidate, primary loser says he's willing |publisher=Nebraska Public Media |date=August 3, 2026 |url=https://nebraskapublicmedia.org/en/news/news-articles/arguing-that-nebraska-democrats-must-have-a-senate-candidate-primary-loser-says-hes-willing/}}</ref> An initial ruling by a Lancaster County judge stated that the attempt to force the party to field a candidate was unlikely to succeed and raised "serious constitutional concerns."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ashford |first=Molly |date=August 7, 2026 |title=Judge says effort to force Nebraska Dems to replace vacancy on ballot unlikely to succeed |url=https://nebraskapublicmedia.org/en/news/news-articles/judge-says-effort-to-force-nebraska-dems-to-replace-vacancy-on-ballot-unlikely-to-succeed/ |url-status=live |access-date=August 9, 2026 |publisher=[[Nebraska Public Media]] |language=en-US}}</ref> The case was dismissed on August 26, 2026.<ref>{{cite court|litigants=''Forbes v. Nebraska Democratic Party''|vol=CI 26-2807|court=District Court of Lancaster County, Nebraska|date=August 26, 2026|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/forbes-v-nebraska-democratic-party-defendant-order-summary-judgment.pdf|title=Order on Summary Judgment|access-date=October 21, 2026}}</ref>

[[America First Party (2026)|America First Party]] organizers submitted completed petitions to form a new party on July 15, 2026; registered voter signatures required to do so were verified by the Nebraska Secretary of State on August 7, 2026.<ref name="auto1">{{cite press release |last=State of Nebraska Secretary of State |title=Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party meet signature threshold for political party formation |publisher=State of Nebraska |date=August 7, 2026 |url=https://sos.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/doc/news-releases/Nebraska%20Working%20People%20Party%20and%20America%20First%20Party%20meet%20signature%20threshold%20for%20political%20party%20formation.pdf |access-date=September 3, 2026}}</ref> After a ruling by the [[Nebraska Supreme Court]] on August 26, 2026, against the [[Nebraska Republican Party]] objections (which claimed the party's name would cause confusion for voters) the secretary confirmed the party's formation.<ref name="auto2">{{cite news |last=Salinas II |first=Juan |title=Nebraska Supreme Court clears the way for two new Nebraska political parties|newspaper=The Nebraska Examiner |date=August 26, 2026 |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2026/08/26/nebraska-supreme-court-clears-the-way-for-two-new-nebraska-political-parties/|access-date=September 4, 2026}}</ref> Chuck Conboy, an account manager, is the party's nominee in this race.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Newly formed America First Party announces five candidates for Nebraska elections |url=https://nebraskapublicmedia.org/en/news/news-articles/newly-formed-america-first-party-announces-five-candidates-for-nebraska-elections/ |last=Olberding |first=Matt |work=[[Nebraska Public Media]] |language=en |date=September 1, 2026 |access-date=September 2, 2026}}</ref>

'If Ricketts can throw his money around then so can I!'}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Browning |first=Kellen |date=May 11, 2026 |title=G.O.P. Plant? Democratic Ruse? Nebraska Working People Party organizers submitted completed petitions to form a new party on July 14 and was verified by the Secretary of State on August 7, 2026.<ref name="auto1"/> After a ruling by the [[Nebraska Supreme Court]] on August 26, 2026, that the [[Nebraska Democratic Party]]'s objection (claiming that the name is too similar to the [[Working Families Party]]) had been filed too late, the secretary confirmed the party's formation.<ref name="auto2"/> Robin Richards, the party's chair, is the party's nominee in this race.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 1, 2026|title=Nebraska Working People Party Chair Richards running for U.S. Senate herself |url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/briefs/nebraska-working-people-party-chair-richards-running-for-u-s-senate-herself/ |access-date=September 3, 2026 |website=[[Nebraska Examiner]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

The '''2026 United States Senate election in New Hampshire''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[New Hampshire]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] congressman [[Chris Pappas (American politician)|Chris Pappas]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former senator [[John E. Sununu|John Sununu]] are the nominees for their respective parties. Democratic incumbent [[Jeanne Shaheen]] is not seeking re-election to a fourth term.

[[Primary elections]] were held on September 8. Pappas won the Democratic nomination with 65% of the vote against medical scientist Karishma Manzur. Sununu, who held the seat for one term until he was defeated by Shaheen in [[2008 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|2008]], won the Republican nomination with 68.5% of the vote against former Massachusetts senator [[Scott Brown (politician)|Scott Brown]]. If elected, Pappas will be the first openly gay man in the U.S. Senate.

This will be the first open Senate election in New Hampshire since [[2010 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|2010]]. Republicans have not won a Senate election in New Hampshire since that race.

{{toclimit|3}}

== Background ==
New Hampshire is considered to be a [[Red states and blue states|slightly to moderately blue]] state at the federal level, with [[Kamala Harris]] carrying the state by roughly 3 percentage points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in New Hampshire|2024 presidential election]]. The state's congressional delegation has been entirely Democratic since 2017. However, Republicans control the [[Governor of New Hampshire|governorship]], both state legislative chambers, and a majority in the [[Executive Council of New Hampshire|executive council]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-05 |title=New Hampshire keeps all-Democratic delegation with Pappas, Goodlander wins in US House races |url=https://apnews.com/article/new-hampshire-congress-election-2024-b9a8e05a7847c3ba93c424c2094a49a7 |access-date=2024-12-10 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-06 |title=NH Republicans claim big State House wins and strengthen majorities in House and Senate |url=https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2024-11-06/nh-republicans-claim-big-state-house-wins-and-strengthen-majorities-in-house-and-senate |access-date=2024-12-10 |website=New Hampshire Public Radio |language=en}}</ref>

Shaheen was first elected in [[2008 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|2008]], defeating incumbent [[John E. Sununu|John Sununu]] in a rematch of [[2002 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|2002]], and was reelected in [[2014 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|2014]] and [[2020 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|2020]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Castronuovo |first=Celine |date=2020-11-04 |title=Shaheen wins reelection in New Hampshire |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/523894-shaheen-wins-reelection-in-new-hampshire/ |access-date=2024-12-10 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref> Republicans have not won a U.S. Senate race in New Hampshire since [[2010 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|2010]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Rating change: Sununu's entry boosts Republican chances in New Hampshire | date=October 22, 2025 | url=https://rollcall.com/2025/10/22/new-hampshire-john-sununu-race-rating/ }}</ref>

{{ElectionsNJ}}
The '''2026 United States Senate election in New Jersey''' will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the [[United States Senate]] to represent the state of [[New Jersey]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Cory Booker]] is seeking a third full term.<ref name="FCC filing" /> He is being challenged by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former [[Tabernacle Township, New Jersey|Tabernacle]] deputy mayor Justin Murphy.

[[Primary elections]] were held on June 2. Booker ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination. In the Republican primary, Murphy won the nomination with 33.3% of the vote over state trooper Richard Tabor and journalist Alex Zdan.

Republicans have not won a Senate election in New Jersey since [[1972 United States Senate election in New Jersey|1972]].
